*THE SERMON OF THE MOSS. The wilderness was stretching out before him, He had no human guide,— Who shall the firmness of his faith restore him, So long, so solely tried. Pitied by none, unwept by human eye, In that vast desert must he drop and die. He thought of home, and of the loving faces, He might behold no more, Never again to meet the fond embraces. So dear to him of yore,— Alter the toils and perils he had past, Must he lie down and perish here at last? His eyes desponding on the ground are set, What do they rest on there? The tiniest 121083 that God. has made; and yet It kept him from despair. That little plant possessed the preacher's power To comfort him in his extremest hour. " Can the great Being," who to such perfection Has brought this pig=y Plant, Fail to afford me His Divine protection, Or suffer me to waet,'?" His spirit, reassured, has lost its fear, He felt, though in a desert, "God is new!" Chr istian,who through th is toilsome world art straying, Do fears and doubts prevail? The weary waste that stretches nut surveying„.. Say, does thy courage fail? No desert is so wide, but thou twa.sreA see A token of the love of God ler thee! --Aurt Judy's Dfagasinc. E. Dorm what owe de firm will settle wid me, and dent what de fires owe will settle wid Moss." A story wh:ch comes from South Carolina will serve as an offset to a considerable number of instances of church steeples struck by lightning. In the course of some exten- sive forest fires, it is averred, the flames parted three times to go around churches, and in a fourth instance "the fires passed under and around the building, burning straw, wood, and lumber around it, but doing no injury to the church itself." This occurred at a place called Pine Tree. A Moastow ENOAGCNIENT.—" My dear," said a Mormon wife to her husband, "I should think that you would be ashamed of yourself, Eirting with that Miss B. as you did in church to-day." "Flirting with her!" he replied in astonish- ment, "why, we have been engaged for more than three months. It's all over town." "Oh, I beg your pardon," said his wife indifferently. "If you are engaged to her I suppose itis'ell right. Whendoes the happy event occur ?" Everybody who has experienced the disappointments which a stranger meets upon going to an undeveloped region which is undergoing the "booming" process will enjoy the reply made by a San Francisco man on being asked how he was pleased with Nlashington territory. "Well, sir," he answered, "every bunch of willows is a mighty forest, every frog pond a sylvan lake, every waterfall a seccnd Minneapolis, every ridge of rocks a gold mine, every town a county seat, and every man a liar." "Ten days, or forty shillings." said the magistrate ; and the prisoner, a sullen-looking fellow, chose the latter alter- native, paid the fine, and was discharged. He walked moodily out of the court, but, when he reached thadoor, turned and showered a wholes'ale tirade of profane abuse uto the magistrate. Then he ran into the corridor; but losfore he could retch the street the officers gave chase. Be w.s cap-ured, and stood again at the bar. "Forty shillings mole," said the court. The money was paid. • "If you had used-mere chaste and refined language," the magis- trate con I ined, waving the fellow away, "you would not h.as e 1:Ron chasoi and re-fined. Mrs. Deintywell, one of the neatest and mod " particular" of women, wood always say to her husband when he-was objecting to the clean shirt which she insisted upon laying out for him every morning," Just reflect, Tom! What if you should meet with an accident—be ran over by a cab, or something of that kind, and people should find you had on a shirt yon had worn for a week! I should suet die of mor- tification." One day Mr. Dainty well really met with the predicted accident, and was brought home upon a con- venient abutter. His wife rushed to the door when she-sew I him coming, her face so pale that her husband, who was fully conscious, feared that she WAS going to faint. "Cheer up, my dear;" he cried, "cheer up. I stepped into an un- suspected hatchway, and broke my leg; bat don't worry—l had on a clean shirt !" Ills needless to say that this quite restored her composure. • EASTEE Wasaisayroa.-one of the events of the year in Washington lathe children's egg-rolling festival on Easter- Monday. It used to take place on the grassy terrace i.ust west of the Capitol, the incline of which is very steep. The sport is described as follows: A dozen or more boys and girls scratched their initials on their gaudy Easter-eggs.. They then stood in a row at the top of the terrace, each holding an egg on the grass. At a signal from one of the party all hands were withdrawn from the eggs, and each chased his or her egg down the terrace. The owner of the unbroken egg arriving first at the foot of the terrace was entitled to all the other eggs. The young egg-rollers at- tracted such a throng five years ago that the grass was killed, and sines then the sport has been carried on in the White House grounds, just south of the mansion.— IT orper?.; Weekly. On this account it was that beta ran high at Leamington one season among WM X.'s friends that the lovely blush which man- tled her cheek was of nature's own bestowing. To end the controversy, which was becoming exciting, one gallant gen- tleman, less timidithan the rest, proposed to ask the beauty for a proof that !would settle the dispute. In an unfor- tunate moment, and perhaps trembling at his own temerity, he said, "Miss X., do you paint ?" "Bring me a glass of water," the syren said sweetly, "and you shall see." The water was brought, and she handed him a spotless cambric handkerchief. "Vow, dip that in the water and rub it on here," she said, presenting him a peachy cheek so tempt- ingly near that his heart stood still as he gently and depre- catingly chafed it. •" Now look at the handkerchief !" she said somewhat sternly. It was as spotless as before. "Are you satisfied ?" she demanded, more sternly yet. ‘• Yes," quavered he, "I am satisfied."" And so am I!" said the insulted beauty, as tyke dashed the water in his face. A WRCNG INTERPRETATION.—An /WWII coloured party named Jake was very late a few days ago in getting down to the store. His emploger, Col. Allspice, rebuked Jake in • aomewhat ,cevere language. "I want you to understand this trifling will never do. If you can't get down to your work In time I'll hire somebody who can." "Boss, don't be hard .on me," and the negro's eyes filled with tears. " Wky what's-the matter with you? Anybody sick ?" "Sick! don't know which am gwinter die fast, my wife or my o madder." " I am sorry I spoke so harshly as that. We won't need. yen about the store to-day." "Thank you, boss. Thank you kindly," and off he went. Next morning, Col. Allspice asked Jake what he meant by saying that his wife and mother were dying, when he had seen both on the ,atreet the day before. " Dyiu'," exclaimed Jake, opening his mouth wide enough to admit of a coffee mill being thrown into it, and elevating his eyebrows in amazement "Yes, dying. You caid they were dying, and half an hour after you left your wife came here to see if you had draws your wages for last month." "I neber said dey was dying. El you was to see de way dey opens dar motifs and takes in chunks of bacon, you wouldn't 'epect dam ob dying. I be- lave I did say I didn't k‘now which of 'em was gwinter die lust, and I don't know that yet; days bofe got such good appetites—l knows one ch 'em got ter die filet, but—" Here Col. Allspice interrupted the orator with an axe helve, and the business relations heretofore existing between them have been severed. The compensation to farmers for damage to the land it, the neighbourhood of Portsdown Hill on the ocessieri of the Easter Volunteer manceavres has been estimated at about £650. Foot and mouth disease shows an important decline. At I the close of the week ended May 10 there were E9l animals remaining affected in England, and none in Ireland, Scot- land, or Wales. The decrease has been 125 during the week. A pair of tomtits have built their nest in the letter-box at the Ronne), Union Workhouse. The moat curious part of this freak is that every letter or paper dropped into the box falls on the back of the bird. On Tuesday a heavy newspaper was dropped in, and it was feared that the hen was killed, but on the paper being removed she was found alive and well. CoNcessicare To CROFTER TENANTSLY.—Sir J. T. Sin- clair, M.P., has made some important concessions to his crofter tenants in Caith.ness-shire. Crofters paying a rental of £3O or under will be granted a permanent reduction of 10 per cent. and leases of 14 or 19 years, together with aid in improving the breed of their cattle. Those wishing to emigrate will be assisted to do so, and the holding thus vacated will be added to contigueue lots, was to make them more adequate to the support of v. family. HEREFORDS.—Lest week a meeting of breeders of Here- ford cattle was held at Hereford, under the presidency of Lord Bateman, to establish an association of breeders of pedigree Hereford cattle, and a large representative com- mittee, with Lord Bateman es its chairman, was appointed to settle the details. The objects of the Association are to supply general information about the Herefords through the 1 committee to the Press, arrange for the exhibition of Here- fords at distant shows, and otherwise to promote the inter- ests of the breed. REMISSIONS OF RENT.—EarI Manvers has made a return Of 4.0 per cent, to his Lincolnshire tenantry on their last year's rents. Mr. Rowland Winn, M.P., has remitted 20 per vent. to all his Yorkshire and Lincolnshire agricultural tenants for the past halleyear. The Duke of Manchester, in view of the recent unfavourable seasons, has notified to the \ tenants of his English estates that, owing to the unfavour- able seasons and the low price of corn, he has decided to make a permanent reduction of 15 per cent, on the rental of arable land. PROFEE3OR SHELDON ON ENSlLLGE.—Professor Sheldon, speaking at Ayr at a meeting on dairying, said some people in England were going mad over ensilage just as two years ago they were going mad over exhaust fans. He did not believe more than a certain percentage of what was said in favour of ensilage, and the warnings of men of such emi- nence as Sir John Lawes and Dr. Voelcker should make them cautious. La the same time he was prepared to admit that there was some good in ensilage. The testimony he had get from American and Canadian farmers was that they might use it up to a third of their feeding, bat not more. The fermentation through which the ensilage passed must affect the milk of the cattle using it. He believed as good results could be got from using roots; and as they could produce turnips here as good and as cheap as anywhere, he thoaght they would do better to stick to their roots in the meantime. There had been complaints about the flavour of butter being affected by turnips; but he was informed this ' could-abe obviated by taking off the crowns of the turnips. INTERESTING EXPERIMENT IN ENSILAGE, —LOCAL INVEN- TIoN.—There has this week been inspected an invention by a respected farmer of the Ormskirk neighbourhood—Mr. Thomas Rinemer, Ben Farm, Bickerstaffe—which cannot fail to be of beneficial, service to agricaltarists. Approving of the principle of ensilage, Mr. Rummer was of opinion that potatoes, after being mashed, might be kept in a similar manner. To crush a sufficient quantity to store would, however, be a work of great labour with the old masher, and, therefore the idea of storing potatoes had to be put aside if ' no better means could be adopted. Mr. Rimmer thought well over the matter, and eventeally got a machine to work which now acts most admirably. It is fixed in the engine- house, and consists of an ordinary steaming cistern, where the potatoes are steamed and softened with steam from the the boiler. At the bottom ef the cistern is a revolving drum, worked by the engine, so that when the potatoes are allowed to drop from the cistern into the pan below, this drum drives them against the pan and they are deposited in the bin as fine as flour. Some idea of the amount of labour the machine is capable of saving may be gathered from the tact that in two minutes it will mash as many potatoes as two men could in an hour. CI coarse the value of the machine will be most felt where the plan adopted by Mr. Rimmer is carried out. After the potatoes are mashed they Itre wheeled to a hole in the adjoining field, and there covered p.nd allowed to remain until wanted. Potatoes which were pepoeitei in this manner last October arc now as sweet as 4rhen they were pat into the hole, pigs and horses eating 'them readily. The potatoes being mashed and deposited in this manner are a great saving e f time to the farmer, good, sweet food being by this means always ,at hand. All who have seen this machine give Mr. Rimmer. ereat credit for his ingenuity. Sowitme TORNIPS.-1 correspondent merites from Clon- tnel :—I finished the sowing of our farm crop of turnips to- day, the two principal varieties being the Priz e•winner and Champion Purple-top swede, with Sitirvit4's aid two other less known kinds for comparison bymnd-by in more limited extent. Few people in Ireland sow so early; indeed, a very experienced agriculturist took me to task in a local journal last year for advocating early sowiag. for the supposed rea- sons that they would" start" to seed or -keep badly. The result with me, for several years, dieposed of eit her suppoei- -1 tion. Now the main reason why I try and have all my !swede seed in the ground by May 10 is to avoid the ravages of the turnip fly or black turnip beetle. Let me, enter into some details. How many farmers have to sow tleeir turnip crops twice or thrice? This entails labour, expe nee, partial failure, and at best, as I have frequently noted, a late crop, that can never compete with the early one. The g, irdener has the same enemy to contend against, and a host of. expedients as remedies have been devised. In one category we have soot, then lime, then sulphur' and once I saw one intelligent man in desperation—he had put down seed three times—use . a mixture of all three together. Bat one of the peculiarities of the turnip beetle is that the female 'aye her eggs gene- rally on the under side of the soft young leaf, so t hat dust- ing with any of the substances named overhead is ni icessarily ineffective. Another cites of expedients le tar, mil, bird- lime, &c., placed on canvas and drawn over the seedlings as 'a trap to catch the depredators. The subject is tom serious, so I need not say how amazing the occupation (or occa- pators, if the word were permissible) would look in a 10 or 20 acre field! Prevention is better than care, and my re- medy costs nothing, while it makes success certain. From several years' close observation, I have foiled the turnip fly never appears before the first week in June, and probably this year, owing to the relatively low temperature so far, it may be later. By having the turnip crop sown before the present date, say May 10 or thereabouts, it will be in "the rough leaf," and can then defy the fly- before the first week in Jane. I have been thinning Golden Globe and Chick Castle Blackstone to-day, and there has net been the sign of a fly. This point is so important that Miss Ormerod might be asked if it has hitherto come under her notice. "PEDIGREE AND PERFORMANCE.—Mr. Cephas A. Leach, of Cleveland Springs Farm, Missouri, U.S.A., oalls atten- tion in a forcible manner to the utter absurdity of awarding prizes to heavy draught horses merely for their show condi- tion, and he will doubtless be pleased to know that the Shire . ,Borse Society has at last broken loom from the thraliom of • our show system, by beginning to have horses exhibited under its auspices, judged " from the feet upwards." This is a fair beginning in a slow country like England, but we hope that with the assistance of such men as Mr. Leach we shall see, sooner than many may imagine, prizes awarded to heavy draught horses on the bases of strength, -endurance, and staunchness, and their pedigrees valued by results re- corded in competitive trials. Another point brought out by Mr. Leach's letter is that American buyers look upon French stud horses as animas which have been brought up on farms as 'working horses, and on English -stud horses as animals which have never done any work, and which have teen pampered from birth in a manner which tends to lessen their usefulness and impceesiveness se sires ins very marked degree. Broadly speaking, the facts are about as repre- sented, bat there are circarnstances in the two cases which modify them materially. In France a large proportion of /enema in England a very small the horses are stallions, preportion of the horses arc saved entire. Under the one system many a good horse may be Fixed, and under the other many a good horse may be lost; but to save the few which give best promise must be the better plan in the long ran, for the French breeders save very many horses that are worm than useless as stallions. If Americep breeders would buy good colts from farmers in England they could do at least as well as they do under the same system in France. All that is wrong with English stud horses is mainly due to the vicious system of "judging }mesas by their looks," under which showyard prizes have until quite recently been awarded; and this is the one fault to be remedied. One thing is certain, namely, that the day for value in pedigrees which are nothing more than a strike- of names has abso- lutely passed, although there are mansehreeders who cannot, or will not, believe it.-21fark Lane &press. Utszxriteran STROKES OF Goon FORTIINE.—We have heard of a man who had £2,000 a year left to him because he was civil to an infirm old lady in church, finding the hymns for her, setting her hassock, &c. He did not know her name; but she took care to ascertain his, and when eke died he found that she had bequeathed to him the bulk of her property "as a reward for his patient kindness." A clergyman of our acquaintance obtained a living of good value from a baronet in Norfolk for no other reason than that he was the only curate within ten miles round who had not applied for it when it fell vacant. And another clergy- man whom we know got a still better living for having re- fused preferment offered to him under circumstances deroga- tory to his dignity. He was a fair singer; and a vulgar plutocrat who had invited him to dinner promised to give him a living if he would sing a comic song at dessert. The quiet rebuke which the young clergyman administered made the plutocrat ashamed of himself, so that the next day he proffered the living with a letter of apology; but the living was refused, the clergyman stating that it-would be impos- sible for him to forget the circumstances under which it was first tendered. This was the more honourable, as the clergy- man was very badly off. Another patron, hearing of what Le had done appointed him to a benefice as a testimony of his admiration. We may conclude with the story of a man who was suddenly made rich because of hie great stupidity. Ee was the only dull man in a bright-witted family, and going to dine with a wealthy relative who had a horror of foals, he made so many silly remarks, that the old man cried in exasperation—" I must do something for you, for you'll never do anything for yourself. If I don't make a rich man of you, you'll become a laughing-stock to the world and a 'disgrace to your family."—Chambers's Journal. THE DISMAL SWAMF.—This little-visited district, on the borders of Virginia and North Carolina, derives most of its celei.rity from the ballad written by Toni Moore et Norfolk on a supposed legend of a distracted lover who fancied that his lost mistress had gone to the Dismal Swamp, and pad- dled her white canoe over the waters of Lake Drummond. When Mr. Wirt laid out the boundary line of the State, he descrited the swamp as forty miles long and twenty broad, with a black deep soil, covered by a stupendous 'forest of juniper and cypress trees, while below was a thick, en- tangled undergrowth of reeds, woodbine, grape vines, mosses, and creepers interlaced and complicated. Bat man has wrought great changes since this account was given. The Dismal Swamp Canal, connecting the Elizabeth and Pasquo- tank rivers, now traverses the district for twenty miles, while &nether runs from Lake Drummond to the Nanse- mond River. The first attempt to drain the swamp was made by a company organised by General Washington after the close of the Revolutionary war; but although the ori- ginal design of reclaiming the land was never carried out, the land company realised enormous profits from the lamter it took out. Immense quantities of staves, shingles, and the like have been sent from the thick dark groves, and to-day most of the valuable gam, juniper. cypress, and white pine has been cut. The undergrowth is varied and luxuriant, reeds prevail everywhere, and to the south form a sea of verdure. The soil is deep and soft, and large quantities of fallen trunks have been taken from beneath the surface, where they have been preserved by the antiseptic qualities of the water. The water of Lake Drummond and the swamp in general is dark-coloured like coffee, but is pleasant to the taste, and will keep pure for a long time. The spongy nature of the soil renders road-making a difficult task, and the first railroad engineers almost despaired of success. The male roads are simply legs laid tide by tide, over which the shingle-carts pass. The swamp is intersected by some ridges elevated above the watery level which constitutes the greater part of the region, and on them the harder kinds of timber grow. These portions of the swamp are, perhaps, susceptible of being reclaimed. As to the rest, numerous schemes since that of Washington have been proposed for making it available for cultivation, and or using the upper bog surface for fuel resembling peat. INSTRUCTING A YALTKEE l'Ar •BRITISH CIVILE6ATION.— , The Buffalo Sunday News contains a long report of an in- terview with Prof. C. A. Jolmso3' of Hamilton, Canada. The reporter says he found Prof. Johnson "a very agree- . able, intelligent talker. He is a man of considerably more . than average height, with a strongly marked African face , and a voice characteristic of his race, easy manners, ready , speech, and a good deal of the satio:re faire which is sup- , posed to be the exclusive property cf the white face. In I reply to a question whether he himself was ever a slave, the • I professor stated that he was born a free man and was a I native of Toronto, where he was educated for a clergyman." .1 The following extract illustrates the character of the inter- , view :—"Do not the people of year race in this city knew . that they are the superiors of the freedmen in educational , and business pursuits?" "There are no business men in But- •I falo among our people. Their glory lies in the whitewash brush, waiters, barbers, Pullman car porters and jubilee I onagers." "Have they no desire to fill other prominent , business positions ?" "1 believe they feel that they have been born to be servants to white Man." "your conclusion [ is that the proper representatives of your people must be , found in the South?" "Yes. The South is to be the , future heaven of our race on earth from a business point of view." "What is the condition of your people i Canada?" "It is very good. They have their magistrates, lawyers, bankers, editors, and men of high financial inquange.” "Have you a separate school system there ?" " Tat. tut, sir," the educator replied ; "you must remember yau are now referring to a thoroughly civilised people." "What do you mean by that ?" "The English people are an excep- tion to the general rule of people; one man is as good as I another under the English flag, you know." Mr. Johnson spoke with much enthusiasm of the good Queen's country and Government, and declared himself a thorough Britou..--, Canaeian Paper.

SCIENTIFIC NOla At the last meeting of the Royal Astronomical Society, the Rev. S. J. Perry, of Stonyhurst College, showed a series of large drawings of sun spots made at that institution. Be described small greyish clouds, seven or eight seconds in diameter, which he and his assistant have observed from

time to time on all parts of the sun's surface; they disap- pear rapidly, lasting only for a few minutes. Somewhat similar veiled spots are described by Trouvelot, but other observers have not been successful in seeing them. UTILISING NIAGARA FALLS.—It is now nearly two years aeo that the question of utilising the water power of Niagara for generating electricity was first raised, the pro- moter being Mr. or Colonel" Leonard Henkle, of New York. There seems to be at last some probability that his scheme will be carried out. The inventor proposes to transmit elec- tricity for lighting purposes to sixty-five cities in the . .
. . . United States:froni central batteries stationed at Niagara The
Falla, and driven by the immense water power there.

_ power generated will be transmitted though a silver wire about the size of a straw, laid underground, enclosed in heavy pipes made of asphalte. Such a wire can, it is stated, with a 40-foot battery at the Niagara Falls end, transmit in four hours to :Rochester enough electricity to light that city for twelve hours. The sixty-five cities are all over 30,000 population. Lockport and Buffalo will probably be the first places where the inventor will introduce his ap- paratus as experimental points, and he hopes that he will be able to make those experiments next autumn. He expects to overcome the resistance usually found in transmitting currents through long distances by a properly constructed means for the conservation of electric energy.—lron. THE Exxisclecisr OF AsTissats.—lt is stated by Engineer Phillips (late of the Northern Pacific Railroad) that no fewer than 20,000 elk, antelope, and mule deer are slaugh- tered every winter in Minnesota, Montana, and Wyoming alone. There is every prospect that three of the noblest game animals on the American continent will soon be entirely extinct. Elk, which formerly ranged from the Middle States to the Pacific, are now never found east of the Mis- souri River. Twenty-five years ago they were plentiful in Kansas and Nebraska, but civilisation has driven them into the dense and uninhabited regions of Minnesota and the Northern Territories. The hide hunters effect the most sweeping destruction. The average price of an elk skin is $3. The hide heaters use repeating rifles, and frequently kill from six to twelve elk in a herd before they get oat of range. Mr. Phillips affirms that, besides the slaughter of the animals named, in the year 1882 more than 25,000 buffaloes were killed for the traders between the Yellow- stone and the head waters of the Little Missouri. If there is to be sport in the Great West in the future, those in- terested will be compelled to move for legislation which will give protection to game in the Western States and terri- tories. Otherwise there will be very few elk, buffalo, mule deer, or antelope left to hunt in five years. CORROSIVE ACTION OF CEMENTS UPON METALS.—MT. J. C. Trautwine, the late eminent American engineer, pub- lished a brief memorandum, shortly before his death, giving the result of some experiments which he had made to deter- mine the corrosive action of hydraulic cements upon metal embedded in them. The cements used were English Port- land and Louisville, in addition to which he tried plaster of paris pure, and also mixed with equal measures of the ce- ments. All were of the consistency of common mortar, and all were kept in an upper room during ten years, unexposed to moisture otherthan that of the indoor atmosphere. The metals were partly embedded in the pastes and partly pro- jected from them. They consisted of cat iron nails, some of which were galvanised, smooth iron wire nails, brass in both sheet and wire, zinc in sheet, copper wire, and solid cylinders of lead a inch diameter. The result at the end of the ten years was that all the metals in both the pure ce- ments were absolutely unchanged, and this was also the case with the plaster of paris, with the exception o 9 the ungal- vanised nails, which had become covered with a thin coat- ing of rust, as were also those in the mixtures of plaster and cement, but to a less degree. Mr. Trautwine concludes Ir3m his experiments that if dampness be excluded, both cement and lime mortar will protect from injury all the metals employed in ordinary constructions for an indefinite time. M. PASTEUR ON CANINE MADNESS.—M. Pasteur, who, for the last four years, has been engaged upon experiments in relation to canine madness, has communicated the results of his labours to the Academie des Sciences. M. Pasteur began by recounting the facts established by his experi- ments. They are in substance as follow :—" If the visas of rabies be transmitted from the dog to the monkey, and then from monkey to monkey it will be found that after each transmission the virulence of the virus has become en- feebled. If the virus thus enfeebled be re-transmitted to a dog, or an animal of that species, it will remain still attenu- ated. By a few transmissions of the virus from monkey to monkey, there can easily be obtained a virus so attenuated as shall never communicate, by hypodermic inoculation. the disease to a dog. Inoculations by trepanning of such virus will ;likewise produce no result; but an animal will, notwithstanding, be rendered thereby proof against the disease. The virulence of the virus becomes, on the con- trary, augmented in its passage from rabbit to rabbit If a dog be inoculated with virus thus augmented in power, a far more intense form of the disease will be manifested than that apparent in ordinary canine madness, and it will invari- ably prove fatal." By applying these and other observa- tions. M. Pasteur obtained virus of different degrees of virulence, and succeeded, by inoculations of the milder qualities, in preserving animals from the effects of more active and metal kinds. For example, after several days longer than the shortest incubation term, M. Pasteur ex- tracted virus from the head of a rabbit which had died of the disease, and inocculated successively two other rabbits. Each time a dog was inoculated with the virus, which, as has been seen, would increase each time in virulence. The result was that the dog was ultimately rendered capable of bearing a virus of mortal strength, and became absolutely proof against canine virus. M. Pasteur anticipates that the time is still distant when canine madness will be extin- guished by vaccination, bat pending that consummation, he feels pretty certain that he will be able to avert the conse- quences of a bite from a mad dog. He says :—" Thanks to the duration of incubation after a bite, I have every reason to believe that patiente can be rendered insusceptible before the mortal malady has had time to declare itself." M. Pas- teur stated, in contusion, that he had solicited the Minister of Education to appoint a commission to test his experi. ments. He added :—"The principal experiment that I shall attempt will consist in taking from my kennels 20 dogs in- susceptible to the disease, and placing the same in compari- son wi,h 20 ordinary dogs. I shall then have all these 40 dogs bitten by a number of dogs in a rabid state. If the facts that I have enunciated are exact, the 20 dogs that I believe to be proof against the disease will remain healthy, while the other 20 will become affected. For a :second ex- periment no less decisive, I propose to place before the com- mission 20 vaccinated and 20 unvaccinated dogs. All the 40 I shall then inoculate in the most sentitive parts with virus taken from a rabid dog. The 20 vaccinated dogs will resist, and the other 20 will all die of madness, either para- lytic or furious."

The Standard New York correspondent telegraphs that the weekly reeeipts of the Irish Emergency Fund have largely decreased. A public quarrel has occurred between 'Patrick Ford and Sheridan. The latter impeaches Ford's honesty and capacity. TUMBLE FRATEICIDE.—Thomas Scott Garner, a pot- ter, aged 38, has been arrested by the Burslem police on a charge of killing his brother, Albert Scott Garner, aged 25. The two brothers quarrelled in the street on Saturday night, and ran at each other with their heads lowered, their skulls earning into contact with great force. The younger was knocked to the ground insensible, and died without having t agained consciousness. AN ABSENT•MINDED MAN.—The following incidents in the career of an absent-minded man are authentic and have

never, we believe, before been published. The subject, a savant and a bachelor, was habitually so deeply engrossed in his studies that but for the care of his housekeeper he would soon have degenerated sadly in personal appearance. The housekeeper had no end of trouble in securing that her master should change his linen with proper frequency, and on one occasion, when he was about to spend a week in a distant town on the occasion of a scientific conference, her fears that he would forget to maintain a respectable ex- terior were intensified. Before he departed, however, the good woman exacted his promise that on rising each morn- ing he would put on a clean shirt, and she placed the requisite number in his portmanteau. At the end of the week the savant returned, and his housekeeper was surprised to find his portmanteau contained no shirts, neither clean nor worn. In the exorcise of her customary oversight of her master, she seized his cuff and 'found that he had obeyed the letter of her injunctions and was wearing six shirts! On learning \what was wrong he simply said, "Well, you didn't tell me •to take anything off, you know." The same gentleman was ' once sitting in a friend's study, when he remarked on the comfort of a rug which lay before the fire. Being told that it was purchased at a shop opposite, he at once stepped across and there purchased a new kind of rug, which he insisted on carrying over to show his friend. To test the rug it was laid on the top of the one first noticed. Soon absorbed in scientific conversation, the bringer of the new rug forgot his purchase on leaving, and though he often afterwards put his feet on it he never remembered that he was the owner. For the sake of the lasting joke his friends did not refresh his memory. On a third occasion the same gentleman was going out of town for a day. Having first pinned a card on his study door, "Not in to-day," he set out on foot, and in an hour or two abstractedly wandered back again. On arriving at the study door he read the card, and muttering to himself "I wonder where he's gone" he passed again into the street and made half the journey to the place he had originally started out for. At that point rain came on, and he actually returned home for an umbrella, where his housekeeper roused him to the consciousness that the day was gone. div.p: EUILDING SOCIETY MEETING. The annual meeting of the Warrington Workingmen's Permanent lienefit Building Society was held in the Gol- borne-street schoolroom, Warrington, on Tuesday even- ing when the chair was occupied by the Mayor (Alderman Harrison). There was a moderate atten- dance of members.—The SECRETARY, Mr. Peter Dal- ton, read the fourteenth annual report and balance sheet. The report stated that the sum of £1430 2s 3d had been received during the year as subscriptions, and £1430 2s 8i for repayments, making the total receipts £2814 4a 11d. The withdrawals during the year amounted to £1236 17s 7d. The sum of £2llO had been advanced to members on their property during the year. There were 202 subscribers holding 2991 shares, and 37 borrowers hold- ing 145/ shares, making a total of 239 members holding 445 shares. The profits for the year after deducting working expenses amounted to £276 17s Id, out of which the mana- gers recommended a dividend of 4 per cent., which would take £249 15s 2d, leaving a balance of £27 Is lid to be car- ried forward to next year's account. The reserve fund amounted to £350, and the contingent fund to £5B 13s 11d. The CHAIRMAN said that although they could not congratu- late the society on paying a dividend of 15 per cent or on a large accession of numbers, it was a matter for congratula- tion that it had been prudently and wisely managed during the past year, and although 4 per cent might appear small compared to what the dividends had been in the past, it must be remembered that the present were hard times. Trade and commerce were so very much demoralised that he almost marvelled that the society could pay 4 per cent. It was practically in the same sound condition as it was two months ago, and he thought that was a matter upon which every member of it could congratulate himself. Considering the way,in fvhich the society had been used in the past, and the difficulties and prejudices that it lead to contend with, he thought that it had progressed wonderfully, and that it mug have beeu well managed to do so.—The report and balance sheet were then adopted on the motion of Mr. HAT.. TON, seconded by Mr. ISHERWOOD.—Mr. KENWORTHY pro- posed that a dividend of 4 per cent be paid to the members. He remarked that on looking over the balance sheet he found that something like £7OO more had been invested or lent on mortgage than seas the Case in the previous year. He also found on looking over the expenditure tha-, leaving out the modest salary paid to the Secretary, the total expenses of the society during the past year had not exceeded £l5. When the expenses were kept so low they might safely say the society was in a sound condition. When the value of money at the present day as compared with what it was some time ago was considered, they might safely congratu- late themselves on having a dividend of 4 per cent.—Mr. FENTON seconded. He thought that the dividend was highly satisfactory, and that the members should be pleased that they catried forward a small balance to the next year.—The motion was then carried.—Mr. POTTER proposed the re-elec- tion as managers of Messrs. James Harding, W. T. Wilkin- son, E. Wallington, Ed. Fenton, John Taylor, and Robert Isherwood. He Was sure that the satisfactory man ler in , which they had conducted the business during the past year spoke volumes in their favour.—Mr. Mimes seconded the motion, which was carried, six additional managers to be taken from the register in rotation.—lt was resolved on the motion of Mr. PERRY, that Messrs. John Edward Wright and Thomas Domville be re-appointed surveyors for the next twelve mcnths.—On the motion of Mr. WALLINGTON, seconded by Mr. NORBORY, Messrs. William Ford and Isaac Leeson were re-elected auditors for the ensuing year.—lt was resolved on the motion of Mr. Ham, seconded by Mr. WEAVER, that the managers of the society receive an allow- ance of 64 for each attendance during the past year,—On the motion of Mr. KENWORTHY, seconded by Mr. Lawn, Messrs. Thomas Jolley, Thomas Tunstall, R. Crowther Wal- lington, and T. B. Carter were appointed arbitrators Of the society.—ln replying to a vote of thanks to the chairman the MAYOR remarked that it spoke well for the good man- agement of the society that during the whole year they had not spent a penny on a lawyer's bill. He sympathised with Mr. White, who was their learned lawyer, that for him it I was not a very profitable society. (Laughter).—Mr. FEN.. TON : It is said that "To go to law is no easy matter, and they that win the day come off no better."—The MAYCift remarked that as the subject had been mentioned he might say that there used to be an estimable gentleman who lived at Tlaelwall, and who was buried there. On his tombstone he (the Mayor) remembered reading the epitaph : • Here lies a faithful, honest friend, Deny it if you can; • He never paid a lawyer's bill, Nor c.used another man. (Laughter.) The meeting then terminated. THE CHARGE OF FALSE PRETFITCES AGAINST A SOLDIER. At the Warringtoa Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) Alderman Holmes, and Mr. John Fairclough, William Rose Campbell, a private soldier, was brought up on remand charged with obtaining by false pretences on the 14th May, from John Henry Nor- bury, household furniture to the value of £47 8s 91d, with intent to cheat and defraud.—Mr. Moore appeared on behalf of Mrs. Mulholland, who had purchased some of the goods from the prisoner, who was undefended.—Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) said that the prosecutor was a furniture dealer residing in Scotland-road. The prisoner was a private sol- dier in the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, which regiment he joined about five and a half years ago, at Or- ford Barracks, and since then he had been drafted to India. having returned about six months ago. When he joined, the regiment he gave it to be understood that he was a bandsman, but, Mr. Hunt believed, he was tested and failed. About the 12th of the present month he went to the prose- cutor's shop and represented himself as a teacher of music and said that he had several first-class pupils in Warrington and Liverpool, and that lie had been attached to the band at the Warrington barracks. He also stated that he was about to be married, and that he had taken a house at 116 Bat- tereby-lane, and that he wanted it furnished from top to bottom. The prisoner selected varioas articles, which were to be delivered on the 16th inst. He also took the house in Battersby-lane from Mr. Tunstall. The goods were delivered on the 16th, and payment for them was to have been made on the 20th. On the morning of that date prisoner met Mr. Norbury in the street and told him that he had an important engagement at Liverpool in the evening and that it would be impossible for him to meet him (Mr. Norbury) according to their previous arrangement. When the prisoner went to Mr. Norbury's he was always in private clothes. He was arrested on the Thursday previocs at the house ef his wife's mother on the charge of being an absentee, and was brought to the police station. Meanwhile information had been re- ceived by Mr. Norbury that some of the goods had been re- moved from the house in Battersby-lane, and from enquiries that were made it was found that the prisoner had sold to a Mrs. Mulholland, a second-hand •clothes dealer, articles to the value of about £ll for the sum of £4. He (Mr. Hunt) then instituted proceedings against him. On tbe prisoner was found a memorandum, showing that he was about to borrow £lO from a loan society in Manchester, and the police had further information that it was his intention to go to America.—The prosecutor then bore out the opening statements of the Chief Constable regarding his dealings with the prisoner.—Michael Vralle, provo-sergeant at Orford barracks, identified the prisoner as a private in the South Lancashire Regiment; he was not a music teacher and had had no authority to wear plain clothes.—James George Kerr, manager for Mr. Morton, pawnbroker, St. James - street, Latchford, spoke to receiving some of the goods in qnestion in pledge, and Mary Mulholland, second-hand clothes dealer, 80 Mersey-street, deposed to purchasing some of the articles. Examined by Mr. Moore this witness said that the £4 she gave for the goods was a reasonable price for second-hand f urni, u She made all possible enquiries and fully underetoed het the goods were the prisoner's pro- perty. She went to Use police station with the prisoner to make enquiries.—Prisoner, who reserved his defence, was committed far trial at the next Quarter Sessions.—The Bench declined to assent to an application made by Mr. Moore that the furniture bought by Mrs. Mulholland should be given up to her, at least, until the prisoner was tried. as argued that he had purchased the goods, believing them to be the property of the prisoner, and that she was now en- titled to them.

SERIOUS CHAIM AGAINST A SOLICITOR.—Mr. Edmund George Tatterahall, who had been practising as a solicitor, surrendered at the CentrAl Criminal Court on Saturday to take his trial for having unlawfully misappropriated £3OOO, which had been entrus ed to hira for a specific purpose. The defence was that prisoner had no fraudulent intention, and that the suddenness of the order prevented him from paying the money.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced to twelve months' hard labour.

ATTEMPTED DOUBLE MURDER AT MANCIIEBTER.—At Manchester, Joseph James Donald was remanded on a charge of attempting to murder his mother and sister and attempt- ing to commit suicide. On Sunday night the prisoner went home drunk and caused a disturbance, in the course of which he produced a razor and cut the throats of his mother and sister, and subsequently attempted to take his own life in a similar manner. The mother's injuries are serious, and shales in a precarious condition. The prisoner injuries are slight. THE ANTIQUARIAN DISCOVERY AT CRESTER.—A fort- night ago some workmen engaged by Mr. Bailin, J.P., of Chester,, in digging out the foundations for a cottage in Whitefriars, Chester, struck into two columns, which anti- quarians have reason to believe formed portions of a Roman temple. These discoveries have been seen by Dean Howson and other gentlemen belonging to the Chester Archseological Society, and pronounced to be of great antiquarian value. Since then fresh discoveries have been made. The workmen have now unearthed a platform composed of blocks of sand- stone, some 4 feet 6 inches square, upon which, at intervals of 14 feet, are square pedestals of the same size, which bore columns some 2 feet in diameter. Thus' there are clearly the foundations laid bare of what was once a large Roman temple. Portions of the Corinthian capitals carved in the sandstone, and much worn by the weather, have also been found. The pavement outside the temple was composed of a mixture of broken Roman tiles and other materials, and, while the pillars and platform have been left as they were found, the tiles have been removed ; but Mr. Bullin has very generously placed all the ancient remains found on the spot at the disposal of the Chester Archeological Society. The base of the temple, it is found, was 7 feet below the present street level. Over the fallen pillars, but at a depth of 3 feet only, is now disclosed the second portion of this extraerdinary "find "—in the shape of the medieval tiles which formed part of tb, flooring of the Carmelite Monas- tery or establishment of White Friars, which existed on this spot. Between the mediaeval remains and the Roman ones a laver of charcoal was found, which seems to Indic P jt, that the Vandals in Chester of those days—probably so ' invading horde—burnt the woodwork of the temple as i as threw down its columns.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. A fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room, at the Workhouse. on Wednesday morning. There were present Messrs. Greening (in the chair), Dr. Mackie, Appleton, Jolley, Harrison, Ildajor Cartwright, Cooper, Blackhurst, Caldwell, Derbyshire, Jeans, Bonnellt W. Houghton, Roberts, Brown, Gibson, Grange, John Houghton, Owen, Siddeley, Swinton, Worthington, and Sut- ton (clerk). 1 THE DINING-HOWL l The House Committee recommended that the tender of I Mr. Whalley of £6l 10s for the re-laying of the dining' room floor at the workhouse be accepted.—On the motion of Mr. JOLLY this recommendation was adopted.—The 1 Cumnatast also mentioned that some of the members of the ; committee thought it very desirable to have new seats and tables in the dining hall, and after some conversation, in which several members characterised the present seats as more like "instruments of torture " than anything else, the matter was referred to the House Committee. PROPOSED EXCURSION, The School Committee recommended that if arrange' ments could be made the children at the schools should have an excursion this year to some suitable place.—On the motion of Mr. DARBYSHIRE this recommendation Was adopted. DR. WATMINS AND HIS FEES: AMUSING CORRESPONDENCE. 'ERIAL PARLIAMENT. _

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MOWDAI. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. THE VfzujaiGTON &realm—Lord GRANYILLB, in answer to Lord Salisbury, stated that no vote would be asked for in the House of Commons for expenses connected with the Wellington statue in addition to the £6,000 already taken. In deference to the vote come to by their lordship? House the other night, the First Commissioner of 'Works sent: a message to the authorities at Woolwich next morning notto Proceed with the work of taking the statue to pieces: but before the workmen at Hyde Park could be coma:unlimited with the head had been cut off. &m ax STRATNIDEN and CAHPSELL, in laying on the table and moving the first reading of a Bill for abating smoke in the metropolis, cited statistics to prove the evils arising from the smoke nuisance and explained that his Bill would place in the hands of local authorities powers in this matter which they did not at present possess. --After some remarks from Lord Mount Temple in favour Of some additional means of suppressing the evil complained of, the Bill was read a first time. Ale Its Gsaitylercs.—Lord CARLINI:I7ORD, answering Lord Midleton,eaid that Mr. Gray, sub-commissioner of land in Ireland, had a knowledge of agriculture which fitted him for the post. The Lord. Lieutenant would not have appointed him had he known that he had taken an active part in land meetings held in the north of Ireland; but, having regard to Mr. Gray's conduct since hi et appointment his Excelbsncy did not feel called upon to take any action in the matter. The noble lord having stated that Mr. Gray was recom- mended by Lord Hertford and his agent, Lord Harextronn stated that he had net recommended Mr. Gray for the ap- Pointment, but had borne testimony to his knowledge of farming and to his being a respectable man. SHOAT/ BOUNTIVS.—Lord DERBY, in reply to Lord Car- narvon, stated that in reference to the West Indian sugar interest he had little to add to what he stated to the West India Committee on the 4th April. For some reason of their own, France and Germany paid bounties which enabled their manufacturers to sell sugar at such low prices as were very injurious to the West Indian trade. It would be use- less to hold a Conference on the subject, but, through the Foreign Office, he was endeavouring to obtain from the United States a "most favoured nation clause " for that trade. Foot AND MOUTH DIMEASE.—In reply to the Marquis of Huntly, Lord CARLINGEORD stated that several cases of loot and mouth disease bad occurred in Lincolnshire. He was sorry to say there had at first been great neglect in these cases, bat the Government had sent an inspector, who kad put himself in communication with the local authori- ties, and they had complied with all the advice given to Them. The infected case were now being carefully watched and isolated by the police. He should be glad to furnish all the correspondence as to the recent outbreak in Cam- bridgeshire. The Greek Marriages Bill and the Colonial Prisoners' Re- moval Bill were read a third time and passed. Lord GrzaerYttxx declined to answer an inquiry by Lord Ashburnham as to the number of the police force employed in the protection of Her Majesty's Ministers, and the cost Of that protection. Their lordships rose at 7-15. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair ot 4-0. THE WELLINGTON STATUE—Mr. SHAR-LEFEYRE' in re- Ply to Lord John Manners, said all arrangements had been made for the reception of the equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington at Aldershot. The site selected was near the head-quarters. It would be erected on a pedestal under the Supervision of the military authorities, the cost being de- frayed out of the fund raised by the Prince of Wales's Committee. MmatuAwcons.—Mr. Tatton-Egerton was informed by Mr. HIEBERT that the Secretary of State had suspended the order to close Chester Prison until the proposal had been discussed in the' House.--Mr. CHAMBVELLIN informed the House that the Channel Tunnel works at the French end had been suspended on the 17th of March. It had since been ascertained that the water entering the works amounted to 447 gallons a minute, and it had been decided to block the gallery.--Referring to the proposal to remove assizes from certain counties, the ATTORNEY-GENERAL stated that no scheme had been formed, and that there was no intention to increase the number of judges.--The Pains Murrwrna announced that the Government had every hope of passing a measure for intermediate educiation in Wales during the present session. THE FRANCHISE BILL.

The House having gone into Committee, Dr. CAMERON moved an amendment in clause 2 with the object of doing away with the present system of voting in three-cornered constituencies, by giving to each elector as many votes as there are members to be elected.—Mr. GLAD- STONE agreed that the question could not be left in its pre- sent position, but must be dealt with in a settle- ment of Reform. It properly belonged to Redistribution, and, though he could not give any pledge as to form, he ' hoped that it would be dealt with in tbe course of the Present Parliament.—After some remarks from Mr. Raikes, Sir E. Colebrook, and others, the amendment was with- drawn. Sir W. BARTTELOT moved to insert in the clause that the Personal payment of rates shall be a condition of the fran- C 11443.-511% GLADSTONE strongly opposed it as a large dis- franchising proposition. This question was fought out in .1.07 and 1869, and, as his right hon. friend the member for nipon would remember, so clear was the matter held to be then after all the aiscussion which had taken place, that the Act which got, rid finally of the restriction of personal pay- Ment of rates was not subject to serious controversy. It Was impossible that this amendment could be accepted.— Lord ELono and Mr. GORST also spoke against it, while Mr. FELL maintained that everybody ought to be obliged to pay their own rates.—Sir S. NORTUCOTE, while approving of the principle of the clause, reminded Sir W. Barttelot of the trouble caused by the "compound householder" in 1887, and deprecated a revival of those difficulties.—After some further oonvorsation the amendment was negatived. Sir E. WATIIN next moved an amendment providing that a household qualification should mean a tenement contain- ing not less than two habitable apartments; but Mr. Glad- stone also objected to this, on the ground that it would have a disfranchising operation, and without dwelling on the case pointed out that in the large Scotch towns one-fourth and oven one-third of the constituency would be disfranchised; and in Glasgow, out of 110,000 families, 39,000 were fami- lies or persons living in one room. Of the 39,000 persons in Glasgow living in one room 7,000 were single individuals. In Aberdeen the amendment would sweep away a fourth of the whole constituency, and he did not know anybody in Aberdeen who was not tit for the franchise. (Laughter.)— The amendment was discussed for a considerable time, and the Government were pressed to frame a definition of a dwelling-house, but ultimately was withdrawn, and clause 2 WAS agreed to. Clause S—the service franchise—was discussed in some detail, but seas ultimately agreed to without amendment. On Clause 4—restriction of faggot votes—Mr. INFL.sawer moved to add a subsection embodying the "one man one vote" principle, and allowing a voter who is entitled to be registered in more than one county or borough to elect for which county or borough he will be registered.—Mr. GLAD- !TONE opposed the amendment as inopportune, and urged its withdrawal; and Mr. J. MORLEY gave the same advice, and expressed a hope that other gentlemen on his side who had amendments would facilitate the progress of the Bill by reserving them for some future occasion.—Sir R. CROSS thought they had better not say much about faggot votes. The first to advocate the creation of faggot votes was the late Richard Cobden. Mr. GLAD- STONE admired the courtesy of the right hon. gentleman. A slur had been cast upon the memory of Mr. Cobden, who sought not to multiply sham or non-residents' votes but to afford easy means of enfranchisement to men competent to exercise the franchise.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE wished to point oat that the right hon: gentleman had himself and the Gov- ernment to blame for the difficulties of misrepresentations to Which they might be exposed because of the manner in which they had chosen to deal with the whole question.— Upon a division, taken after Mr. Dillwyn, Mr. John Morley, and others had walked out of the House. the amendment was negatived by 235 to 43. Progress was reported on the motion of Mr. GLADSTONE, and the House resumed at 11-35. THS NATIONAL DEBT BILL.—The CriaNcuLost of the EXCHEQUER moved the second reading of the National Debt (Conversion of eqock) Bill. He explained that the total amount of three per cent. stock was D 312,000,000, and that the offer would he made to the three descriptions—Consols, reduced, and new—and that the two and a half per cent. stock would be offered at 108, and the two and three-quarters at 102. Among other inducements to conversion, he men- tioned that if it became necessary to make another voluntary offer it would not be on such favourable terms and that the payment of dividends would be quarterly. terms, gross sav- ing of interest, he estimated, would be £1,830,000. but he proposed to establish a small sinking fund of £490,000 to pay off this nominal increase in the capital of the debt, which would reduce the saving to £1,310,000.—Mr. CHIT, DER,S then made some remarks on the policy of reducing in- terest, and concluded by maintaining that the Acts consolida- ting the debt gave a compulsory power to convert.—Mr. Iltrustam, who moved the rejection of the bill, denied that there was any compulsory power of conversion, and oh- jected to the reduction of the interest at the expense of in- creasing the nominal amount of the debt. In the name of the widows and orphans be protested against robbing the pre- sent for the benefit of the future, and in answer to Mr. Chit- der's arguments for the policy of the bill, he said that his 24 colleagues on the Direction of the Bank of England were without exception opposed to it.—On the motion of Mr. W. FOWLER, the debate was adjourned. Blisctwolsous.—The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill was read a second time. Leave was given to Colonel Colt- burst to bring in a bill to amend the Tramways (Ireland) Act, 1843. Mr. Trevelyan having moved for leave to bring in a bill to amend the Irish Land Act, and to provide facili- ties for the sale and purchase of land in Ireland, the debate was at once adjourned.—The LORD ADVOCATE moved for leave to bring in a bill for the better administration and endowment of the Universities of Scotland, and explained in what respects the measure eliffered from that which was - brought forwaid last year—The motion was agreed to. The House adjourned at 1-30. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIIISDAY. Their lordships met at 4-15. hitscztultl3ns —The Liverpool, Southport, and Preston • Junctiodltailway Bill was read a third time and passed.— , The Earl of Caroperdown laid on the table a bill imposing Certain - regfilations in the case of water companies. The bill was read a first time.—The Commons Regulation Pro- visional Order Bill passed through Committee.—The Settled Laud Bill was read a third time and passed.

Ti &ivPruitt QUNSTION.—The Earl of CArtatAttvon in- quired whether, as the House was about to rise for the holi- days, Her Majesty's Government should give any informa- tion relative to negotiations which it was understood were proceeding between Her Majesty's Government and the French Government as to Egyptian affairs, and whether it was the case that any arrangement had been made or pro- mise given to withdraw Her Majesty's troops at a given time P—Earl GRAtevnia replied that it was absolutely necessary that an arrangement of Egyptian finance should take place and in the opinion of Pier Majesty's Government it was needful to make alterations in the law of liquidation. With that object they had addressed the Powers, proposing a Conference to deal with the matter, and their lordships were aware of the terms of the circular of invitation, and also that all the Powers had agreed to a Conference. France having agreed to it in principle, there had been an inter- change of views between the two Governments. As to Egyptian affairs, communications between the French Go- vernment and Her Majesty's Government had gone on, and were still going on, in a friendly way, and it was impossible for him at that moment to say what the final result would be. When that result had been come to, Her Majesty's Government would consult the other Powers, and as soon as that had been done the result of the communications would be communicated to both Houses of Parliament. He might add that that would be done before they entered into the Conference. (Cheers.)— The Marquis of SALIM:MY supposed that the Government had found the custom of carrying on business by imposing silence on their supporters so successful, not only in facilitat- ing business, but in avoiding answering disagreeable ques- tions, but they were proposing to extend it from the House of Commons to the House of Lords. The crisis was grave, but, of course, he could net force them to speak. He hoped, under the circumstances, that so long a recess as the noble earl proposed would not be agreed to. (Cheers.)—Earl GuArgirthur was perfectly prepared to shorten the holiday if the noble marquis wished it, but he had listened with some astonishment at the courage of the leader of the Opposition in declaring the amount of openness necessary with Parliament before entering into important negociations. (Cheers.) The Government had been accused of wishing to shrink Parliamentary discussion but their very object in promising to lay the proposals before Parliament before going into the Conference was to give Parliament the fullest opportunity of discussing the whole question.— Answering the Earl of Wemyss, Earl Calcevutat said there was a difference between taking measures, if necessary, for General Gordon's safety, and making war in the midst of the Soudan, to reconquer which had never been the policy of the Liberal party.—The Marquis of SALISNUHY wanted to know whether Turkish troops were to be employed in the Soudan ?—Earl GuArrynne said it was not the case that Turkish troops were going to be sent, in the absence of British troops at this time of the year, to the relief of General Gordon. HIGHER EDUCATION IN WALES.—Lord CARLINGFORD, answering Lord Norton, said a commission, which sat two or three years ago, recommended that a moderate grant should be made from the Treasury to enable the people of North and South Wales to establish a college, and a grant of £4,000 had accordingly been made. Ihen a question arose whether the college at Aberystwith should be discon- tinued, anti in consequence of strong representations a grant of £1,500 a year had been made to keep it up. Their lordships, after some little discussion as to the date, adjourned till Monday, the 9th of June.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuasnAs. Tim CONFERENCE ON Envvr.—At the morning sitting of the House of Commons, Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. Bourke, stated that in the event of England coming to any understanding with France on matters now under discus- sion, and after those conclusions bad been communicated to the Powers, they should be presented to Parliament before the Conference meets. The Premier was subjected to severe cross-examination by Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, Mr. A. Balfour, Lord Randolph Churchill, Sir Stafford Northcote, and Sir Walter Barttelot, but nothing beyond this was extracted from him.—Sir H. Wow., after the undertaking given by the Prime Minister, would not proceed with the motion by which he had proposed to raise a debate on the Con-

ference. MISCHLLANHOUS. Dealing with the business of the House, the Psnursa consented not to take the Franchise Bill on Friday in next week, postponing it till the Monday following. The National Debt will be taken en Friday.— Mr. AsHmEAD-SARTLBTT inciaired whether any actual pre- paration had been made for an expedition for the relief of General Gordon.—Mr. GLADSTONE fell back upon the state. meat of Lord Hartingtor, who had recognised on the part of the Government their obligation with regard to Gordon and their especial duty to keep themselves in a position to fulfil that obligation—Mr. CtraxesaLinr, challenged by Mr. Gorst, cheerfully gave him assurance that the Government had no pressnt intention of abandoning the Merchant Ship- ping Bill.-Mr. GLADSTONE moved that the House at its rising adjourn till Thursday, the sth of June. Mr. Bar, POHR, whilst admitting that that the Premier had met the House on the question of the Conference in a fair and open spirit, nevertkeless made two or three observations on affairs in Egypt. Mr. Wands and Mr. O'Donnell followed. The conversation was continued by Mr. Labouchere, who com- plained that those—Mr. A. Balfour and Mr. Rylands— had almost shaken hands over his head; Mr. Bourke, Mr. Cowen, Mr. Rathbone, Baron de Worms, and Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett. After this discussion took divers turns, Dr. CAMERON complaining of the neglect of Scotch business, more especially with respect to the report of the Crofters Commission, and Mr. NORWOOD anxious ahout the second ' reading of the Merchant Shipping Bill. TizE SHIPPING BILL.—At five o'clock Lord Hain-mown appealed to the hon. members to allow the conversation to drop so that Mr. Trevelyan might explain the Bill dealing with the purchase clauses of the Irish Land Act. The im- mediate result of this appeal was the appearance of Mr. MACITER, who, three times called to order by the Speaker, desired to discuss the case of Captain Hatfield, "an honest, good fellow, and one of my constituents." Mr. MACITER challenging Mr. Chemberlain's statement with respect to Captain Hatfield in his speech on the second reading of the Merchant Shipping Bill, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN observed that he had read a letter from Captain Hatfield, in which he ad- mitted the accuracy of his statement, which was that he had had twelve ships, and that within a space of seven years he had lost eleven of them. PURCHASE Or IRISH LAND: LIBERAL PROPOSALS.

On the order for the adjourned debate on the motion for leave to bring in a bill for the purchase of land in Ireland, Mr. TREVELYAN said the purchase clauses of the Acts of 1870 and 1880 had to a great extent failed, not more than one farmer in 400 having become the possessor of his hold- ing. Under the operation of both measures the average sales of the Landed Estates Court had fallen from £1,500,000 in former years to less than £250,000 in the last three years. The principle obstacle to the purchase of land was that the tenants were waiting for better terms, and the Government in the bill now before the House had gone to the uttermost extent they could probably propose so that tenants might know what was the full limitation they had to look forward to. The legal obstacles, which were now considerable, would be almost entirely removed by this bill. The machinery of the Sales of the Settled Estates Act of 1882, which enabled limited owners to make their titles through the Land Com- missioners to the fee simple of the estate would be applied, and it was also proposed to give the purchaser an absolute statutory Parliamentary title:without legal expense to the purchaser except he choose to engage a solicitor. There would also be little or no delay in the completion of the transfer. To facilitate the purchase of land by the best class of tenants the Treasury had consented to reduce the rate of interests from 3 to 3i per cent. In the case of limited owners, part of the pur- chase money might remain on mortgage of the farms—on condition ef the Land Commissioners being assured that the price was fair, the security good, and the transaction such as would benefit the tenant and the community alike; they might advance the whole of the purchase money at the rate of interest just stated. The result would be that by paying £5 every year a tenant would be able to become the full and absolute owner of his farm at the end of 32 years, an offer such as was never before made by any State to any class of individuals. It was also proposed to make the county gess responsible for any deficiencies on the payments by the pur- chasers, the experience of the Land Commissioners being that this liability was very small, sanction to the advance for which the county news was thus to be responsible being given by the County Boards, elected partly by the Board of Guardians anl partly by the Grand Juries. In order to grapple with the arrears in the Appeal Court, it was pro- posed to strengthen the Land Commission by the appoint- ment of a fourth lay commissioner for two years certain, the Lord-Lieutenant to select two chairmen of counties to serve in the Appeal Courts, of which two would sit, one to be pre- sided over by Lord O'llagan. It was also proposed to limit the amonnt of money lent by the State to five millions in any one year, and to a total of twenty millions. Mr. PLUNBET hoped the bill would be printed as soon as possible. Colonel KING-HARMAN trusted the Government would give ample time to consider the bill. Mr. PARNELL thought the proposal that there should be a local guarantee for the payment of the whole of the money where the tenant did not advance any portion of it was serious, and that the constitution of a second Court of Appeal was unfortunate. Leave was given to bring in the bill, which was read a • first time. ,f The House then adjourned for Whitsuntide to June sth. _pre-

_ RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—figar! on Thursday morning the l• bridge crossing the Donaia; , katham, and Dover Railway, near Denmark Hill Station, elf while an engine was pas- sing under it. The engine buried itself in the ruins, and left the rails, but both the driver and stoker escaped with their lives. The accident was caused by the snapping of the iron girders which carries the roadway over the line. The driver and stoker were saved by the fact that they were protected by the iron canopy under which they were standing. TIIE ALLEGED ABDUCTION OF A Glut. AT BOOTLE.—At Bootle, on Thursday, Thomas Read, a married man with a family, was *charged with the abduction of a girl named Nelson, under 16 years of age. Prisoner lodged at the house of the girl's parents, and induced her to leave home with him, giving her money to put up the banns and promising her marriage. They lived together three weeks in Liver- pool, and then went to Manchester, where he was arrested. The girl said the prisoner swore he was a single man. In consequence of his misconduct she had to go to the hospital He threatened to cut her throat. Prisoner said that the girl was immoral, and that her mother connived at it, which Mrs. Nelson denied. He also said he took her away because the bailiffs were in the house, and kept her, but found she was not faithful to him. Prisoner was committed to the asaizea for trial.
