EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. REASSURING NEWS FROM KEIARTOII3I.—THE P.ROPOSED EXPEDITION. CAIRO, SATURDAY.—IiaIt ot the Egyptian battalion which was despatched from Assouan has arrived at Wadi Haifa without encountering opposition, and has occupied a forti- fied position. Captain Bedford, of Her Majesty's ship Monarch, has gone to Assiout to superintend the armour- plating of the patrol boats. CAIRO, SUNDAY.—TeII messengers are now on their way to Khartoum, in addition to which fresh messengers are being sent wit Dongola, as the best watered route. One thousand rifles have been despatched to the Governor of Dongola, whose loyalty is considered to be no longer doubtful since the formation of a British flotilla on the Nile has been de- cided upon. The flotilla will at present only consist of three steamers, each manned by 20 blue-jackets. Five British naval officers and eleven artificers are now at Assouan order to make the necessary arrangements. The remainder of the crews will leave Alexandria on the 27th inst., when the river patrol will commence. The flotilla will act inde- pendently of the Egyptian army, being under Lieut.- General Stephenson. No preparations for an autumn cam- paign have yet been made at British headquarters here be- yond preparation of plans, which are all ready. The British military authorities are decidedly in favour of the S nakim- Berber route to Khartoum, as offering fewest difficulties. in this case the Egyptian army would go up the Nile in order to divert the attention of the rebels. CAIRO, MONDAY.—The report that Major Kitchener had started across the iesert with 1,200 Arabs for Abu Hamad is not correct. Major Kitchener is still at Koroso. He has collected 500 gagaaras, and is now awaiting orders before starting on the desert journey. A telegram from Koroko at ten o'clock this morning announces that the rising of the Nile has commenced, the waters of the river having risen five inches within the last 43 hours. A report is current that Berber has not yet surrendered, but that hostilities have been suspended; Hussein Pasha Khalifa, the governor. having been engaged to give up the place as soon as Khar- toum shall have surrendered. M. Barrire, the French diplomatic agent, has left for France via Ismailia. Mr. Clif- ford Lloyd is expected to leave for London by the next Brindisi mail. fie will not return to Egypt. The English officials appointed by him in the Ministry of the Interior will be dismissed almost immediately, Nubar Pasha insist- ing that no European shall be employed in that department. It is expected that Abd-el-Kader Pasha, Minister of the In- terior, and Ahmed Pasha Nasbaat, Assistant Under-Secretary of that department, will tender their resignations. Scream, MONDAY, 4 PAL—The latest reports received here confirm Osman Digna's inaction, and state that his in- fluence has become greatly weakened with the tribesmen. He is now coquetting with the friendly tribes, but the latter do not respond to his advances, and are clamouring for assis- tance in the shape of arms and stores from Suakim, in order to avenge their blood-feud against him. The road to Khar- toum, via Suakim and Berber, is not vet open, but the intel- ligence which has come through from Khartoum and Berber represents the condition of both towns to be satisfactory.- 6 P.m.—The messenger on his way here from Berber, which town he left ten days ago, was captured to-day by Osman Digna just outside Suakim, his companions, however, suc- ceeded in escaping, and have arrived here. They report that the insurrection does not appear serious in any part, except near Shendy. The False Prophet is prevented from leaving Kordofan owing to the hostile attitude taken up by the Bagara, Kabalich, and other tribes. According to their ac- counts, neither Berber nor Khartoum is invested by the rebels; but the tribes are pressing round Khartoum. VVany liaise, MONDAY, 5 par.—Twenty soldiers belong- ing to the Dongola garrison arrived here to-day to take over the thousand rifles and ammunition despatched by the Egyptian Government for the Governor of Dongola. REBEL DEFEAT AT DONGOLA. CAIRO, TUESDAY —The Governor of Dongola telegraphs that he has visited the disaffacted districts, and has suc- ceeded by persuasion in tranqnilising them. The tribes have even intimated their readiness to pay taxes. The Governor engages to pacify the whole of the Soudan if 7,000 troops are despatched to him. Cacao, TUESDAY EVENING.—Owing to mistranslation, the last despatch of the Mudir of Dongola has been misread. The Governor telegraphs that he has tranquilised the dis- affected districts by totally defeating the rebels, who have tendered their submission. Assoiram, TUESDAY, IC a.m.—Messengers have returned hither who were despatched from Dongola to Darfour five months ago. They bring a letter from Slatin Bey, who says, after contending" against the rebels for two years and ex- hausting his supplies, he was reduced to the expedient of casting copper balls, which had no effect upon the enemy. Having waited in vain for the assistance he had repeatedly applied for, he at length surrendered to avoid further blood- shed. ZEBEHR'S ATTEMPT TO RESCUE GENERAL GORDON. Cargo, THURSDAY, 2-30 P.M.—Zebehr Pasha has sent several messengers to Khartoum to communicate with General Gordon if practicable. His three sons have all started on this mission, and it is hoped that some at least of the messengers will succeed in getting to Khartoum. In order to facilitate the passage of the messengers through hostile districts, Zebehr has furnished each messenger with a circular letter to the rebel chief.

The formation of a new balloon corps in connection with the Royal Engineers at Chatham, is now complete. The officers appointed to the corps are Major Elsdale, Major Templer, and Lieut. Macdonald. The corps will consist of telegraphists, carpenters, riggers, kc. They will leave shortly for the Soudan to join the autumn expedition. THE PRINCE OF WALES. ROYAT, Mccathay.—The Prince of Wales and his suite will leave Rovat by special train at three o'clock this afternoon for La Bourbole. His Royal Highness, after spending two days there, will proceed by road to Mont Dore, where he will pass the night. The Prince will subsequently return to Paris, on his way to Wiesbaden, where a large gathering of English and foreign royal and distinguished personages is expected. NEW ENGLISH CHURCH IN BERLIN. BERLIN, SATURDAY—The ceremony of laying the founda- tion stone of the new English church took place this morn- ing, in the grounds of the Monbijon Palace. The Crown Prince and Princess and their family, attended by many distinguished personages, were present. The Crown Prin- cess laid the stone "To the honour of God and His holy Church." FRANCE.—THE REVISION BILL. PARIS, SATURDAY.—M. Jules Ferry to-day presented to the Chamber of Deputies the bill for the revision of the Constitution. The bill consists of one clause only, in which are indicated the points of the Constitution which, in the view of the Government, require modification. In sub- stance the bill proposes—that the law of February 24th, 1875, relating to the election of Senators, shall lose its con- stitutional character; that irremovable Senators shall no longer hold their seats for life, but that their term of office be reduced to nine years, this provision however, not to be retrospective ; that provision be made for filling vacant irremovable Senatorslaips by means of elections in which both the Senate and Chamber of Deputies shall participate; that the number of Senatorial Delegates with whoa, the election of ordinary Senators rests be increased in proportion to the number of municipal Councillors; that, with regard to the financial rights of the Senate, the existing state of things be modified to the extent involved by making Ibe word Chamber the last word in the text of the present law; that public prayers at the opening of the Legislature be no longer held; and, finally, thit Clause 8 of the Fundamental Law of February 25th, 1875, shall be revised in such a way that in no case shall revision touch the Republican form of government. The Premier, in laying the bill before the Chamber, read the preamble, which sets forth the views of the Government upon the above points, and without formu- lating a precise text, the drawing up of which is left to the Congress of both Houses, insists on the necessity of limiting the revision to the points indicated in the body of the bill. The reading of the preamble was applauded by the majority in the Chamber, but was frequently interrupted by ironical laughter from the benches of the Extreme Left. MADAME SARAH BERNHARDT. PARIS, MONDAY.—The Seine Court of Assizes to-day : heard the action brought by Madame Sarah Bernhardt against Mdlle. Marie Colombier for libel and defamation , contained in the book " Sarah Barnum," of which defendant . was the author. The Court found that Madame Bernhardt , had made out her case, and sentenced Madame Colombier to , three months' imprisonment and to pay a fine of 1,0001. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—M. Jules Ferry and Vice-Admiral _ . . . .

programme had had .to be accepted as, containing the minimum of the sacrifices demanded of the Com- pany, for whom It was onerous in its effects. M. de Les- seps protested against this interpretatien of kis words. Part of the meeting applauded the chairman, while another sec- tion supported the skareholder, who cmtinuing his remarks amidst considerable interruption, declared that the promises made to the shareholders had been broken. Another share- holder maintained, on the other hand, that the convention concluded with the English shipowers was satisfactory, and ought to be supported. Eventually all the proposals of the Board of Directors were adopted by a,large majority. The last resolution, proposing a modification of the statutes of the company, for the purpose of increasing the number of English directorti by seven, Was approved by 2,608 votes against 556. RAILWAY OUTRAGE IN RUSSIA. ST. PETERSBURG, SUNDAV.--At one o'clock this morning the Moscow express ran off the rails near Bologoe station, and the engine, luggage van, and three second-class passen- ger carriages were precipitated down the embankment. The manager of a Moscow factory. named Date], was killed. M. Beres, Deputy Governor of Orloff, and a lady were severely injured, and five of the railway employes were more or less hurt. ST. PETERSBURG, MONDAY.—From later particulars re- garding the accident to the mail train on the Moscow Rail- way, it appears that the train was intentionally wrecked, the rails at the spot where the disaster occurred having been loosened. Among the injured is the Vice-Governor of Orel. The Grand Duke Sergnis, who was travelling on the line, arrivsd on the scene a few hours after the accident, and rendered great assistance. ZULULAND. _

DURBIN, SkTUßDAY.—General Smith and Mr. Osborn are at Maritzburg. They will cohfer with Sir Henry Bohner preparatory to the adoption of measures for the maintenance of order in the reserve. British troops have left Maritz- burg for the reserve. CETEWAYO,S SON CROWNED KING OF ZULULAND. .

DonneN, WEDNESDAS,-10:1E-eat"—.:—Intelligence received here announces that the Boers crowned Dinizulu, son of the late King Cetewayo, King of Zululand, on the 21st inst., the chiefs Chant and Usibepu having acknowledged his claim.

THE FAILURES IN NEW YORK. NEW YORK, SUNDAY.—The West-side Bank, in this city,° has suspended payment. The teller is stated to be a de- faulter to the amount of 96,000 dohs. The President of the Erie County Savings Bank, who has been absent from his post, has returned, and confessed that he has lost 100,000 dole, belonging to the bank in speculation. NEW YORK, MONDAT.—Mr. James Fish, formerly presi- dent of the Marine National Bank, for whose arrest a war- rant was issued on charges of misappropriation of funds, is still at large, and is supposed to have fled. Mr. Vanderbilt has transferred 5,000,000 dols, four per cent. Government St.ck to his son. The Penn Bank of Pittsburg, which re- cently suspended payment and subsequently re-opened, has again closed its doors owing to the sudden illness of its president. A small bank at Green Bay, Wisconsin, has sus- pended payment. The President of the Erie County Bank has been lodged in gaol in order to prevent acts of violence on the part of the mob' Mr. James Fish has been released on bail. Mr. James B. Keene has asked his creditors te ac- cept notes at 12 and 18 months for their debts, with interest. This extension of time will probably be granted. A col- lision has occurred on the West Shore Railway, between Savannah and New York, in which three persons were killed and many injured. CHARGES AGAINST GENERAL GRAN P. NEW Yonx, MONDLY —A painful impression has been produced by the publication of a statement by Mr. Fish, president of the Marine Bank and a member of the firm of Grant and Ward, that he holds letters written to himself by General Grant, in which the latter vouches for the genuine- ness of the alleged Government contracts upon which certain operations of the firm were conducted. NEW Yona, TUESDAY—It has been made known that in 1882 Mr. Fish wrote to General Grant, stating that he understood that he (Grant) was a partner in the firm of Grant and Ward, and that he presumed he was right in sup- posing that the notes issued by that house were solely for raising money to carry out Government contracts. General Grant replied, confirming the partnership,but saying nothing about the contracts. On the same day that he received the General's reply, however, M. Fish also had a letter written by Mr. Ward and signed by General Grant. This contained a full assurance that Mr. Fish's advance would he perfectly safe, and on the faith of these two document Mr. Fish says he paid over the money, believing everything was straight- forward. It is stated that the counsel who have been in- structed to act for General Grant in this affair will urge that the General signed Mr. Ward's letter as a mere matter of business routine, and without reading its contents, of which he was wholly ignorant.

IForster. In a return compiled from official sources' it is estimated that the coming wheat crop in America will be fifty million bushels over the average. The crew of the steamer Delabole, of Newport, were landed at Ilfracemloa on Thursday morning, their vessel having sunk in collision. Owing to defects in the pedestal of the statue of the late Lord F. Cavendish at Barrow, the ceremony of unveiling has been indefinitely postponed. In their match with Cambridge University the Yorkshire Eleven, on Wednesday, won by an innings and 203 runs. Notts beat Middlesex by six wickets. Sir Bartle Frets died on Thursday morning, at his resi- dence, near London. Sir Bartle had been in a prostrate condition for many weeks. Be was 67 years of age. The Freeman's Journal, the organ of the Nationalist party in the Irish daily press, recognises that in his Purchase Act Mr. Trevelyan has made a real attempt to solve a press-

jug problem. - Dr. George Ridding, late head master of Winchester School, was on Wednesday installed as first Bishop of the newly-founded diocese of Southwell. The ceremony was a very impressive one. The west front of Lichfield Cathedral, which has been restored at a cost of £35,000, was dedicated on Thursday, the Archbishop of Canterbury taking part in the ceremony,

which was of an interesting -charade'''. Considerable delay was caused on Wednesday morning to traffic on the Caledonian Railway by a goods train leaving the metals near Cumbernauld. some waggons fell ever an
embankment and were smashed. The pe-r-manent way was broken up for some distance, and passenger trains were
kept waillog for hours before the 'damage could be re-

paired. Bryan Denis Molloy, a man of 50. was again brought be- fore one of the Dublin magistrates on Wednesday, on a charge of having married a woman in March last notwithstanding the fact that the person to whom he was married 24 years ago was still alive. The prisoner is said to have five " wives " living. Mr. Molloy was again remanded for the production

of another wife. ALAUMING ACCIDENT: Two MEN KILLED —A. serious accident happened Jo Thursday afternoon, at the gasworks, East Cowes, Isle of Wight, through the wall of the coal store giving way. Three men—named Saunders, Brown, and Legg—were buried under a mass of coal 20 feet high. On its removal Brown was found to be dead, and Saunders died shortly after being extricated; but Legg was not

seriously hurt. THE PREMIER AT Homn.—Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs. and Miss Gladstone, left Downing-street at 4-30 p.m. on Tuesday, and drove in an open carriage to Euston Station, leaving for Hawarden by the five o'clock express. The right hon. gentleman wore a white felt hat and a thick overcoat He was understood to be in very good health, with the exception of a slight cough, which at times is somewhat troublesome. Sir S. Northcote spoke on Wednesday night at a some- what disorderly meeting ot the Marylebone Conservative Union, held in the St. Pancras Vestry Hall, under the pre- sidency of Lord John Manners. The leader of the Opposi- tion, who reminded his hearers that he was a native of the borough, pleaded for freedom of speech, and proceeded amidst considerable interruption to criticise the Liberal watchwords of 'Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform." ALLEGED LIBEL ON MRS. WELDON.—In the Queen's Bench, on Monday, the hearing was commenced of the action in which Mrs. Weldon claimed £4,000 damages from Mr. T. Johnson, London correspondent of the Paris Figaro, for an slimed libel arising out of differences between plain- tiff and M. Gounod, on the production of the latter's oratorio "The Redemption," at the Birmingham Festival of 1882. The jury gave a verdict for plaintiff, damages £5OO. Judgment was given on Wednesday, in the case of Westinghouse v. The Lancashire and York- shire Railway, which was an action for infringe- ment of the plaintiff's railway brake, and came up on appeal. Mr. Justice Grove and Mr. Baron Huddleston held yesterday that there was no reasonable evidence of in- fringement before the jury, and gave judgment for the defendants. It was intimated that there would probably be an appeal against the decision. FEMALE Sultsmom.—The memorial which is to be pre- sented to Mr. Gladstone after Whitsuntide in favour of leav- ing open the question of female suffrage when Mr. Woodall's amendment to the Franchise Rill came on has received the following among the many other signatures, and is daily re- ceiving fresh adherents:—James Stansfeld, Jacob Bright, Arthur Arnold, John Slagg. Thos. Shaw, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, Robert Leake, William Agnew, Henry Fawcett, Thos. Burt, Isaac Holden, Benjamin Armitage. SODDEN DEATH OF AN IRISH M.P.—The Press Associa- tion learns that the death of Sir John Ennis, M.P. for Athlone, which occurred at his London residence at 3-15 on Wednesday afternoon, from apoplexy, was almost entirely unexpected. The honourable baronet's illness was very brief, and he had taken part in all the important divisions during the present session. He was returned for Athldne at the general election by a majority of only one vote over Mr. Shell, and the Nationalists are now hopeful of carrying the seat. SPEECH BY MR. H. GLatisrorrg, M.P.—Mr. Herbert Glad- stone, presiding at the annual meeting of the London and Counties Liberal Union, on Tuesday, said two great ques- tions monopolised attention—Egypt and the Franchise. As to the Soudan, he believed the country did not distrust the action of the Government present, past, or prospective. It was untrue that they had abandoned Gordon. Regarding tbe Franchise Bill, it was true it might be stopped by the House of Lords, but the immediate effect of such action would be to precipitate the reform of that venerable insti- tution. POISONED BY TINNED Sermow.—An inquest was opened at Wolverhampton, on Monday, on the body of a young man named Frederick William Dewin, who died from the effects, it is believed, of eating tinned salmon. On Thurs- day night, Dewin, his sister, and mother ate some tinned salmon for supper. The next day all three were taken seriously ill, the chief sympton being severe vomiting. The young man died on Saturday, and his decease has been followed by the death of his mother. The daughter has recovered. The inquest was adjourned for ji post-mortem examination.

----- PORTOBELLO COLLIERY ON FIRE: SEVEN LIVES LOST. —A fire broke out on Saturday in one of the pits of the Niddrie Collieries, near Portobello. Sixteen mea were in the lower workings at the time, and their fate was for several hours uncertain, as they could not be reached by 'volunteer parties or explorers owing to the density of smoke. About six o'clock in the evening a rescue party was enabled to descend to No. 12 pit, and suc- ceeded in rescuing nine of the imprisoned mea. Their names are James Kerr and son, Robert John Ferguson (a boy), Patrick Shavelin, William Hamilton (a boy), John Fleming, Archibald M‘Cartney, Patrick Corrigan, and Alex- ander Ferguson. The other seven were suffocated, having been unable to reach the crossing where the rescued men were found. THE SLIGO MURDER CONSPIRACY.—The magisterial in- vestigation of the Sligo conspiracy was continued on Satur- day. Patrick Delaney. who is under sentence of penal servitude for life for taking part in the Pheenix Park murder, stated that James Tynan, known as "No. 1," was present when Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke were murdered; and Thomas Brennand, late secretary of the Laud League, was a member of the London directors of the Fenian organisation which encouraged crime. Evidence was also given to show that Daly, arrested with infernal machines in his possession at Liverpool, was present at the meetings of the Tubbercurry conspirators.—The case was not concluded until Tuesday, when all the eleven prisoners were committed for trial for conspiracy to murder and treason-felony. PAINFUL SUICIDE or THE DEAN Or RANGOII.—The greatest consternation was excited throughout North Wales on Saturday, at ehe report, unfortunately only too well founded, that the Dean of Bangor, the Very Rev. Henry Thomas Edwards, M.A., had been found dead in his bed- room at the residence of his brother, the Vicar of Ruabon (the Rev. E. W. Edwards), and that his end had been caused by his own hand. The deceased had been unwell for several months, and early in the present year, by the advice of his medical men, he took a long voyage in the Mediterranean. He found but little benefit from this, however, and shortly after his return to Wales he went to Ben Rhydding, near Ilkley, in Yorkshire, where he remained for three weeks. On Friday week, in the company ef his brother, the Vicar of Ruabon, he returned from Ben Rhyditing, and came to stay at Ruabon Vicarage, where he still continued to suffer from excessive nervous depression. It was not, however, thought that his end was immediately near, and certainly not anticipated that he would do anything to cause it, but on his bedroom being entered en Saturday morning by his brother, for the purpose of handing him his letters, he found him suspended by a leather strap from one of the posts of his bedstead. On a medical man being called in it was found that life was quite extinct, and it is surmised that he had been dead for more than an hour.—At the inquest on Mon- day a verdict of temporary insanity was returned. It was stated that the deceased had dreaded attacks of insanity for nine months past, having said that something gave way in his brain like the snapping of a watch spring.—At Ranger, on Wednesday, the remains of the late Dean were conveyed to their last resting place amid universal demonstrations of sympathy and sorrow. The Mayor and Corporation and other public bodies attended at the railway station and joined in the funeral procession to the Cathedral. as did also a detachment of Carnarvonshire and Flintshire Volunteers, to whom the Dean was honorary chaplain. About two hundred of the clergy of the diocese were present, but a still more striking testimony to the esteem in which Dr. Edwards was held was afforded by the Welsh Wesleyan Conference, which adjourned its session in order that the members might attend the funeral service at the Cathedral. The attendance of the general public was also very large, a great many people being conveyed to Bangor from surrounding towns by special trains. div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The number of visitors to the Health Exhibition for last week was 83,220. Total since the opening 179,222. Mr. Alfred Dearman, an estate agent, Sheffield, was killed by jumping from his carriage, the horse having run away. Several great demonstrations in support of the Franchise Bill have been held near Leeds and Bradford, non-electors attending in thapnds. A Cabinet Cdilliken was held at the Premier's official resi- dence at 12-30 on Tuesday. Earl Granville had previously an interview with the Premier. Mr. Justice Chitty, on Monday, after hearing arguments in private, authorised the Duke of Marlborough to sell cer- train of the Blenheim heirlooms. A receiving order was made in bankruptcy, on Tuesday, against James Davis, secretary of tbe London and San Fran- cisco Bank, the debtor having absconded. Major G. A. Elliott, 19th Regiment, threw himself over- board from a steamer in the Irish Channel on Monday night. He was rescued, but died shortly afterwards. The Premier, replying to the Sunderland Shipowners' ISociety, writes pointing out that the Press is open to those who disagree with the Board of Trade's statements. The will of the late Mr. M. T. Bass, formerly M.P. for Derby, has been proved, the personalty being sworn at £1,800,000. There are numerous legacies to friends. Sir Henry Wilmot presided at the spring meeting of the National Rifle Association. The report stated that the Council bad largely increased the contribution to the prize fund. The Limerick Corporation on Tuesday again refused to levy a rate for about £2,000 for extra police during the recent agitation. A mandamus is issued against the Cor- poration. Robert Black, found guilty of murdering a woman at Tox- teth Park, Liverpool, by throwing a lighted paraffin lamp at her, and sentenced to death at Liverpool Assizes, has received a respite. The report for the past year of the Suez Canal Company states that the nett profits of the undertaking amount to £1.436,520, and that the distribution amongst the various classes of shareholders will reach £3 103. lUid. per share, against £3 ss. for the year preceding. EXECUTION AT Dunnam.—Joseph Lawson was executed on Tuesday morning, at Durham, for the Butterknowle mur- der. The culprit was very cheerful, and kept talking to Berry, the executioner. He said Hodgson struck the first blow, and then he helped him. He hoped Siddle would be looked after (liberated). DEMOLITION OF A CATHOLIC CHURCH: MIN KILLED.— During the taking down of St. Mary's Catholic Church, Liverpool, to make room for the Lancashire and Yorkshire extension, on Tuesday, a portion of the roof fell in with a groat crash, killing one man, a labourer, who leaves a widow and numerous family. THE CONGREGATIONAL UNlON.—Acknowledging a letter from the Rev. Dr. Parker, expressing, on behalf of the Con- gregational Union, continued confidence in the Premier's policy and administration, Mr. Gladstone says he knows he may always rely that justice will be done to himself and his policy by the Nonconformist community. Lord Wolseley presided, on Saturday evening, at the an- nual dinner of the Artists' General Benevolent Institution, in London. In proposing " Tbe Army, Navy, and Auxiliary Forces," he said he had a high opinion of the militia. He believed it to be the backbone of the army, for he knew it to be the force from which they received most men at the present moment. THE GOVERNMENT OF LONDON.—This is the title of an important pamphlet by Mr. W. M. Torress, M.P., published at sixpence by Messrs. Regan, Paul, Trench and Co. It is quite a little history in its way. and bristles with facts, figures, and quotations from official reports. It will be read and studied with interest in view of the bill before Parlia- ment on the Reform in the Government of the metropolis.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
The Daily/Voss says :—We understand that within three hours of the decision of the Lords' Committee on the Man- _ __ .

cheater Canal Bill the capital of £5,000,000 stipulated for was subscribed. The operation was carried on chiefly by telegraph with Manchester. It is estimated that the pro- ceedings in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal cost promoters and opponents an aggregate sum a trifle under

£lBO,OOO. _ _ The Manchester Guardian says the committee have held 41 sittings of five hours each, that 151 witnesses have been examined, 99 for the bill and 52 for the opponents, and that 25,36 T questions have been asked, covering 1861 pages of printed matter. Mr. Daniel Adamson, the chairman of the Provisional Committee appointed to promote the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal, obtained an exceedingly hearty welcome from the inhabitants of Didsbury on his return home from London on Saturday afternoon. Triumphal arches had been erected in his honour, and other indications of popular approval of the part he has taken in securing the passing of the Ship Canal Bill were found in various mottoes in conspicuous places. On a triumphal arch erected on the way to his residence, the Towers, were the words "Welcome to the pilot of the Ship Canal Bill ;" another erected on the carriage drive leading to his house, had on it this expression—" Well steeed, so welcome home to port." Mr. Adamson arrived at Stockport from the Me- tropolis about half-past two o'clock, and drove through Burnage and along Fogg-lane in his landau with Mn. Adamson. He was met at the railway station by the Didsbury brass band, which immediatey struck up "See the conquering hero comes." Cheers were raised on their arrival and were continued along the route to the Towers When opposite the Didsbury Hotel, the horses were taken away from the conveyance' and a number of enthusiastic believers in the Ship Canal scheme took their places. While this was being done Mr. Adamson, standing up in the car- riage, addressed a few words to those assembled. After thanking them for their kind reception, he said that although their opponents could bribe all the technical talent in England it did not withstand the evidence brought by the best engineers of the world. It was some consideration for the two and a quarter hours waiting for the verdict whether they should have the bill or not to receive such a kind reception:as he had that day. (Applause.) The com- mittee had given them the bill exactly as they asked for it, and the only condition imposed upon them was what they asked for, that they should get the money before com- mencing operations. (Applause and "three cheers for Pem- ber.") He was told the previous day that it was the greatest fight that ever took place in England, and he was sure the time was not far distant when they would return from the House of Commons with the bill in its entirety. He trusted, then, that they would be ready with their thousands and millions to complete the canal. The carriage afterwards moved off, drawn by willing bands, to Mr. Adamson's resi- dence. After assisting his wife out of the carriage, Mr. Adamson made another short speech, in which he thanked them most sincerely for that kind reception at his ownhome. He was sure that was sufficient compensation for the several ' weeks he had been engaged in London fighting the battle of extended 'commerce oa their account and for a future generation. He knew they had to fight against the wealthiest monopoly this country ever produced, and un- fortunately while they were fighting the monopolists they were being opposed by money paid by the men of Lanca- shire. The people of this county had, however, come to their senses. They had decided not to have the tollbar at Liverpool, but to let Liverpool people keep up their commerce themselves. Their opponents in the Lords' Committee-room looked exceedingly bilious when they (the Provisional Committee) prompted Mr. Pember to tell the noble lords that they did not desire to start the Canal until five mil- lions of money was subscribed. It was the last nail in their coffin. (Applause.) He could assure his hearers they had to fight against prejudice to begin with, but the Committee gradually came round to their side because they had the best talent in the world ia their favour. (Applause.) A deputation attended at the offices.' of the Provisional Committee in Market-street, Manchester, on Monday after- noon, representing some of the local ward committees inter- ested in the canal scheme for the purpose of congratulating Mr. Adamson and the committee on the passing of the bill by the committee of the House of Lords.—Mr. Alderman Batty, in introducing the deputation, stated on their behalf that he felt that the thanks of the whole of the people of Lancashire and Yorkshire were due to the projectors of this great scheme, which, when completed, would confer such numerous benefits to the whole of this immense district.— Mr. Adamson, in reply, highly eulogised the untiring services of the gentlemen who had worked with him con- spicuons amongst whom were the engineer, Mr. E. Leader Williams, and the solicitor, Mr. Saxon, Messrs. Marshall Stevens, Boddington, Hicks, and other members of the com- mittee, together with Mr. Pember and their otber able counsel. He stated that Mr. Pember's great speech would be specially printed for the use of the committee.—lt was mentioned by Mr. Reuben Spencer that a strong feeling existed that a monstre demonstration should be arranged at an early date, and it was un- derstood that steps were being taken with that view. The Liverpool Mercury says :—lf we may credit the reports which reach us from Manchester and elsewhere, the first and essential condition on which the Select Committee of the House of Lords passed the Ship Canal Bill on Friday has already been complied with. That condition was that before the proposed works were begun the sum of £5,000,000 should not only be subscribed but the payment guaranteed. The object of the committee was to prevent the creation of a mere bogus subscription list, and it must be taken as an in- dication of the practical sagacity of the committee, and of their determination to protect, as far as they were in a posi- tion to do so, the interests of capitalists, great and small, who have sufficient confidence in the ultimate success bf the scheme to induce them to speculate on the venture. It is affirmed that, within three hours I after the decision of the committee was made known, the whole amount was subscribed. It was I -confidently stated during the progress of the inquiry that Ithe money would be forthcoming when required, but no- body seems to have been more surprised than the Manches- ter people themselves that the committee passed the bill without imposing conditions affecting the structure of the works, rather than the financial operations necessary to carry them out, which might have jeopardised the whole scheme. If it be true that the capital has actually been subscribed, not on paper only, but with a substantial cash guarantee, it 'is unquestionably a marvellous instance of commercial en- terprise and an astounding example of boundless faith in the realisation of what has hitherto been regarded by many practical minds as merely an ambitious idea. The Corporation of Manchester, on Thursday, by 28 votes against 10, granted £lO,OOO in aid of the ship canal scheme, on consideration of certain clauses being inserted in the bill "for the benefit and protection of the interests of the city.

The new Speaker of the House of Commons upon reach- ing his Bedfordshire residence at Sandy on Wedne.sclav,waq presented with an address of "welcome," and in the even- ing the inhabitants entertained the right hon. gentleman at a banquet. The attitude of intolerance towards Dissent maintained by some landowners was the subject of complaint at Wed- nesday's sitting of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist Synod. The Synod ultimately appointed a committee to wait upon landowners who had refused to grant chapel sites.

div.p: PRESCOT.

, Barratxrv.—At the Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. H. Willis, James Sephton, sweep, was charged with brutality, and James Taylor with being in company with Sephton, and rendering hint such assistance as to make his escape.—Both prisoners were remanded.—Sephton has only been liberated a few months, having undergone 18 months' imprisonment for a similar offence. PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. . A fortnightly meeting of the Board of Guardians WM held at the Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday, when there tvere present—Mr. J. T. Hall (in the chair), the Rev. T. Chambers, Rev. J. Barnacle' Rev. Father Finegan, Messrs. W. Birchall, W. Newsome, W. Gilbody, J. Matthews, W. J. Ashton, S. Marsh, J. Jackson, J. Lowe, J. Buckley, J. Fid- ler, J. Leatherbarrow, J. G-riffiths, J. Kenwright, W. Tyrer, T. Dobell, T. Sadler, R. Leigh, T. Eatock, R. Tuson, T. F. Hill, J. Fisher, P. Langton, H. Hulme, W. Gerrard, T. Syder, J. Meadows, and S. H. Hartley (clerk.) APPOINTMENT OF MASTER AND MATRON OF THE WORK- HOUSE —The Clerk stated at a special me-tin' of the Board, held on the previous Tuesday, the applications fer the posts of master and matron of the Union Workhouse were considered, and reduced to three in number, and these were—Mr. and Mrs. Arthur fierily Hal., master and matron of the Helper Workhouse, Derby : Mr. and Mrs. John Scannel, Widnes, relieving officer of the Prescot Union ; and Mr. and Mrs. Leonard Forster, of Liverpool, formerly master Fulham Union Workhouse.—The teetimonials and qualifications of each candidate were duly considered, after which the candidates were called into the room and questioned.—Mr. Hale stated that the religion of he and his wife was Church of Englaad and their present joint salary was £l4O per annum with rations. Upon Mr. Scannel and his wife being called, the Chairman remarked that he thought they wuuld be so well known to the Guardians that he scarcely thought it necessary to question them I nrther.—The Guardians agreed with this remark and Mr. and Mrs. Scannel left the room.—Mr. and Mrs. For.ter were briefly questioned, after which the Board proceeded to vote upon the matter.—Before this was done, Mr. Fidler stated that he would like to say a few words upon the election. He thought they should sink all differences that had previously existed and appoint Mr. Hale, who appeared to be a downright good man. (Hear, hear.)—The voting was as follows: For Mr. and Mrs. Hale: Messrs. Meadows, Birchall, Griffiths, Syder, P. Langton, Swift, Kenwright, Lowe,Newsome,Fidler, Dobell, Hulme, Hill, Ashton, Tuson, Leigh, Leatherbarrow, Barnacle, Marsh, Tyaer, and Hall (chairman), 21; for Mr. and Mrs. Scannell : Messrs. E dock, Buckley, Jackson, Gilkody, Chambers, Matthews. Finegan, Sadler, Gerrard, and Fisher' 10; and for M. and Mrs. Forster: none. Mr. and Mrs. Hale were therefore declared elected; and on being again called into the room they were acquainted with the fact, the Chairman expressing the hope that they would be able to conduct the Workhouse as well as it had been conducted previously, and he could assure them that the Guardians would render them all the assist- ance they could.—Mt. Hale sincerely thanked the Guar- dians for their kinddess and confidence, and said he hoped they might fulfil their duties to the entire satisfaction of the Local Government Board and everyone else, both rate- payers and Guardians. Fist( DINNERS.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board acknowledging the receipt of a commu- nication containing the opinion of the Medical Officer of Health as to th 3 effect on the health of the inmates of the fish dinner which the Board on the 6th February last, sanctioned for a further period of three months. The Guardians proposed temporarily ,to discontinue the fish din- ner, and were desirous of having the sanction of the Board to resume tire fish dinner when they consider it expedient to do so. The Local Government Board, however, could not give such ar. assent 83 would enable the guardians to vary the dietary when they thought it desirable to do so. Having regard, however' to the opinion of the Medical Officer with regard to the fish dinner, the Board assented to its permanent adoption as an alternative diet for the inmates of the workhouse. THE VACANCR ON THE BOARD.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board dated the 22nd May, I stating that in compliance with the wishes of the guardians, they would shortly issue an order authorising the special election of a guardian for the urban ward of the township of Eccleston, in the room of Mr. James Penketh, deceased. THE Sr. HELENS CORPORATION AND THE BOARD OF GuARDIANS.—A letter from the Local Government Board, dated 23rd May, was read by the Clerk, enclosing for the observation of the Guardians a copy of a letter from the St. Helens Town Council with reference to the erection of vagrants wards at St. Helens. The letter added that the Local Government Board had been furnished with a copy of the correspondence which had passed between the Town Council and the Guardians on the subject. Mr. Hartley (clerk)explained that since the last meeting he had had an in- terview with Mr. Craik,and informed him that the Guardians would probably sanction a line of telephonic communication between St. Helens relief offices and the workhouse so that if the police wculd render all the assistance they could they (the Guardians) would doubtless make provision for the re- moval of any person from the Town Hall in the cab belonging the Union. Mr. Craik Informed him that he felt confident that that would meet with the approval of the St. Helens Corporation. TELEPHONIC COMMUNICATION WITH ST. HELENS.—Mr. Tyrer moved: "That the offer of the Lancashire and Che- shire Telephonic Exchange Company, Limited, to erect and maintain a telephonic communication between the St. Helens relief offices and the Union offices, dm., as per specification, for the sum of £4O per annum be accepted."—The motion was seconded by Mr. Birchall and carried. WITHDRAWAL OF A Mornow.—Mr. Meadows remarked that at the last meeting he gave notice that he would move that the minutes of the Guardians authorizing the sinking of a well and providing the necessary machinery at the t workhouse and the proposal to borrow £BOO for such works I be rescinded, but he now wished to state that it was not his intention to proceed with the matter at present. TAIE Rrsteistanote OF MR. BICKNELL.—Mr. Leather- barrow expressed the opinion that before Mr. and Mrs. Bicknell left their posts as master and matron of the Work- house some recognition of their services ought to be given.— Mr. Newsome subsequently moved that the Board express re- gret at the loss of Mr. and Mrs. Bicknell's services, and at the same time express the high appreciation and esteem in which they were held.—The Rev. T. Chambers seconded the motioa, which was passed. THE PANTASAPH ORPHANAGE—The Rev. T. Finegan said: I beg to give notice that at the next meeting I will ask the Board to rescind the resolution which prevents children of this Union being sent to the Pantasaph Orphan- age, and that the children removed from that institution be sent back. THE WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 414 inmates of the Workhouse that week,and 427 in the preceding week. There were 185 boys and girls in Kirkdale School.—This was the only business of interest.

div.head: RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

An adjourned meeting of the members of the Rural San:. tary Authority was held at the Union Workhouse, Whistor on Thursday afternoon, when there were present—Messrs. Leatherbarrow (in the chair), Meadows, Newsome, Tyrer, J. T. Hall, Leigh, Eatock, Sydtr, Glilbody, Swift, Ken- wright, and Hartley (clerk). The meeting had been called to consider the application of the assistant overseer for Eccleston township for a sanitary rate of 8d in the pound, and also to consider the report of Mr. Goldsworth (sur- veyor) with reference to the sewerage scheme for Eccleston. Mr. Cook (one of the overseers for Eccleston) and Mr. Dunn (aesistant overseer) attended the meeting.—The Clerk stated that the Authority wished to know why the contribution orders regularly issued and properly served on the overseers of Eccleston had not been met within the time specified, and why they had been disregarded. They wished to know whether the overseers had had funds in hand to meet the requirements; and whether they levied rates at the proper time.—Mr. Dunn explained that they at present required about £l5O, and to meet that they would require a rate of 8d in the £. —The rate books were afterwards produced and examined, and the clerk afterwards stated that the fact was the over- seers had not levied rates sufficient to meet the requirements. and the result was that the ratepayers of to-day were to be asked to pay rates which ought to have been paid several years ago. After the matter had been dismissed for some time, Mr. Dunn promised to do all he could to get the rates collected, and the subject dropped. THE ALLEGED ALTEEATION OF A REPORT.—With refer- ence to the alleged alteration of a report by the. surveyor (Mr. . gthordered k to e abde aprlemateerd ha ey hadt e RuralG so al dn tea, or yr t h A) n after received from Mr. Goldsworth, in which he said new tloori tbye, in at once say for the information of your Authority that when they resolved to have my report printed and asked me to revise the proof that I at once made emendations in the word- ing and arrangement of the matter. I went again over all the calculations, and added appendix notes and altered the scales of the sections, dm., so as to make it as perfect as pos- sible, and in making these alterations I am most wish- ful to say I meant meant no disrespect to the Authority."— Mr. Newsome and Mr. Hall expressed the opinion that no- thing reflecting on the character of Mr.Goldsworth had been said at the last meeting, and Mr. Meadows stated that the original report had not been altered in any material way.— Mr. Leigh: The subject matter is entirely the same.—lt was afterwards decided that the question of paying Mr. Golds- worth's account for £127 for preparing the report should be cmsidered at the next meeting.

DROWNED IN A WASIIING TUB.—On Tuesday at noon, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Saddle Hotel, Westfield-street, St. Helens, on the body of a child named Martha Williamson, daughter of John Williamson, a labourer residing at 53, Eccleston-street, who was acciden- tally drowned tv falling head first into a dolly tub on the precious Friday afternoon. Jane Williamson, mother of the deceased, stated that between five and six o'clock on the Friday afternoon she saw her daughter Martha go into the hack yard to play with one or two other children. From what she was afterwards told she went into the back yard, and found her daughter head first in the dolly tub. there w quantity of soap ends in the water. The girl was not quite dead, e dead, and witness carried her into the house. Dr. I Jardine afterwards attended the girl, but notwithstanding i the girl died about ten o'clock on Sunday morning. Betsy Makin, who resides opposite Mrs. Williamson's house, de- posed that she heard last witness scream, and on running across saw Mrs. Williamson holding the child by the heels, just as she had taken it out of the tub.—The Coroner remarked that the deceased appeared to have met with her death accidentally.—The jury then returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

The corner house is occupied as a shop, and the whole premises contain an area of 993 superficial square yards or thereabouts. The premises are held and will be sold for the residue (except the last day) of a term of 999 years, created by a lease from John Ireland Blackburne, Esq. , dateo Ist November, 1872, subject to the payment of the yearly ground rent of £6 4s. thereby reserved, and to the lessees, covenants, and conditions therein contained. The property is well built, and situate outside the borough boundary, and the rates and taxes are low. For further particulars apply to the AUCTIONEER, Bewsey- street ; or Messrs. W. D. JEANS & Co., Solicitors, 27. Winwick- street. Warrington,

SATURDAY, MAY 31, 1884.

THE Liberal party in Warrington are to be congratulated upon the excellent choice they have made in Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, J.P., of Liverpool, as their candidate for the representation of the borough at the next Parliamentary election. It is not to be de- nied that the announced retirement of Mr. MCMINNIES, the present Liberal member for the borough—although the party were in a measure prepared for it—was something of a shock, and therefore disturbing to their equanimity. Mr. McMINNIEs, always ex- ceedingly popular with the Liberals, has won "golden opinions" from all sorts of men by the ability, tact, and geniality which he has displayed since he became member for War- rington; he represents success in the past, and might be looked upon as "victory organised" for the future How could it be otherwise than that there should be a pang at the thought of parting--especially under cir- cumstances of ill health which deepened the sympathy and heightened the regard of the whole constituency? Tha choice of a suc- cessor was a difficult , and delicate task to turn to; but it has been admirably accom- plished. Let the Tories say what they will about the Caucus—and they bless it as well as curse it—it is the best machinery which has yet been devised for legitimately eliciting wide-reaching and representative opinion. The popular voice named a CROSFIELD as the most suitable man to succeed Mr. McMINNIEs, and it is upon a CROSFIELD that the choice of the party has fallen. Failing Mr. JoHN CROSFIELD and Mr. JEssE COL- LINGS, the Committee did well to try another branch of the CROSFIELD family, and the result is that Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD stands before the constituency to-day as the candi- date of the Liberal party at the next electior As it was fitting that he should do so, he a dressed a well-attended meeting of the Gene:.

Council, on Wednesday evening, before a de- cision was arrived at; and it is due to him to. say that the good opinion which was formed of him, from the report which preceded hun, speeel! was increased a hundredfold by the explanatory of his views, which will be found reported at length in another co!umn% Whatever may be the unhappy position of the Conservative party in Warrington., the Liberals at any rate will have no occasion to blush for their candidate when addressing an audience. MT. CROSFIELD puts forth ne. claim to be an orator, but he is a clear an a effective speaker, impressing his hearers as a man who brings sound common-sense to. bear in the discussion of politics as the .busi- ness of Government. With the experien.c.e of a quarter of a century as an active cian, he has passed beyond his first and not yet reached "his second childishness , ' and certainly does not himself need to act on the advice which he humorously gives as t? feeding on fish as food for the brain. He is in the prime of life ; it is seen at a glane that he is instinct with vitality, mental aria physical, and he comes to Warrington offer- ing his best days in the service of the comUa m. nit)' and of the country. Mr. CROSFIELD lS man of purpose; life with him is real aria earnest; and with such a record as he hal behind him of good work in Liverpool, 10 can well believe that it will be his aim in Par- liament to show that he has at heart the, interests of the masses, not by foul votes belie fair speeches, but by lending a helPl hand to those who are toiling in season an out of season to bless their fellow-Inel'; i There s something in breed ; and we 11311,7,; therefore, the more faith in Mr. Caosrit7, in that he comes of a good stock. father earned a reputation in Warrington ° which the son may well be proud—the In°r,e, so as he has himself brightened rather ti1a.,1," tarnished it. We may trust men who 1.71, their sires have fought hard and made sacils fices for the establishment of civil and religions liberty rather than we can those " dr°,llhe of the community who feed on ~`"fee mechanic's labour ;" and make the end 01 1,1 t; the gratification of puerile vanity by the P 0 15 display of an empty title. If the Liberah of Warrington cannot win with silc„ a candidate as they have just chose,' as opposed to the Brewer of Wilderspo°,; who makes his own friends miserable wile: he opens his month, they deserve to .ve whipped with the scorpions of a blunderint representative and a plundering Governmen, But we have no fear of such a result; Liberal partythroughout the country areuult,ee in the main issues before the nation, and t'e " Two Hundred" of Warrington are, we ar.„ glad to observe, united and enthusiastic 1" their choice of Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD their champion in the coming contest. It I, no secret that he was asked some time ago t; allow his name to be brought forward as a candidate for Liverpool, for he has sustained the Liberal party there through ill all through good fortune, and it was felt that. Ded would be equal to all that might be requite., of him as the representative of a great Cu We mention this to show that Mr CaosFisL, is "ripe for the hour," and that the Liberals of Warrington, in the wise step they havted taken, have simply anticipated what won't doubtless have been the action of some atile constituency on the look-out fora represeritat- tive of recognised ability, sound judgniell and high character. Such. a man we del Mr. CROSFIELD to be, and as sucn we bespea's him a befitting welcome when he collie before a mass meeting of Liberal electors/ as he will ere long, for that ratification of file choice of the General Council which we aAre quite sure will be enthusiastically accord' "The world "Emerson says, "is upheld bi the veracity of good men," and we believe that Warrington, as a part of the world, will bef upheld in the future by the veracitY ° WILLIAM CROSFIELD. It would be perfectly fair t." retort as to what he speaks of, on his oft! side, as "the evidence of the best engineer.' ofthe world" that this better talent was perhaP'n secured by bigger bribes. There has been,: good deal of "hard swearing" on he' sides ; but this was inevitable on the thecl of the Q.C. of large experience in slic.t matters, who laid it down as an axiom -tri,4,4 "there were liars, and liars, and: witnesses." But truth " lies " somewh paradoxical as it may seem, and we trust may be found in the Manchester Ship G"ell• if not at the proverbial bottom of a w It is an ill-wind that blows nobody goe" and, apart from any consideration of tlic

RUNCORN. AND THE QUEEN,S BIRTHDAY—On Saturday, 111 honour of the Queen's birthday, flags floated from various Prominent positions in the town, and the bells ot the Parish Church sent forth a merry peal. WESLEYAN SALE OF WORK, WIDNES.—This sale of work, which was held on Thursday and Friday last week, in aid of the Albert-road Chapel, realised upwards of £llO, being Considerably above the anticipations of the promoters. RUNCORN Peatesu Cntracm—Special sermons in aid of the Additional Curate's Fund were preeched in this church °0 Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. R. Edwards, curate 'in charge of Newtown Mission Church, and in the evening I-7 the Rev. Percy Alexander, vicar of Alvanley. There were fair congregations. RLIDI RIBBON ARMY, RUNCORN.—In connection with this teetotal organisation a seryme of song entitled "Poor Mike" was rendered in Runcorn Co-operative Hall on '•eceday evening by a choir composed of members of the "Star of Temperance" Lodge of 1.0.G.T Mr. Bullivant °onducted, and the music was rendered in a yrry efTicient Unfortunately the audience was of but scant pro- Portions. MOORE WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.— The anniversary services connected with this school were held on Sunday. The Rev. Sidney Mee, of Halton, was the special preacher, afternoon and evening, the chapel being crowded at each service. The children sang special hymns, Mr. Booth being at the harmonium. The sum collected on behalf of the Bchool was £2l 18s 6J, being upwards of £4 ip advance of last year. POLICE CHANGES AT RUNCORN.—We understand that Acting Superintendent Leah, of Crewe, has been appointed late of county police at Runcorn, in place of the 'ate Superintendent Williamson. Inspector Hollingworth, who has been stationed at Runcorn for a period of nearly nfoor years, has been promoted to Mr. Leah's position at 'ewe; and he will be succ,teded at Runcorn by Inspector Atherton, of S'ockport. „Thant OF THE REF. W. W. DUKE, LATE OF RUNCORN.— death of this esteemed Wesleyan minister took place at welshpool, at his residence, on Thursday. The deceased gentleman had suffered from paralysis for several years. Re 'was superintendent of the Runcorn circuit for a period of three years, during which time he won the esteem and raiection of the members throughout the circuit. He was a ,thful and earnest preacher of the gospel, and even now e_ln Runcorn many of his quaint utterances are remem- bered and quoted by those who were once under his spiritual Charge. eSID DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.—On Saturday , -0V named Charles Garner, son of Mr. Garner, an officer , boy flamed Majesty's customs, was drowned in the Mersey. A Playmate had wheeled him in a barrow along the edge of ;JlO man's land." The barrow was left sten ling a few eet from the side, when it upset and threw Garner from the Wall into the river. As there was a rather strong tide run- ni „ ng at the time the body was washed away before any aid `°nid be obtained. The body has not been recovered. SLEEPING OUT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, John Travner, Charles Jennings, and Edward Johnson, boatmen, pleaded guilty to sleeping in the stable belonging to Mr. Samuel Crosby, provision dealer, High- street, Runcorn, early that morning.—Each prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. „ ENGLISH JOURNALISTS.—Mesers. A. and F. Pears, we proprietors of Pears' soap, have issued an interesting sheet of the leading English journalists, including those of the "Times," "Standard," "Daily News," "Punch," "Illus- trated London News," "Graphic," ice. Each portrait is shown in the centre of reduced pages of the newspaper with which it is identified, and the artistic execution of the work makes the sheet one well worthy of preservation. DISORDERLY CHARACTERS AT WlDNES.—Elihabeth Cross was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, charged with committing a breach of the peace in Beamont- street, Widnes, on Monday night. P.C. Thompson proved the case, and the prisoner was hound over to keep the peace for three months, herself in £lO, and two sureties in £5 each.—Catherine Corney, for committing a similar offence in Irwell-street, was dealt with in a similar manner. OUTEREAS Olt MEASLES AT WIDNES.—Some alarm has been caused in Widnes during the present week through the statement published in a Liverpool contemporary that there were 500 cases of measles in the town. It may be some satisfaction to know that this statement is most grossly exaggerated. That there is an outbreak of measles of a rather extended character is certain, but we are informed by reliable authority that there are not more than forty or fifty cases in the entire township, and these are generally of a mild type. During the past month about six •deaths have occurred from the disease. WHITSUNTIDE PREPARATIONS AT RUNCORN AND Win- aces—At Runcorn on Whit-Monday, about ten friendly societies will parade the town accompanied by brass bands and in the afternoon there will be a procession of scholars in cannection with the various Sunday schools. The 'fair " will be located in its usual situation. Trips by train and packet leave the town on Tuesday. The railway companies have organised special excursions from Widnes to Buxton, Southport, Blackpool, Jac, on Monday and Tuesday, while for the amusement of the children at home, merry- go-rounds are being erected on the beach near the promenade. , ROBBERY FROM WIDNES MARKET.— kt Whines Police Court, on Monday, Mary Marr was charged with stealing from a stall in the market a frock, the property of John Finn.—lt appears that Finn is a second-hand clothes dealer, and keeps a stall in the market. On Saturday night the prisoner was at the stall for a period of fifteen minutes, and after examining a great many articles went away without making a purchase. Shortly afterwards the frock, which is worth 3s. 6d., was missed. About eleven o'clock the same night P.C. Evans apprehended the prisoner at her own home, and found the frock (produced) hanging on a bed. She stated that she had purchased the article for 45., and paid 2s. as a deposit, but she now pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to a month's hard labour. THE FOREIGN IRON TRADE.—There has been no great changes in the iron markets of the C ntinent since our last report. The state of the Belgian iron trade continues dis- couraging. The iron markets of France are gaining in strength, owing partly to the action of the ironmasters of the Nord in raising their quotations, referred to last week, partly to the settlement of matters with China, partly be the large orders for locomotives given out by the iailway com- panies. The improvement in the German iron market noted in our last impression is maintained. The American iron market is quiet. Scotch pig iron is dull at New York, with prices nominally unchanged. American anthracite pig No. lis scarce and firmer, and No. 2 steady. Bar iron is stiffer in anticipation of a strike of mill operatives on June 1, against a proposed reduction of 10 per cent.—lron. TRESPASSERS AT WlDNES.—William Cairo% Patrick Stevens, John Rogers, P itrick Foy, and Charles Matthews, young men, were brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, charged with trespassing upon the land of Mr. Peter Longton.—Mr. Knowles prosecuted, and said Mr. Longton occupied a farm in Mdton-road. During the past twelve months Mr. Lonetot had bad a considerable amount of damage done to hie fields by people making a road over them from Appleton village, near the Cross Keys Hotel, to the Widnes police station, and new fences and deep ditches and a notice board had been of no avail in stopping the trespassers. Mr. Longton had been obliged tn ask for the assistance of the police, and on the 19th inst. P.C. Almond took the names of the defendants as they crossed the land. —P.C. Almond proved the trespass, and Mr. Walter Longton stated the damage to be a penny each.—Each defendant was fined 103, including costs. A STREET SINGER IN TROUBLE AT WIDNES —At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. G. Pilkingten, an elderly man named Joseph Robinson was brought up in custody charged with being drunk.—P.C. Holbrook said at a quarter-past eight o'clock on Monday night the prisoner was drunk and disorderly in Victoria-road. He had cau- tioned the prisoner before, and ordered him away.—The prisoner: Me drunk !—Witness : Yes —The prisener : I was singing "Jesus, lover of my soul," and a gentleman came up and "gen" you in charge with me.—P.S. Clarkson said the prisoner was singing and waving his arms, and he was ordered to go away by Inepector Wood, but be refused, and they were obliged to lock him up.—lnspector Wood corro- borated. The prisoner was pretending to sing, but nobody could tell what he was singing. At one time he said, "I want a bit of bread only," and he (the inspector) ordered him off as a bagger. He was certainly drunk.—Mr. Pilking- ton: You are fined 5s and costs.—The prisoner: You never saw me in a public house in yourllife.—Mr. Lewin: You mast go to gaol for seven days if you cannot pay. ON PR! MISES FOR AN UNLAWFUL PURPOSE AT RITNCORN. —At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr.l James Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies, Peter Rogers, a young man, was brought up in custody charged with being on the enclosed premises of Mr. R. Roberts, draper, Bridge- street, Runcorn, for an unlawful purpose, and also with assaulting P.C. Bason.—Evidence was given by a domestic servant named Elizabeth Owen that at midnight on Saturday she beard some one trying to unfasten the window from the yard. A policeman was sent for, and P.C. Baeon entered the yard, where he encountered the prisoner. Rogers struck at the officer with a broom, and as he refused to leave the yard he seized him, and a struggle took place. Ultimately Barn got the man opposite the police station, and with the assistance of P.C. Smith he was locked up. Whilst being searched prisoner struck Bason two violent blows in the stoma? h.--There were several previous convictions against the prisoner, and he was committed to gaol on the first charge for three months with bard Labour, and for assaulting the constable he Was ordered to he imprisoned for a month, with hard labour.

TIE REPRESENTATION 01 MID AND WEST CRESEIRE Two of the sitting Conservative members for the divisions of Mid and West Cheshire retire at the next general election, and do not again offer themselves—namely, Mr. Piers Eger- ton Warburton (Mid-Cheshire) and the lion. W. F. Tolle- mache (West Cheshire). Preparations are being made by the Liberal party,with a view to securing not only the vacan- cies, but to return two Liberals for each division. The selection of Mr. 3.5. Leadam and Mr. Thomas Rigby to contest the mid division has been received with a great deal of favour. Both gentlemen are well-known locally, and are likely to make a good fight. The constituency com- prises a large number of agriculturists, and Mr.ltigby,whose services in connection with the Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural Society and the Cheshire Chamber of Agri- culture have rendered him very popular, may be expected to carry the whole of these with him. The Liberal candi- dates will be opposed by Mr. Alan Tatton Egerton, one of the present members, and Mr. John Brooke, a Conservative. In the West Division Mr. Henry Tollemache. M.P., and Captain Cotton will be opposed by Mr. Tornkinson and Mr. David Duncan, the Liberal candidates. ADULTERATION <)lf SPLEITS AT WIDNES.-At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Gibbons, landlord of the Wellington Inn, Ditton, was charged with selling whis- key which was not of the nature and substance demanded. —lnspector Wood said on the 6th May he purchased a. pint and half a pint of whiskey, for the purpose of analysis, at the defendant's house. He paid 33 for it.—Supt. Barker said the public analyst certified that the whiskey was 30 per cent, under proof, being 5 per cent. weaker than was allowed by the Amendment Act.—Defendant said he put one quart of water to a gallon of prooof spirits, according to the instructions of the spirit merchant—Superinteudent Barker observed that publicans could test their spirits each day if they wished. If they water their spirits it means profit.—Mr. Brock: If they sell water for whiskey it is all profit.—A fine of 40s and costs £1 was imposef.--Jobn Ashley, keeper of the Crown Inn, Birchfield--oad, was sum- moned to answer a charge of selling adulterated rum.—On the 6th May Inspector Wood purchased a pint and a half of rum from the defendant's wife, and paid 33 for it. The public analyst certified that the spirit was 30 per cent under proof, or 5 per cent. weaker than was allowed by the Amendment Ad.—Defendant was fined £2 and costa ,£l.
