div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 31. 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 31. 1884.

A RUNCORN CONTICT.—At Runcorn Police Court, yester- day, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Cap:ain C. W. Haztehuret, William Poever, farm labourer, Halton, a returned convict, was charged with failing to report his change of residence, as required by the Prevention of Crime Act. 1871.—The Bench ordered the license to be forfeited, and committed the prisoner to gaol to serve the unexpired five months of his sentence. A VIOLENT PRISONER AT WlDNES.—William Egan was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly.—P.C. Davie stated that on Saturday he was on duty in Ann-street, when he saw the prisoner turned out of a hedging-house. His eyes were in- jured, and his face was besmeared with blood. In conse- quence of his violent conduct he (witness) locked the pri- soner up. The prisoner damaged the cell.—The prisoner accused three constables of assaulting him, but this was denied, and the prisoner was fined 59. and costs. AppLETON RECREATION GROUNDS, WIDNES. On Saturday afternoon there was decided, at the above grounds, the match between James Cencannon, of Widnes, and Alexander Clark, of Glasgow. The match was origin- ally, made for £2O aside, Clark to concede 60 yards start in one mile hut subeeqnently Mr. Mellor laid Concaunon's backer £:3O to £2O, and thus the amount of stakes was raised to £9O. Slowly, but surely, Concannon drew away in the I race, and he eventually won by at least 15 yards. Mr. T. R. Allison, of Manchester, officiated as referee, and Mr. W. H. Fowler, the proprietor of the grounds, as starter. DAMAGING GAS LAMPS AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Hill, a boy, was charged with wilfully damagiuga gas lamp belonging to the Widnes Local Local Board, on the 27th April.—Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. J. I'. Allen, clerk to the Board, prosecuted, and stated that he was instructed to bring the case before the Bench because there had been much damage done to the gas lamps in the town. They had something like 400 lamps in the district and they were constantly being broken. It was very seldom they were able to trace the person who did the damage, but he thought he should be able to clearly prove it in this case. He called David Hatton, of Dock-street. who deposed that on the evening of the day in question a number of Irish boys and English boys were fighting in the streets. The Irish boys were standing near the lamp, and the Englsh boys were throwing stones at them. The defen- dant sent a stone which struck the lamp and smashed it.— Mr. Carr, the manager of the gas works, stated that 2s had been expended in repairing the lamp.—Mr. Allen said the case had been brought as a warning, and if the defendant would pay the costs be would agree to withdrawal of the summons.—The defendant promised to pay the costs, 15s, and the Bench dismissed the case, Mr. Brock observing that the magistrates were bound to put a stop to each practices, and any fresh offender would be severely punished. TUE BRUTAL OUTRAGE BY A CAPTAIN AT RUNCORN.—At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mews. James Reynolds and G. L. Davies, Michael Murphy, mister of the schooner Eclipse, of Fleetwood, was brought up on remand charged with unlawfully and maliciously causing grievous bodily harm to William Stringer, 29, Lower Port- land-street, with intent to disable him —The facts of the case were gird c in last Siturday'e Examieer.—Evidence was given by Win. Hardley to the effect that he was at the Darwell's Vaults on Saturday, the 17th inst., and saw the prisoner seize Stringer by the shoulders and throw him over his head against the wall. He was picked up in an uncon- scious state, and had to be wheeled home in a barrew.—Dr. Bagnall stated that the injured man was still paralysed from the effects of the prisoner's violence, and was still unable to appear.—Mrs. Bradburn, of Darwell's Vaults, stated that there was DO quarrel going on in the house, and that the prisoner was very kind to Stringer.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Edmondson, solicitor, of Fleetwood, who represented prisoner Hardley, said that the prisoner was talking about wrestling, and was showing them how it was done, and Murphy did not think that he bad hart Stringer.—Mr. Edmondson held that there had been no felonious intent proved, and applied for the prisoner's release on bail until the ease could,be thoroughly gone into.—The Bench refused the application, and remanded the prisoner until to-day (Saturday). ASSAULTS AT Wrreeus.—On Wednesday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, Mary eullivan was summoned for assaulting Mary Rosevere, an elderly woman.—lt was alleged that on Saturday night. the 24th instant, Mrs. Rosevere and her husband were returning home from the market, when, as they were passing the defendant's house, the defendant rushed into the street and struck her on the temple. She gave her no provocation whatever. Later in the evening Mrs. Rosevere was again passing the house, when tbe de- fendant struck her on the mouth..—Several witnesses cor- roborated this statement, and Superintendent Barker said the defendant had been several times convicted of assaults, and there was now a commitment against her for an offence committed in 1873.—Mr. Brock said the Bench felt bound to enforce the commitment. She would therefore be fined 5s and costs, or days for the present offence, and goto gaol for a month on the commitment.--Mary Jane Widders sum- I moned Charlotte Coombes for assaulting her on the 24th May.—Conaplainant said the defendant wed very had lan- I pelage to her. And after pushing her twice, struck her on the breast—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed--Cor- nelius Starkee, a young man, was summoned for assault. ing Mary Al ularkey, a married woman, living in Widnes.— Complainant alleged that on the 24th inst she entered Mr. Quinn's public-house to see her brother-in-law. The de- fendant followed, and "making a dart at her," seized her by the dress and threatened to murder her.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the defendant, cross-examined witness, who stated the defendant pushed her.—Several witnesses were called, and the defendant was fined Sc and costs. AN ILLMATcrIED PAIR AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Kenny, John Broxton, and Elizabeth Broxton were summoned to answer a charge of committing a breach of the peace.—P.C. Moores stated that on Sunday the 18th instant, about half-past three, Broxton and his wife were shouting, cursing, and fighting with each other in Warrington-road, Widnes. Kenny was standing amongst a crowd of persons, at length he went to Broxton and struck him two or three blows on the mouth with his fist. —Mrs. Broxton said her husband had not lived with her for eight weeks. She did not wish to have any- thing to do with him. She wished to get her own livieg in an honest way. On Sunday afternoon her husband came into the house, knocked her to the ground, and knelt upon her chest, and pulled nearly all the hair off her head. Kenny was passing the house at the time, and he protected her when she shouted " murder." If he had not done so she did not know what would have been the consequence. She did not call murder until she was fainting from loss of blood.—Broxton said his wife spent all the money be gave her in drink. Every day for three weeks i the last month she had been drunk, and when he came home from his work he could not get anything to eat.—The constable was re-called, and said he knew that Broxton had been teetotal for two years. He had heard Mrs. Broxton complain that her husband did not give her any money.—Mr. Brock: Have you seen Mrs. Broxton drunk ?--Witness: Yes.—The Bench bound Mrs. Broxton over to keep the peace for three menthe, herself in £lO and one surety in £5. Broxton was ordered to be bound over for a similar period, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each. Kenny was discharged. SAVAGE ASSAULT AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, .junr., Thomas Noon, an intelligent-looking man, who lives an Hope-street, Widnes, was brought up on remand charged with unlawfally wounding John McConachy, of 71, Church-street—The pro- secutor said he was foreman at No. I works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., and the prisoner was a labourer under the same employers. On Saturday afternoon there was a fire in No. 2 works, and himself, the prisoner and others, were engaged assisting to put it out. The prisoner was work- ing at the pumping engine. During the afternoon he (wit- ness) supplied the prisoner and other men with a pint of beer each. The prisoner asked him for some more beer, but he gave him some tobacco, and promised to him another pint of beer in an hour's time. Shortly aW• eight o'clock he was standing near the fire when the prisoner came behind him. He asked him ,what he was doing there, and he said what had that got to do with him. He (witness) ordered the prisoner to his work, but he replied that he had as good a right there as him (witnees.) He put his band loosely upon the prisoner's shoulder, and the prisoner slipped on the Staves. He slipped also. The prisoner on rising said "I will cut the head off you," and he (witness) replied come along then, and got hold of his arm to take him to his work. He had no sooner done so than he got a blow on the right cheek with a wooden stave similar to the one produced. The prisoner was the person who struck him. He got the prisoner down, and held him until the witness Betney took him off. He was blind with blood from a wound and he lost a great quantity of blood. Hie left arm was black through guarding a second blow which would have struck him somewhere about the face. Betney wrap- ped his head up and took him to DT. McLennan's surgery, where the wound was dressed. He gave the prisoner no provocation. He was sober. The prisoner was net drunk and knew what be was doing.—William Betney, a cooper at ' Messrs. Hutclainsons works, living at 10, Lord-street, Run- corn, deposed that the prosecutor pushed the prisoner several ' times, and gave other corroborative evidence. After being cautioned by the magistrate, the prisoner alleged that the prosecutor pushed him down twice and knocked him %down twice before he struck him.—The prisoner was committed to Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial, but was admitted to bail, himself in £4O and two sureties of £2O.
wickedness and vice and of preserving that good law and order which was absolutely necessary for the well biing of the public at large it would be impossible to find a better man. -
- The remarks he had _made embraced, he was sure,

the feelings of the whole of the magistrates. and he was sure they joined with him is sending a cordial vote of sympathy with the widow and children who had suffered by his death an irreparable lofts. Mr. A. E. Linaker, on behalf of the solicitors practicing in the Court, said he had to offer his sincerest sympathy with Mrs. Williamson in her bereavement. He was sorry
that an older member of the profession vras.not in Court to
rcply, bat as the chairman had mentioned it, he felt it to be his duty to reply. Since Mr. Williamson had been .at Runcorn he bad been found very fair in discharging his duties.
lie was courteous, and to a very great: degree
obliging, and be only hoped that they would be able to se- cure as good a man in the future. He begged to second Mr. Reynolds' suggestion that they offered a vote of condo- lence to Mrs. Williamson.
The remains of the late Superintendent Williamson were interred at the Runcorn cemetery on Monday afternoon. . .

About an hour previous to the time fixed for the funeral cortege to leave the police station, half-past two, a large number of people had assembled in front of the building, and in various parts of the thoroughfare, through which the procession would have to pass. The shops in the vicinity were closed. At the head of the procession walked the fol- lowing gentlemen :—Messrs. H. Hankinson, J. L. Jones, Wm. Sutton, W. Brookes, M. Barker, T. Jones, Charles Dutton, Thomas Price, Thomas Cliff, H. Jackson, W. Croley, Wm. Ward, William Blythe, J. Beesley, T. Capper, E. Cootie, T. Blease, S. Spann, C. W. Phillips:(Daresbary), William Chad- wick, James Ditcbfield, William Baker (Rock Savage), T. Hotsefield, W. Cunningham. Next in order were the following members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Free and ac- cepted Masons, each wearing a sprig of acacia .—Messrs. E. Marwood, WM. ; T. D. Timmins, J. J. Waterwortb, L. Rosenberg, T. Wright. T. H. Hitchen (Secretary to the Bridgewater Chapter), F. A. Lake, 1.G., J. H. Salkeld (Secretary), J. S. Davies, T. Houghton (tyler), Lewis Thomas, Richard Oldbury, S.W. ; Wm. Mellor, P.M.; Cap- tain Le Couteur ; A. Buck, P.M.; George Moss, P.M.; W. R. Wass, P.M.; R. Rigby, P.P.G J.D.; and Revs J. Lock- wood (chaplain) and R. Edwards (curate in charge of New- town Mission Church). Then came the hearse containing the body of the deceased, followed by Mr. A. Williamson • '
Deputy Clerk: The salaries of the schoolmaster and school- mistreszt are paid by Government as well.—The discussion then ceased. There was no other business of public im- portance.

div.head: LATE SUPERINTRNDENT WILLIAMSON, OF
div.p: THE LATE SUPERINTRNDENT WILLIAMSON, OF
RUNCORN: MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE AND FUNERAL.

Before commencing the ordinary business of the Court at the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, the presiding magistrate (Mr. James Reynolds) said he had the painful duty to make known the almost sudden and early death of Mr. Williamson. He wished that someone who had been longer a member of that bench had been present to discharge that duty, but he might say that daring the whole of the time he had sat in that Court he had found Mr. Williamson fully up to the duties which he had to perform, and his courtesy and general kindness of manner endeared him to all who were acquainted with him. In his early life he was at Crewe, where he won considerable esteem among the inhabitants, and when he left he had a substantial memento given to him that he had discharged his duties faithfully and with good effect. After that he was moved to Chester to an advanced position, and while in a new branch of the office he showed an adaptability for the particular branch of werk under his care that the authorities said they had in him a very valuable servant and one that was sere to ob- tain promotion. Time was not long before there was a vacancy at Runcorn, tend he was appointed superintendent of police at Runcorn, sorne six years ago. That office he held up to the last and he had tilled it with very consider- able ability. He would not say that it would be impossible to fill his place with so gaud or a better man, but this he would say, that in the quality ha possessed of restraining

div.head: DISASTROUS FIRE AT WIDNES.
div.p: DISASTROUS FIRE AT WIDNES.

On Saturday afternoon a serious fife broke out at the cooperage yard at Messrs. Hutchinson and bon's chemical works. Widnes, which resulted in the destruction of con- siderable property. About two o'clock a woman named Clare, who lives in John-street, observed flames issuing from a sheitin the yard, and she immediately raised an alarm. In the yard were piled several hundred thousand stools used in the making of casks, which were in piles of about nine feet high. One by one these piles caught fire, and by the time the works engine could be brought into play the flames had obtained good hold of several piles, which they enveloped in a fierce, lurid sheet. The eftorts of the men I were at first directed towards preventing the spread of the fire to the houses in John-street, which overlook the yard, but in this they were only rewarded with partial success. Before a hose could be connected at this point a shed near the houses had caught fire, and it was quickly burned down. Then the element set on fire the stable of Mr. Atherton, but before it had proceeded far the hose was attached, and a stream of water soon extinguished the flames. So tierce was the heat, however, that the woodwork on the houses in Johc-street was scorched, and the occupants hurriedly began to remove their furniture. Thus 16 houses were emptied amid the greatest excitement. The heat in the houses was intense, and the work was rendered still more dangerous by the clouds of smoke which filled the rooms. Besides the hose from the works engine, a pipe was attached to the main in Mersey-road, while a third had connection with a hydrant in the works of Messrs. Grossage and Son. The un- touched piles of timber were removed in order to prevent the spread of the fire towards the works of the firm. The adjoin- ing buildings are stored with rail mai tallow, and if once seized by the tire nothing could have checked an immense confl tgration. The fire continued burning amongst the timber until past. midnight, and the damage done is esti- mated at about £1,500, which is covered by insurance in the Metual Insurance Society. The fire is supposed to have originated through boys smoking in one of tile sheds in the yard, and throwing down lighted matches. Inspector Wood, with several officers, was on the scene of the fire, and rendered good service in the work of saving pro- perty.

The whole costs of the deputation, legal charges, &c., was .£l2B 12s 4d, and the bill had been taxed by the Clerk of the Peace at Cheater.—Mr. Aaron: That is money well spent —Mr. Linaker Our Engineer tells us that if they have to provide a new scheme it will cost them nearly £lO,OOO. AN EPIDEMIC OF TYPHOID FEVER. The Rev. J. Lockwood observed that he had been in- formed that there were four cases of typhus fever and three of typhoid fever at Sutton, and he asked if there was any report from the medical officer.—An intimation was given in the negative.—The Rev. J. Lockwood: Seven cases of fever in one little village, and yet no report from the in- spector or • medical officer.—lnspector Farrington said he was at Sutton on Tuesdny last, and he heard of these cases. he sent a report to the medical officer of health, and on Friday afternoon Dr. Adams inspected the case of Johnson, who lives,at Sutton Weaver station. The case was repre- sented to him verbally as typhus, but the doctor said it was a specific case of typhoid.—The Rev. J. Lockwood said Mr. J. 0. Jackson, of The Cedars, Sutton, had told him and the chairman that morning that there were four cases of typhus and three of typhoid fever. The names of the patients were Cawley, Taylor, Leach, Howard, Egerton, Johnson, and Mrs. Jackson. Mrs. Jackson was attended by Dr. Daly, of Chester, and her own medical attendant, Dr. Robinson, of Runcorn. There was no doubt there was quite an epi- demic.—The Inspector said Taylor was suffering from typhoid, but he was convalescent now.—Mr. Aaron thought it very wrong that the doctor had not made a report on the matter.—lnspector Farrington said he had reported the matter to Dr. Adams, and he had expected him to visit Sutton that morning. There was a little bit more made of this outbreak than what was really substantial. From in- formation he had received he understood that Dr. Robinson, of Runcorn, had made certain statements about the drainage if Sutton. He should like such a gentleman as Dr. Robin- son to be more particular in his statements, because the assertions he made were of a kind to affect the position of the Authority. When there was the outbreak of scarlet fever at Weston he told Mr. W. Banks, the magistrate, that there were no less than three hundred cases of scarlet fever at Weston and Runcorn. The statement got into the newspapers, and then Dr. Robinson repudiated the thing altogether. He should be careful about making these assertions. Mr. Banks told him (Mr. Farrington) and he thought Mr. Bankes as reliable as Dr. Robinson. But re- ferring to the subject under consideration. Mrs. Aston the other day told him that a medical man (who could only be Dr. Robinson), had said that there was not a worse drained place in Cheshire than Sutton. He denied that most em- phatically. Sutton was not badly drained. There was a good culvert, about two feet six inches. running through the village, and it took all the drainage. There was a little mat- ter or two that wanted some attention with respect to the main sewer, but they were not matters that would produce typhoid fever. He had received a letter from Mr. J. 0. IJackson who stated that the public pump at Sutton had been ; out of order sometime and that he should be glkd if Mr. I Farrington would have it put right. There were many people drinking impure water in consequence, and it was also s. great inconvenience to them. He feared this was the cause of the fever being about them so long. He (Mr. Farrington) received that letter on the 17th May, and the primp was re- paired on the 21st. It was now in working order. Dr. Robin- son, of Frodsham, bad intimated that these cases of fever had arisen from drinking the water supply of a certain pump in Sutton village belonging tie Phillip Taylor. All the people had been in the habit of using that water pre- , vious to the public pump being out of order. To set the matter at rest he would have a full report on the drainage of Sutton, and he should advise that the water at the public pump and Taylor's pump be submitted for analysis. He must say again that Dr. Robinson when he made assertions very annoying and very startling to the public, ought to be prepared to prove them. He (Mr. Farrington) knew that Dr. Robinson knew no more about the drainage of Sutton than that book (striking a book on the table.) In reply to a question, Mr. Farrington said Mr. Jackson stated a medical man, and the medical man was Dr. Robinson attending on Mrs. Jackson and other cases.— Dr. Adams, the medical officer of health, and Dr. Robinson, medical officer to the house, then entered the room.—Dr. Adams said he had no report about Sutton. He had pre- paced a special report on the case of Mr. Johnson at Sutton Weaver, but that morning Mr. Farrington notified an out- break in several other families, and be thought it best to give a report as a Whole because the cases must have a con- nection, fle was on his way to Sutton that afternoon, and he thcught he would call and let the Board know.—The Chairman said in a matter of this sort it was well that some- thing should be done at once. I was like an epidemic.— Dr. Robinson said all the cases at Sutton were typhoid fever. —The Chairman: Not typhus.—Dr. Robinson : No. He added that the pump opposite Mr. Jackson's house had been out of order about three weeks, and was only put in repair last Wednesday. Well, the people had been getting water during that time from a parno where Taylor lived. Close to this pump was a grid, and although Mrs. Taylor said the carried her slops to the midien, which was six or seven yards away, there was no doubt she rinsed her various utensils at the grid. All the people at Sutton had got water from that pump because the other pump was out of order. Taylor was first affected with the disease on the 27th April.—Dr. Adams said it would be the duty of the Board to prevent any further consumption of that water.— The Chairman : Better have it analysed to see if it is had. —Dr. Adams said they might have the water reeking with the germs of typhoid fever, and yet not contain sufficient organic matter to shew it as a bad water on analysis.—ln- spector Farrington said the people fetched water from both pumps when they were both in order. Some preferred one and some the other.—Mr. Weir moved, and Mr. Derbyshire seconded a motion that the water at Taylor's well be an of lysed.—Cirried.—Dr. Adams said at the next meeting .l the Authority he should be prepared to give a report on the whole outbreak.—lt was understood that in the meant orne Dr. Adams and Mr. Farrington should take all necees steps for preventing the spread of the disease.

div.p: otl Ft LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

. - - - I happened to be in the House of Lords on the night, six years ago, when Lord Salisbury was questioned with respect to the Secret Treaty, the existence of which Mr. Charles Marvin had just inconveniently disclosed in the columns of the Mat. "I: was," the marquis said with indignant re- buke, intended for his unpatriotic interrogator " not authentic." To the young and ingenuous mind this settled the matter. It was impossible ID believe that a statesman of historic name should in the most public place in the world tell a deliberate lie, especially when there seemed scarcely any doubt that the discloser of the secret was in a position to verify his statement. I was in the House again on Tues- day last, when Lord Salisbury, speaking from the other side' raising his voice to terrible tones, and scowling upon the j Foreign Secretary, demanded that Parliament should be i taken into the full confidence of Ministers even in respect of a delicate matter of foreign affairs still being negotiated. There is nothing prettier in the House of Lords than, Lord Granville's manner with the Leader of the Opposition unless it be the Muquis of Salisbury's attitude towards Earl Granville. On Tuesday, Lord Salisbury was not good. He was playing a part simulating indignation, and rather over did it; but Earl Granville was delightful at no time more than when with eyebrows slightly raivid and on air of genuine surprise upon his fees he observed, " I have listened to the noble marquis with astoniehrnent at his courage in declaring what ainanut of opeuness is necersary in Parliament before entering into iinpertatr, negotiations." That was all he said ; but it brought back to every mind the Secret Treaty of 1878, its startling disclosure, and the lying and wriggling to which a British Minister stooped in desperate effort to deny it.

This whole scene in the House of Lords WAS as cartfully and deliberately planned as if it had been a charade. In both HOUSES a statement had been made which went un- expectedly far towards easing the mind of the Opposition. They say—having for the moment dropped General Gordon --that the Government are going into Conference on the Egyptian question with the intavion to despoil this country of the advantages it may have purchased by its military oc- cupation of Egypt. Lord Salisbury on Tuesday night went into remarkably full details on the subject. The Govern- ment had decided upon a course which " woald stain the honour and affect the position of England for years to come." "It will smite us with a weakness equal to that of a great defeat," and so on. Admitting this absurd talk, which is really not worth serious denial, there remains the fact that Mr. Gladstone in one House and Earl Granville in the other, announced that before England went into Conference the Government would communicate to Parliament the re- sult of the negotiations now going forward with France. Therefore, supposing all that Lord Salisbury's vivid imagi- nation pictures be true, Parliament will have an op- portunity of saying "no," and there will be an end alike of the thsbonour and thie wicked Ministry.

This was acknowledged in the House of Commons where a projected debate was postponed, there being from all shades.of opinion a frank admission that the Government had fully met their desire. Lord Salisbury happened to be in a fighting mood, and bearing of what had taken place in the Comm-ns, be fretted And fumed and declared that a splendid opportunity had been thrown away. This he de- termined to make up in the Lords, and the outbreak which followed upon Earl Granville's statement was as deliber- ately prepared as are the proceedings of the gang of hired loafers who go about London interrupting meetings of the Municial Reformers. It is not a creditable proceeding from any point of view. But for Lord Salisbury, of all men in the world, to affect indignation because, as he, with charac- tenstic unveracity, says the Government are hiding things from Parliament, is enough to take one's breath away.

I The Academy is still too densely crowded for full oppor- tunity to view the pictures in comfort. The general opinion, truly expressed, I think, is that on the whole the Exhibi- tion is not up to some that have gone before it. Neverthe- less everyone must see it, and everyone goes. For those , who cainot go, and still more for those who can, Mr. Henry Blackburn's "Academy Notes" is an indispensable com- panion. It is much more convenient and handy than the official catalogue, and half an hour's preliminary study will I save hours wasted in looking round for pictures. For those r who cannot go or are deferring their visit the Notes give an excellent idea of the show, as they contain over a hundred and fifty illustrations, the greater part of them being fac similes from sketches by the artists. As for the Academy itself, there is rising over it a ()loud at present no bigger than a man's hand, but which may have disastrous consequences. There is more in what Sir Robert Peel says on the subject than people are inclined to accept from such a reckless authority. Amongst other things there is a good deal of talk about the disposition of the Chantry Bequest, which is not silenced by the purchase of this year. It is alleged the fund is not used primarily for the encouragement of art, but for the enrichment of Royal Academicians. It is added that instead of disposing of the fixed uum every year its dispensors "save it up," and when it reaches what they regard as an adequate sum they buy one of their own pictures with it. Mr.Pettie's "Vigil' is undoubtedly a fine picture; but perhaps it would have been better if it had found a purchaser other than the body of which he is a distinguished member.

It was an odd coincidence, perhaps not altogether acci- dental, that the great commercial crisis in America should have burst forth when Mr. Vanderbilt was on the sea. This great man has a curious way of taking his pleasure. Once or twice a year he hires the best state cabin on board an atlantic steamer and sets off for England, stays there a week or so, and goes back like a giant refreshed. Last autumn he arrived in Liverpool on Saturday, and went back on the Thursday following. The richer son of a rich father, his wealth is positively fabulous, and is now being engaged in steadying the disturbance in the American market. Father aid sou live as neighbours in a massive brown stone man- sion on Fifth Avenue. It is a double house, each family h,ving its own residence, but with connections between which allow the heuses on occasion to be thrown into one. Mr. Vanderbilt is one of a group of Americans whose per- sonal wealth exceeds that of anything that can be done in the Older World. He has the advantage of being in the second generation. Some others, especially the San Fran- cisco men, are of the first, and prominently carry about them reminiscences of the manner which became thfam when they were working millers or kept a small grocery store. In San Francisco, I had the honour of dining with a man who lives in a palatial residence, whose property would realise in the market eeven millions sterling, who began life as a lad in the mine, and who married a washerwoman. These things are net talked of now, at least not in the house on the hill. But San Francisco recalls thorn with pride, and 1 is pleased to relate them in the ears of a stranger. One distinct disadvantage which a Liberal Ministry labours under as compared with a Conservative, is that the course of its legislation constantly makes for it enemies. The explanation of the bitter personal hatred cherished for Mr. latadstone is that all his life, and more particularly during the last 25 years, be has been attacking vested interests, whieh is generally another name for encrusted injustice. A Government bent upon leaving things better than they find them cannot help on one point or other upsetting the calcu- lations and arrangements of monied men.. At the present time the artificial political furore which is maintained in London against the policy in Egypt, rinds its explanation on the Stock Exchange and in its wide ramifications throughout society. The great friend of the stock-jobber was the late Mr. Disraeli. Nobody could tell from day to day what he would do or what he migkt not do. The con- ecquence was that the air was full of rumours, stocks went up or down, fortunes were made by some, and brokerages were earned by maii• Mr. Gladstone's Government is not good for the Stock Exchange. They do not embark noon hazardous pursuit of glory, nor do they make secreteeeartPireisz,et9hien indviasclosure of which brings mad ex. citement into the market. When a man goes into court he can- not make things comfortable for himself, leaving the court without a stain on his character and in his ' t f ren o to fifteen shillings in the pound Poe" "- f his creditors 1` PIO,V. Bankruptcy therefore has gone out f h c tin 0 fashion. with . set class of traders, and the occupation of solicitors and aCCOII n- tants is curta4ed accordingly. It is urged by the aggrieved ' classes that the average is made up by arrangements made out of cc,art. If that be so, which I very much doubt, it is again to the advantage of the creditors. They now b.ild

Rather than do that the manag- ing, not to say fraudulent debtor, would mah:! considerable sacrifice, dividing with his creditors much more of their iown money then he originally intended to do. What ix thought of the'Bankruptcy Act by the class against which it is chiefly directed is shown by the extraordinary rush made to benefit by the old law on the eve of the introduction of the new one. .

Students and connoisseurs who wish to study some of the freaks of the French school of painting, and learn from it what to avoid and what to admire, would do well to visit the Dudley Gallery, where are now being exhi- bited about sixty pictures by a group of fatisian artists. While looking at same of these curious produe- tions, one cannot help sympathising with Mr. Ruskin, who, I believe, looks upon " impressionist " tendencies as the very acme of all that is dangerous in art. Mr. Whistler, on the other hand, would doubtless delight in these examples of haste, as he delights to imitate them. He would End hero not only landscapes and trees that are" a puzzle to the botanist "—which according to his latest theory is one of the definition.; of a masterpiece—but also boats and ships that would be a puzzle to to the ship builder, and figures that would make the anatomist gad. There is really something to learn, though, in the c!eyer photographis dexterity with which M. de .Nittis seizes momentary attitudes. The three works which he exhibits are drawn in paste—not a happy medium as far as colour is concerned. In the scenes represented people are looking on at races. One wet-weather picture called "in the Tribune," might also be called "a study of umbrel- las." Along a lawn, below the chief group in the fore. ground, stand crowds of people of whom nought is visible but dripping umbrellas. Other notable contents of the gallery are M. Henri Gervex's "The first communion at l'Eglise de la Trinite," a large picture occupying a central place; M. Bonnet's "Portrait of Victor Hugo " sitting with one hand to his head, and his arm resting on a book, a care- ful portrait not of the impressionist style: M. Barau's large crude, depressing landscapes and several paintings of Rochelle by Marie Flamang, Which might have been more pleasing if they had been less scattered-looking and puzzling Six contributions by M. Charnay stand apart from the others as being excellent little works, highly finished, and still are not in the least laboured.

Mr. Hootley McCarthy has had a happy thought in writing a history of "England under Gladstone." The iveord covers only four years from 1880 to 1884, but it makes a stout and closely-printed volume written in clear and vivacious style. The volume practically forms a con- tinuation of Mr. Justin McCarthy's " History of Our Own Times," bringing the record up to so recent a date that the death of Henry Byron is' noted. It is instructive, and in some sense astonishing, when reading this volume to recall bow much has happened since 1880. and to be reminded of how much one has forgotten. A full index cempletes the value ot the book:
UNDENIABLE FACT.

0I& CURT. SATURDAY —Befere Alderman Burgess. B.EG&M.—Samuel Hu:se was charged with having been begging in Bold-street on the prey ous evening.—lt was stated by a police officer that the prisoner first asked for alms, but when refused pulled some tracts out of his pocket and offered to sell them. It was further stated that hitherto Hulse had lived respectably, and on promising to leave the town he was discharged. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the chair, Mr. John Fairclough, and Alderman Davies. BEGGING.—Edward Bradbury, charged with begging °Li Saturday evening, was allowed to go on promising to leave the town. Dmatizicists.—Wm. Fitzgerald, charged with being drunk in Church-atreet, was dismis,ed on payment of costs.—A young woman named Loftus, an old offender, was fined 108 and costs, or 14 days, for being drunk and disorderly in B .ttei market- street on Saturday.—Htoter Ann Harrison, who said ohs came from Ashton-under-Lyne, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-strees on Saturday evening. Not having been preciously convicted she was only fined is includ- ing costs.—Mary Flannery, for committing a similar °Hulce in Scotland-road, at midnight on Saturday, was also fined 5s in- eluding casts.—Michael Foley, charged with being drunk and disorderly in St. James's-street, on the 17th May, was ordered to pay the costs.—Luke Tulley was fined 5s acid Bs costs, or 7 days.for being drunk and disorderly in St. James's-street, on the 17th hist —Joseph Bibby, tor being drunk on the 20th inst, was fined 10s and costs. or 14 days. A WIFE DESERTER —Wm, Fearney, a labourer, was charged with leaving his two children chargeable to the Warrington Union, and also with having assaulted his wife. The prisoner deserted his wife and family on the 3rd of April. and the Children have been eh .rgeable ever since.--For that offence he was committed for two months' hard labour, the case of as- sault being adjourned as the wife was n A, present. POACHING.—Two yonng men, named Lewis Losh and James Crank, were charged with having trespassed on land in the occupation of Thomas Wall. at Acton Grange, in search of game, on the 11th instant.—Mr. Buckley, a gamekeeper, said that on the day in question he saw the defendants in a field with three dogs. One of them slipped one of the dogs after a hare. He went up to them and asked what they were doing there, when they replied that they had come to "have a bit of sport."—They were each fined 2s. 6,3 and costs; er, in default of payment, seven days' imprisonment.

He told them they were trespassing, and called their attention to the notice board. There was a good deal of shunting going on at the time--ICI- - who had given a false name, was fined Ss and costs, and the other three defendants were fined 23 6d and costs each. ASSAULTING AN AUNT —William Houghton was summoned for assaulting his aunt Mary Hall, at,the Royal Oak beerhouse, Langtree-street, Parr. on the 19th inst. It appeared that com- plainant was too busy to prepare defendant's tea at the moment he required it, and the latter followed her into the bar and struck her in the face, blackening both eyes.—He was fined 20s and c Mita. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Mr. A. Sinclair. CHARGE AGAINST • Lao.— Bcarry, aged 15, who has been more than once con .cted of larceny, was charged with being in the shop of Thomas Birch, tobacconist, Liver- pool-road, for the purpose of committing a felony.—Mrs. Birch said that on Friday afternoon she saw three boys there. the prisoner being one of them. Two of the lads had their hands in the cigar case, and she called to her husband that boys were in the shop stealing cigars. They then ran out, and her husband followed, bringing back the prisoner. hhe missed about twenty cigars from the case. There was nothing found on him but a halfpenny.—The prisoner was committed to gaol for fourteen days. MONDAY.—Betore Messrs. R. Pennington, J. C. Gamble, and H. S. Hall. ASLEEP ON THE HIGHWAY.—James Blatter and Owen Ken- nedy. y mng men, were summoned for being drunk and asleep in Crank-road, near the Crank Hotel, Rainford, at noon on dunday week.—The defendants alleged that they were sleep- ing on a plot of land adjoining the highway.—The Bench im- posed a tine of 5s and costs in each case. ON LICENSED PREMISES DURING PROHIBITED HOURS.— Edward Byrom, Evan Cross, Edward Lomax, and Thomas Derbyshire were summoned for being on licensed premises during prohibited hours.—P.O. Millington deposed that on the 11th inst. he visited the Bottle and Glass beerhous., Eccieston- lane end, and in the taproom found the four defendants, with a quart jug and glasses before them. They said they had coins from Park-road, but he afterwards ascertained that they lived in Rock View, which was only about two miles from the public-house.—Each of the defendants was fined lOs and costs. MAINTENANCE OF A DAUGHTER IN A REFORMATORT.—Wm. Waterwortk. a labourer, was summoned by Superintendent Johnston for failing to comply with an order of the Dints - trates ordering him to contribute Is 6cl per week towards the maintenance of his daughter in the Kirkdale Industrial School. —Superintendent Johnston stated that the Beneh made the order in question on the 16th March, 1883, but the defendant had not paid anything since the 14th July last, the arrears amounting to £2 15s 6d.—The Bench made an order for the payment of the arrears. TUESDAT.—Before Aldermen Cook and Mcßryde. DRUNKENNESS —Thomas Callaghan, ter being drunk and re- fusing to quit the licensed premises, the Emelt Bull Inn, Bridge street. was fined Ts 61 and costs.--John Crosby. who appeared fur the 31st time. was fined 103 a A costs for drunken- ness.

HAYDOCK. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT HAYDOCE.—The annual ser- mons in aid of the funds of the Haydock Colliery and Blackbrook Sunday Schools were preached en Sunday last. The morning preacher was tke Rev. R. J. Ward, of St. Helens; and the evening preacher was Mr. John Fairhurst, of Haydock. There was a good attendance, and the collec- tions were of a satisfactory character. SALE OF WORE AT St. JAMES'S ScnooL. The annual sale of articles worked by the school children was held in St. James's School, on Saturday afternoo last. The goods consisted chiefly of pinafores and other small articles of clothing, the majority ef which had been very tastefully and excellently worked by the young children, for presentation to the school inspector at the annual examination in April last. The scholars had evidently been well trained by Miss Cording, the mistress, assisted by the members of the Ladies Sewing Committee. The goods were neatly arranged about the room, and throughout the afternoon a goodly number of ladies and friends attended the "sale." The majority of the articles were dispose.d:of, a fair sum being realised.

HAYDOCK LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of the Havdock Local Board was held in the Boardroom on Mondai afternoon, when there were present Messrs. W. Balharry (in the chair), Thomas Jackson, John Jackson, Cunliffe, Alker, and T. Turnbull (clerk).—Toe minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed; and accounts amounting to £93 12s id were examined and passed for payment, on the motion of Mr. Thomas Jackson, seconded by Mr. Alker.—Vedical Officer's Annual Report.--The Medical Officer's annual report (which has been p.eviously published) again came up for discussion, and after a few remarks from one or two members, Mr. John moved, and Mr. Cunliffe seconded that the report be ac- cepted.—The motion was agreed to.—lnadequate Water Supply: Singular Complaint —The Clerk stated that he had received the following anonymous letter :—" Haydock, , May 12th, 1884. Dear Sir,—l am very sorry that I have to inform you that during the past bit of dry weather we have been compelled to carry and wheel our washing and drink- ing water, as we have not any water put in our houses yet. We have two wells at the back, but they are unfit for drink- ing as there has fallen down one of our small animals which has never been got out, and I think it is high time that we had water put in if it lies in your power. Please to avail us of it and oblige yours truly, Haydock, near toll bar."— As no name or place was indicated the Board could not con- sider the matter, but It was understood that the clerk would inquire into the question.—Plan of Stables.—Plans of stables proposed to be erected at Haydock for Dr. Hayward were submitted, and after being briefly considered were ordered to lie on the table.—The Clerk's House.—The Clerk drew the attention of the Board to the fact that his house required papering, and it was decided that tenders for papering he asked for.—School Attendance.—The School Attendance Officer reported that there were two cases of non-attendance of children at school, and it was resolved that the parents be summoned before the Board at the next meeting.—This was the only business of interest.

Elizabeth Donelly, who was so severely wounded by her brother, Joseph James Donelly, on Sunday last, died on Wednesday in the Manchester Infirmary. Donelly's mother —whom he also did his best to murder—still lies in a pre- carious condition. Aworrans Sulam n WALES.—Another lamentable suicide is reported from North Wales. On Wednesday morning Mr. C. E. Darby, one of the largest coal and iron masters in the Wrexham district, did not appear in the domestic circle at the usual boar, and upon his room being entered it was found he had hanged himself. For some time Mr. Darby had been in depressed spirits, and his melan- cnoly has been incieased by the death of his brother. fie was a prominent member of the Society of Friends, a magis- trate, a member of the local School Board, a director of several industrial undertakings, and took an active interest in temperance work and social improvements generally. THE DERIST.—The race for the Derby, on Wednesday, proved exceptionally sensational. A dead heat for the blue riband of the turf has only occurred once before in the whole course of its history of a hundred and six years, and that was in 1828, between the Duke of Rutland' Cadland and the Hon. E. Petrie's The Colonel, a tie which was run off and won by Cadland. Harvester, which divided the first honours with St. Gatien, is in the same stable with Queen Adelaide, which was third, so that Sir J. Willoughby and his followers had two strings to their bow. The son of Sterling-Wheather was the favourite till the close of last week, and the race was otherwise so open that, though much , money must have changed hands, there would be fewer heavy losses than usual. It is a curious coincidence that • St. Gatien and Harvester were numbered respectively first and last on the card.

&Lam CHAMPAGNE.—The champagne districts of the Conti- nent produce some 300,000,000 bottles annually. Onlv one- halt of this quantity is exported, and yet England and America alone are said to consume more than twice this vast production. From whence does the balance come? From the apple orchards on both sides the Atlantic! Yes, It is these apple orchards that are responsible for most of the cheaper Champagnes. IfoW CAMMACK & CO. are offering an AMERICAN CIDER CHAMPAGNE—the PURE JUICE of American apples—which they might easily pass off as a champagne at ten times the price: but they prefer to call a spade a spade! They are confident that everyone who tastes this most delicious and wholesome beverage, will, like Oliver Twist, ask for more.—Advt.

div.head: ME EXAMINER. SATURDAY. MAY 31, 1884.
div.p: ME EXAMINER. SATURDAY. MAY 31, 1884.
THE REP RESENT ATION OF

WARRINGTON. SELECTION OF A LIBERAL CANDIDATE. ENTHUSIASTIC RECEPTION ,OF MR. WILLIAM CROSFIELD. For some time it has been well known that Mr. MeMin- Mee, M.P., who has for so lenge time been the faithful repre- sentative of the borough of Warrinzton in :he Liberal in- terest, would not, in consequence of continued ill-health, feel himself justified in again offering his seryices to the party at the next election. As soon as it was theroughly understood that the decision of the present member for War- rington was of necessity unavoidable, attention was at once turned to the duty of selecting a successor. After due con- sideration a sub-committee that had been formed to deal with the question, selected the names of three gentlemen whom it was thought desirable to ask that their names should be submitted to the general COuncil, For rerteene that could not be lightly Overlooked, die first two gentle- titan, Mr. John Crosfield and Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., found themselves unable to entertain the proposition, but the third gentleman, Mr. William Crosfield, of Liverpool, at once offered to place his services at the disposal of the con- stituency, should his views meet with the approval of the Liberal electors. As a result ef the action of the sub-com- mittee a large gathering of the General Council (" the 200") of the Warrington Liberal AVY.TMOTI,- wa4 beld iii th 9 Wycliffe Hail, Bewsey-street, on Wednesday evening, called by circular "to receive and to consider the report and re- commendation of the sub-committee appointed by the General Council, and to decide what course of action shall be adop- ted in referenCe therefe." The chair was occupied by Mr. Samuel Rigby, J.Pa oresidesf of the association, and amongst those also preeent were the following gentlemen, viz :—Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., Aldertean• C. J. Holmes, J.P.; Councillors John Crosfield, J.P , C. Broadbent, JP., F. Monks, J.P., Joh:. Platt, John Greening, George Walling- ton, John Brown, and F. Dixon; Revs. John Tonge, Thos. Rippon, and E. Moore ; Messrs. F. A. Roberts, J. H. Ger- nall, Roger Bate, J. J. Sanderson, J. Walker, T. S. Fair- dough, T. H. Poole, W. Wright, Joseph Mounfield, P. T. Winskill, W. Barker, W. C. Baines, John Podmore, J. W. Hall, W. Bibby, G. Holford, Thomas Miller, James Kilduff, John Conroy, Thomas Flynn, George Blackhurst, J. Winser, F. W. Monks, E. J. Guest, J. H. Fleming, A. IL Browne, William Perry, John Bonne!, W. Stirrup, W. Grimshaw, I. J. Biddle. T. Birchall, W. Jeffery, ,N. Legge, F. Brown, T. Burton, H. Whitham, L. Gilooley, John Burke, IL Highley, S. Dunbobbin, Anthony Connor, Alban Stirrup, J. McCon- ville, James Haynes, T. Dignum, &c. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the meeting, remarked that they were assembled in consequence of a sub-committee having been appointed at a meeting of the General Council to take into consideration the question of selecting a suit- able candidate for the representation of the borough of War- rington at the next general election—(hear, hear)—in place of their friend Mr. McMinnies, who, as they would all be aware, had decided to retire. Nothing weuld have pleased them better than to have been able to retain Mr. McMinnies' services—(applause—but that not being possible, they were, of course, under the necessity of procuring another candidate. Ile then called upon the Secretary to explain what had been done by the sub committee since their last meeting, and remarked that it would be for the meeting, after hearing the report, to declare what should be done that evening. (Applause.) Mr. H. ROBERTS, Secretary, said that the sub-committee duly considered the names that had been sent in to them, for the purpose of making a selection, by various members of the Association, and came to the conclusion to ask three gentlemen, out of the list of naines, to allow themselves to- be submitted to the General Council for consideration. The names were, first, Mr. John CrosSeld, J.P.—(applause) —second, Mr. Jesse Coliings, M.P.—(applause)—and third, Mr. William Crosfield, of Liverpool. (Applause.) Depu- tations were appointed to wait upon each of the three gentle- men whose names had been selected, and•in due course thee was done. As the meeting was already aware, Mr. John Crosfield, in reply to the deputation that waited upon him, while appreciating the honour that the Liberal party pro- posed to confer upon him, and at the same time being ex- ceedingly desirous of rendering every possible assistance that was in his power, felt that in consequence of the state of his health and the requirements of his business, he was, utterly unable to comply with the request. Mr. Collings was waited upon in London, at the Westminster Palace Hotel, and every argument and effort was used to induce him to consent to allow his name to be submitted to the Council. Bat in reply Mr. Collings lengthily explained the position which he held in reference to the people of Ipswich, and while fully desirous of aiding the Liberal party in Warrington to the utmost extent of his power, he felt strongly that his duty at present compelled him to decline the invitation, and to allow his services to be again placed at the disposal of the Liberals et Ipswich, so tong as they wished to retain him. In reference to Mr. Wm. Crosfield—(applause)—that gentleman was waited upon by a deputation in Liverpool, and when the matter had been fully explained to him, and the situation gone into fully. Mr. Crosfield at once placed his services at the disposal of the party. (Cheers.) A meeting of the sub- committee was called as soon as possible afterwards to receive the reports of the various deputations, and all the members of the committee were present except Mr. McMin- nies, M.P., who was detained in London. After careful and lengthy consideration it was unanimously and enthusiasti- cally resolved to recommend to the General Council that Mr. William Crosfield—(applause)—be the Liberal candi- date for Warrington at the next election, (Renewed applause.) Mr. Roberts proceeded to say that in Mr. Crosfield, if he met with the approval of the Council, they would have a man of sterling worth and excel- lent ability, a man who bore a name honouredin Warring- ton whose father was formerly in business in Warrington, and who consequently did not come as a stranger amongst thetn. (Applause.) If the Council accepted Mr. Crosfield they would not have to do the whole of the work of the con- , test themselves, as Mr. Crosfield had the reputation of being a eood political worker, and would undoubtedly do every- thing that lay in his power to secure to the party that which lay in their own hands, if they chose to take it—triumphant victory at the next election. (Applause). The CRLIRMAN then asked if any gentleman had any suggestion to make in reference to the report. Mr. A. H. BROWN suggested that if Mr. Crosfield were in the neighbourhood be should be requested to deliver a short address to the meeting, as it would be much better to see and hear him before any decision was arrived at. (Applause). The meeting having adopted that suggestion in reply to the Chairman, Mr. McMinnies left the room and returned irt a few minutes accompanied by Mr. Crostield. Their en- trance was the signal for a round of enthusiastic applause, the meeting rising en masse and cheering heartily. After the applause had subsided The CRLIRMAN, addressing Mr. Crosfield, said :—Mr. Crosfield, your name has been mentioned in this meeting, and I think you will see some intelligent faces here, and, .I may say, without fear of contradiction, many kind friends, who, if they once hold out their hands to a an and give him their good wishes, do not withdraw them readily. They expect good, kind treatment. They expect a fair represen- tation of their cause—(hear)—and I am quite sure, sir, that if they are anxious to hear you it is simply, that they may be assured that you are the person upon whom they may fix, shall I say their desires and affections. They are very warm people in Warrington. (Laughter.) They call it affection here and they mean it. (Applause.) There are many friends here who, if they once think you are the proper person-and you mast assure them of that yourself— will withhold no energy, no personal exertion, nor any- thing else, even to forgetting their own night's rest, to secure that on which they have set their minds. Sir, get their trust and confidence, and I do not fear the result, and I think then we may fairly say " We were going to have a Crosfield, and we have got one." (Applause.) Mr. W. CROSFIELD, en rising to address the meeting, was received with loud and continued applause. He said : I can hardly say "unaccustomed as I am to public speak- ing" but I may say that I am certainly unaccustomed to the position in which I find myself at this moment, and I do not occupy this position without feeling very grave res- ponsibility. (Hear, hear.) Mr. CEOSFIELD, in reply, said he had not words to ex- press his gratitude to them for the confidence they had seen fit to place in him. He felt they were placing in him a great trust. They had but very little knowleege of him, but he trusted that their further acquaintance would justify the confidence they had placed in Lim. He might say that from that time, se far as health, strength, and time would permit, he should place himself at their service. He trusted that they would together achieve a victory—(bear, hear, and great applause)--a victory not for themselves alone. He felt that he was not merely going in for personal honour, but to maintain a position which their friend Mr. McMin- nles had achieved for them, and that they were together fighting a battle for the Liberal party. (Great cheering.) If they lost sight of themselves, and looked at the great end which they had in view—the good of their country and the nation at large—they would ultimately win the victory if they only deserved it. (Loud and enthusiastic cheering.) Councillor MONKS, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. McMinnies, expressed his concurrence with the decision arrived at. Mr. Crosfield, of whom he had had opportuni- ties of judging, was ha every way most suitable for the posi- lion in which he had been placed. They were glad to see their chairman (Mt. Mcninnies) back amongst them, and glad to believe that his health was very much better, and that they would yet have the benefit of Iris assistance and advice.

Mr.T. A. ROBERTS, in second*, said that he did not look upon the retirement of their present member as by any means an unqualified misfortune. No one knew what they had lost during the absence of Mr. McHinnies from the party during the last few years and they wauld now have him again amongst them as their chairman and president, and with the benefit of his advice and guidance there was no doubt at all' as to what the isst..Ne of the contest would be. Mr. McMinnies had fought and won a way for himself, and he was able and willing to assist in the return of his suc• COMM (Applause.) Mr. MCMITBRES replying, said, that he need nct remind them that so long as he lived and his health permitted any- thing and everything that he could do for the Liberal, party, he would have pleasure in doing. The proceedings, which had throughout been most in- , thusiastic, were them brought to a close.

•. EARLESTOWN. MISCELLANEOUS, t3NCRIIT.—On Saturday evening a con- cert was given in the Arioduct Institute, Earlestown, when an attractive programme was readered. The artistes were Miss Lewis, Miss Rothwell, Miss Bertha Jackson, Miss Ada Davies, Miss Sarah Marsh, Mrs. Squire, and Megan, .1. White, G. Wright, and, W. Jackson. Mr. H. J. Darman acted as accompanist and choirmaster.. There was a good attendance, over £l6 being realised. Ties EAHLESTOWN Feoratita. Tnear.—The friends and supporters of the Earlestown Football Club will be pleased) Whear that the first teaxp of the club will have silver medals- presented to themby the Liverpool and district Pcotball Association for having played in the-Snal tie et thecompetition for the challenge cup, when they were beaten by Rverton by one pal to none. The secretary of the Euriestown club has received a communication from the Liverpool Association stating that the medals are of a hand- some design and have been inscribed ; and they will be presented tothe Earlestown players on the night of Thurs- day, the 12th June. INTERHSTIEIG CEREMONY AT THE CATHOLIC CHAPEL.— A guild; has recently been established in connection with the Catholic Chapel, Crow-lane,.and the first consecration of schoolchildren, as members, took place on Sunday after- noon, the ceremony being of a very interesting character. The girls were dressed in white, and wore on their breast, ' suspended by a bine ribbon, a medal descriptive of ;le cere- mony, whilst the boys wore the same insignia attached to a red ribbon. The consecration was performed in the after- noon by the Rev. Father Fanning,. af Bedford Leigh, the childroa-taving previously walked in procession from the schoolroom and round the chapel, the girls carrying floral wreaths. The reverend gentleman delivered an earnest ad- dress to the children, the chapel at the time being crowded I with their parents and friends. LIBERAL MEETING AT Aserrog.—An enthusiastic meet- ing in connection with the newly-formed Ashton Liberal I Association was held in the Congregational Schools, on Wednesday evening: The chair was onicupied by Mr. John I ;Smethurst,. and he was supported hy Dr. Latham, and I I Messrs. T. Roberts, S. Wood, W. Francs Jos. Mitchell, W. I 1 Boardman/ F. Lowe, J. McGeever, J. Francs, dtc., Ash- -1 ton; and leSessra. C. M. Percy, 0. Rushton, R. Stuart, J. Wilson, T. Worthington, and 0. Gee, Wigan, who attended , las a deputation.—The 'Chairman said it was a source of ' great satiefaetion to him to see such a large meeting ; It t spoke well for the advancement of Liberal prin- ciples in, Ashton, and was a sure sign that the darkness which had so long reigned over ' the township would SOOB pass away. (Hear, hear.).— Mr. Roberts-proposed "That this meeting of the inhabitants of the Ashton polling district expresses its entire confidence in Mr. Gladstone and his Cabinet." The motion WAS secon- ded by Mr. R. Stuart (Wigan), who congratulated the Ashton Liberals upon their large and enthusiastic gathering and stated that the resolutien was one which would commend itself not only to them but every sappor:Ar of the Liberal cause. He maintained that the Liberals bad done every- thing for the good of the country, and would continue to do so in the future.—Mr. T. Worthington and Mr. 0. Gee sup- ported the motion, which was carried with acclamation.—.- Mr. S. Woods, in an excellent speech, proposed the next 'resolution, as follows :—" That this meeting expresses its , approval of ,the principles øf the Franchise Bill, and firmly believes that the great body of the people will tempest her Majesty's ministers in using all the power the constitution places in their hands for the passing of the same." (Cheere). —Mr. 0. Rushton heartily seconded the motion, which' was supported by Mr. C. M. Percy, and carried unani. monsly.—llearty votes of thanks to the chairman and the speakers concluded the meeting. EXTRAORDINARY DISAPPEARANCE OF Two CHILDREN.— .Daring the present week considerable emcitement has beam occasioned in Earlestown by the strange disappearance lof tefo children. It appears that about nine o'clock on Saturday morning Joseph Hilton, 6 years of age and Richt': Buckley, el. years old, left their homes in Ratllbone-street for the purpose of playing in the street with other children. A short time afterwards, however, they were both missed; and despite the most vigilant search and inquiries in the neighbourhood nothing has since been ascertained about their whereabouts or condition. It was supposed that. they had rambled away and been accidentally drowned in one-of the pits of water in the vicinity, or that they had strolled too far away and been picked up by passing strangers, but the bare fact of their disappearance, and at so young an age, caused much sorrow and pain to their parents, as .well as excited much sympathy for them throughout the tow-n, On Monday it was reported that the two lads were last seen wandering in the direction of the canal, and as it was feared. that they might have fallen in, P.C. LlOyd and a number- of ether men proceeded to .‘ drag "the water throughout the afternoon, but their efforts were unavailing. Notiees in reference to the affair were printed and posted and circulated throughout the district, as well as forwarded to the police stations in the divielon, as follows Lost, Joseph Hilton, aged six, light complexion, straight light hair, tall for his age, very thin, wearing cord suit, black stockings, elastic side boots, blue Scotch cap; from 29e Rathboae-street, Earlestown • missing since nine o'clock I sem, May 24th. Also Richard Buckley (he may call himself Bailey), aged three and a half years, rather stout, wearing cord-trousers, cloth waistcoat, no jacket or cap, red and black stockings, lace up boots; from 26, Rathbone-street, Earlestown; missing since nine o'clock am., May 24th. Information to be given to Mr. Superintendent Jackson, Cbunty Police Office, Leigh, Lancashire e, or the Sergeant of Police, Newton-he-Willows; or the nearest police sta- tion." Since the foregoing was written one of the children (Richard Buckley) has been recovered under somewhat peculiar circumstances. Among other persons. to whom copies of the hand bill was forwarded waa the town crier or bellman of St. Helens, and on Wednesday last that person put in an appearance at Eaneestown, and handed over the boy Buckley to his parents.. He gave the statement that he found the lad wandering in the streets of St. Helens on Saturday afternoon' and as he could notice the lad was "lost" betook him home, where he had wall-fed him until the morning of that day, when ha received the notice. Although the lad is so young, only 3/ years old, he can give a consistent account of his and his friend's disappearanze. In reply to ques- tions, the child, as well as he was able stated that he and Hilton were picked up by some men, Who placed them in a van, containing baskets, and the men made sticks. He did not know bow far he was taken, nor did be know. where he was put down, but as he was picked up in St. Helena on the same day that he was mined it was surmised that he was cruelly and heartlessly put down in that town by his captors. He adds that Hilton was taken on by the men, and here, for the present, all trace of Hilton is lost. There cannot be the least doubt that a party of gipsies who passed through Earlestown on Saturday morning picked the lads up, and released the child Buckley at St. Helens. The utmost efforts are being put forth to recover the other miss- ing lad, and it is to ho hoped that the offenders will soon be brought to justice.

"No—neither 7 rnY liver," Byron replied, with one of those quaint turns speech which he always had ready. UNSPEABABLE."—At the annnaldinner of Sorosis in New °..rk on Monday, Mrs. Croly, the president, in offering the east " The Woman Martyrs," said that "the martyrdom j,,Wotnan was an unspoken agony." Anything " unspeak- " must be a great agony to a woman, that's a fact. , The writer of an article on the subject of clever parrots Very truly remarks that "a parrot has only to go on saying r; Silly thing upon every opportunity that offers, and , the e‘gnt chance is certain to come round at last, when its silly ,?eech becomes the happiest possible." The same fact has ,"° doubt encouraged many men and women to keep on talk- , lng. "He ought to be," aa the reply ; "it cost me almost five hundred pounds to learn how to buy that horse." a HIT 'Ex.—Not long ago a citizen of Michigan avenue • 7 a small house to rent, and he got a paint brush and h„legle and hung out a sign reading: "To Wreut." It was a? tined that the word " wrent" was not exactly in accor- ',„ lee with Webster's latest, and the speller went away C7,4lnbling," Well, if they are so very particular about it I _an change it." Some minutes elapsed before one of the actors was able to inform Romain that his ace had been painted a lustrous black. Anour Poots.—" Stranger," he began, as he shoved ha hat back on his head and sat down on a trunk on the plat- " What is this 'ere about these 'ere railroad pools ?" ' How ?" "Wall, then, what is a railroad pool ?" "Why, a aumber of railavad lines put all their earnings into a bag, !hake it up and divide even." "What's this far ?" "So that all can get-a whack at business." "An' its accordin' to ?" "Yes." The man pulled his hat down, rested his tibows on his knees for a " think " which lasted three or tr,air minutes, and then suddenly arose and said: "Stranger, ,!..ve bin a tarnal fool !" "How ?" "Why, thee,' a chap rho' next door to me at hum, who has allus worked four r,°,arls to my one, and who earns a dollar to my quarter, and .riae never occurred to me to make him pool our wages and "act,. up !" ~,eaa Cams Lam —" Captain" said the reporter as he • "wolted his way into the circle, "how large waves did you lee on the lakes ?" "Well, let's see. Do you mean within Iti;he last five years ?" "I mean any time since you have „eon " Oh—ah ! Well, sir, twenty years ago, when used to sail the bark John B. Skinner, I saw waves on the Bay which must have been—" "Go on." "Say," the captain, "please ask some of these gentlemen iielr opinion." There were six other captains in the circle. "r° of them said they had seen waves 15 feet high, two agreed on 20 feet, and the other pair thought they had a few waves running about loose which mast have been atu of 25 feet high." "Now, then, Captain," said the repor- Zte the first. I took a ladder and tape line and mea- then', 'eat, and I know I knocked off at least 10 inches of narLtops in reaching up.". He came last, and the other Tina could only mime their desperation. /3,,-„ItaPPED INTO A PROMISE OF MARRIAGI.—A young I"ruand man who is about as innocent as a dove, though t'arti-IY so wise as a serpent, is said to have been ensnared Lnto matrimony by a device which has the charm of novelty. is a handsome fellow, and earns good wages at his trade, of course, a favourite with the fair sex. One of his 'clung lady friends, who has always shown an especial fond- ness for him, asked him point blank in the course of a recent Sunday evening tete-a-tete "Who are you going to marry?" ‘‘ You!" he said, jokingly. "Really?" "Yes." " Shake hands on it !" the business-like maiden demanded. The Young man did so, thinking it the most amusing incident he had ever borne a part in. The young lady, however, told her father that Mr. Blank and she were engaged, and the young man was immediately waited upon by the interested parent, and has decided to marry the girl rather than stand a threatened suit for breach of promise. YANKEE Doorms—A well-known " reithete" has been lecturing recently on the United States. He visited Lead- 'Ville, the chief characteristic of whose inhabitants, he says, Was the constant use of the revolver. He lectured to them upon Benvento Cellini, his Life and Works," and was re- proved by his hearers for not having brought the artist with him. The explanation that he had keen dead for some little time elicited the inquiry "Who shot him ?" Among the More elderly inhabitants Of the Routh he found a melan- ,ch°lY tendency to date every event of importance by the "abellion. " How beautiful the moon is to-night! "he °ace remarked to a gentleman who vets standing next to "-`4l- "Yes," was the reply, "but ym should have aZen it before the war." An art-patron west of the Rocky Mountains sued the raiP-oad-company for damages °cleanse a plaster cast of the Venus ot Milo, which he had imported from Paris, had be-n delivered minus the arms! What was more surprising still, he gaincd the case and the damages.

It came to pass that at a farmers' market- %liner the talk turned upon Mr. Eke's performances, when ' 81°Ille one present protested that what had been narrated was '.°aPossibie. The 7alt was killed, the bones were cutout, the flesh was chopped it. 41,0 minute particles and apportioned into seventeen enor- b °Lis pastiea, the outer crust of when was a thin film of f sitter, made lovely and tempting to every sense, but care- er kept from any ingredients that could cloy the palate. I.3'was called in, he having agreed to the wager with evident delight, and was told he might fall to. He did as, nit, steadily gorged. He had ma 'e no difficulty of the first fiae Pasties ; but when a tenth was brought in he seemed to Per To the horror of his backers he sighed and looked • I)'esci It was but for a moment; he desired only to ii.: 130stulate. 'I say, mas'r, I ain't got nuthin' to say agin 441 loik 'em arnazin' ; but I'm a-thinkin' et's aYnt time as I should begin upon that ther calf!'"

Secretaries of Cricket Ohms are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning. CROSSLEY STREET V. LATCHFORD STA.R.—Played on Satur- day; tho latter being beaten ov 11 and 10 wickets to tall; bowlers. Oliver Devison and Peter La wlesa. ST. PAUL'S STAR V. PEOPLE'S COLLE.GB (IST ELEVEN).— Played on Saturday, and resulted in an easy victory for St. Paul's Star by 67 runs. Score :---St. Paul's Star, 13; Peoples College, 6. WESTON PoINT V.,CO-OPERATIVE STORES.—WestOn Point. Si; Co-operative Stores, first innings. 21; second innings, 16. Wes- ton Point played well, beating their opponents by an innings and 17 runs. LATCHFORD V. OLD TRAFFORD (2ND ELEVEN.)—Thts match was played at Old Trafford. on Saturday, and terminated in a draw greatly in favour of Latchford. Score: Latchford (four wickets), 79; Old Trafford. 98 BEWSEY WHITE STAR V. SLACK Smot.—Playea on Satur- day, on the ground of the latter, and resulted en a victory for the White Star by 10 run.' and 4 wickets to fall. Score : Bewsey White Star 51. and 4 wiskets to fall; Black Star, 41. WARRINGTON WESLRYANS V ST. CLEMENT'S, SALFORD.— Tilts match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and resulted in an easy victory for the home team. H. Ostle bowled well for the Wesleyans, taking eight wickets for ' three runs, four of which he took in one over. Score :—Wes- leyans, 187; Clement's, 9. BURTONWOOD V. RUNCORN (2nd) —This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday, and resulted in an easy victory for the home team. Messrs. Stubbs and Fryer shared the wickets equally, each obtaining five wickets for six runs. Messrs. Knowles, Norman, Fryer, and Leathwood did most of the run- getting for Runcorn. Score: Runcorn 134: Burtonwood 15, ST. JOHN'S CO. V. PENKETH 0 C.—This match was played at Penketh on Saturday, and resulted io a victory for the St. John's team by 25 runs. The visitors weat in to bat first, and were all out for 60 runs.
