div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 31, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 31, 1884.

LODGE PRESENTATION. Oa Saturday afternoon, the members of the Late Spring , Rose Lodge of the Ancient Order of Shepherds, Ashton Unity, met at the Workrnen'e Club, Warrington, to present a testimonial to Secretary P.M. Joseph Whitlow, as a mark of their esteem and appreciation of his services. The testi- monial took the form of a silver lever watch and a hand- some framed emblem of merit. Prior to the presentation a substantial tea was provided, at which about 150 of the members and their wives and sweethearts sat down. Sub- sequently a well attended meeting was held, over which Bro. D.P.C.S. Edmund Wrigley presided.—Mr. Timson, organist of Stockton Heath Church, opened the proceedings by a pianoforte selection.—The Chairman said that one of their objects in being met togethsr was to place the benefits of such societies as they represented prominently before the public Of Warrington. No doubt there weie many young men who had not joined a friendly society, but it wiaLld be to their benefit to do so, and they wished to make it known that there was such a society as theirs in existence, and to encourage the young men to joinit. In the second place, they had, a very important duty to perform, and that was to pay a mark of respect to their secretary for his valuable services in connection wilh the lodge during the past six or seven, years.—Mr. Timson having sung "Hearts of Oak," the Chairman proposed "The Queen and the Royal Family," remarking that the Queen had won the universal esteem of her subjects, and was admired by every nation throughout the length and breadth of the civilised world.—The Chair- man next gave "The Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds, Warrington District," calling upon the previous Corres- ponding Secretary, Mr. Mather, to respond:—Mr. Mather, replying, said that at the special meeting of the district called for him to give in his report, it was a pleasure to tim to be able inform the delegates present that never since the establishment of the Order in the district had they been in such a flourishing position, either numerically or financi- ally. To give them an idea of the benefits to be derived from joining an tinstitution like theirs, he would read them a few particulard from the annual report. During the year 1883 the amount of money received as contributions to the sick and funeral fund was £916 Is 41; the interest upon the money in the district £52 12s 51. Amongst payments were £604 63 61 for sickness, £l6O for lunerale, and £125 18 llid for medical aid. The providential fund was sup- ported by subscription, and was devoted to the relief of members in distress, who by reason of continual sickness or accidents were incapacitated -from following their usual employment. Each member paid one penny per quarter to this fund, which was established in 1876, and from which £BO is had been paid to distressed members since that date. (Applause.) The fund at present was worth £4l 183 Id. They had also in connection with the district an educational fund. They, as Shepherds, did not like to see a deceased member's widow applying to the School Committee for re- mission of fees, because they liked to be independent. They had therefore levied themselves a halfpenny each per quarter to pay the school fees of deceased members children. That fund was established in 1879, and they had paid from it the sum of £l9 Os 41, and a balance of £2O Os 9.1 i-d remained. They had sick and funeral fund £2,512 4s 21, provi- dential fund £4l 18s Id, educational fund £2O 93 93/4d, and management fund £47 178 41, miking a total of £2.622 93 81. The total amount of receipts from the whole Order last year was £59,699 us 103, and the payments were £49,349 18s 7d, being a gain on the year of £10,349 13s 3d. (Ap- plause ) The total number of members comprised in the 70 districts that sent in returns was 64,857, and the total amount of the funds of the society was £145,864 193 01.— Song by Bro. Taylor, "The Anchor's Weighed."—The Chairman, referring to the remarks of Mr. Mather, said he could fully bear out what that gentleman had said. Mr. Mather had stimulated the officers and members to greater exertion, hence the success of the Lodge.—P.M. John Parr, in felicitious terms, then introduced the subject of the testi- monial, and the Chairman made the presentation.—Mr. Whitlow briefly replied in suitable terms, and the remainder of the evening was spent in an enjoyable manner, several songs being given and heartily applanded.—The watch presented bore the following inscription: "Presented to J. Whitlow by the members of the Late Spring Rose Lodge, L.0.A.5., Ashton 'Unity, Warrington District, for services rendered as secretary. May, 1884." IRISH LAND LEAGUe; MEETING AT WARRINGTON. On Monday a well attended meeting in furtherance of the objects of the Irish National Land League of Great Britain was held in the Workingmen's Hall, Warrington. The chair was occupied by Mr. Kilduff, who was supported on the I platform by Mr. B. Hughes, President of the central branch, Liverpool; Mr. M. Conway, of Blackburn, district organiser; Mr. Stirrup, and Mr. Mannion. The CHAIRMAN said that at a former meeting of Irishmen in Warrington there was a committee, pro tern, appointed to get up another meeting of the Irish electors of Warring- ton. That committee, he might say, dwindled down to five, but they were determined to carry the thing out and nee what could be done amongst their people in Warrington, hecauSe for seine time they had been so scattcrett as to scarcely know one another. He had always voted and worked for the Liberal interests in Warrington, and it was not for him to say they were hot going to do so still, but it was for that meeting to appoint a committee when they would have an understanding as to whom they were going to vote for. They would support the man who promised them and their countrymen his support. (Applause.) Mr. M.Conwev said that some time ago it Wae his good fortune to meet some of his countryrnen ia one of the public halls of Warrington, and there after a good meeting they formed a committee. On that committee were men whose names he thought would win the respect of the Irishmen of Warrington—he thought that from hearsay. There were other Irishmen in the town whose names were given to him as those of men likely to help on the cause of old Ireland. But one of those gentlemen, in particular, re- fused to give him a helping hand and threw discourage- ment in his way. This gentleman told him that it was no use appealing to the Irishmen of Warrington; they were apathetic in the cause of Ireland; that they were lost to the sense of the duty which Ireland enjoined upon them, and that the prospect of a branch of the Land League was very remote indeed. Judging, however, from the numbers before them that night there was every prospect of a very suc- cessful branch of the Land League being formed. He took it that the Irishmen of Warrington would belie the asper- sions of those who said they were wanting in love of their country. He thought it just wanted a word or two to be put before them in order that that branch of the Land League might be successfully formed, and in order that the Irish public opinion of Warrington might centre in that branch, and thus prevent any Irishman as an individual from going out of his way to pledge the suffrages of other Irishmen to any cause without the consent of his fellow- countrymen in this town. He might tell them confiden- tially that the individual who said there was no hope of a branck being formed in Warrington actually wrote to the executive in London asking for Mr. McMinnies's votes on the Coercion Acts and desiring their consent to start a sort of organisation in this town for the purpose of getting two or three leading Irieh members down so as to provoke Irish opinion in the channels he himself was there that night to do. It was not, however, to the interests of Ireland that any individual should step out of his place contrary to the wishes of the executive and attempt to get up a great demonstration. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Conway then gave an account of the work which had been done and was being done by the Irish members of Parliament, and concluded by saying that it was now that the Irishmen of Warrington must rise in their political strength. They were strong be- cause no member could be returned from this borough with- out their aesistance. They must say that neither Mr. Cros- field nor Mr. McMinnies, nor anybody else should receive their suffrages without those suffrages using considered by the leaders of the Irish people, and whatever they advised they shoold stand true to it and place their votes at the dis- posal of their mother country, Ireland. (Applause.) Mr. B. HUGHES then gave an interesting address, .in the course of which he touched upon various subjects in con- nection with the Irish question. After a few remarks from the CHAIRMAN, in which he in- vited those present to form a branch of the Land League, Mr. CONWAY repeated that neither party in Warrington could send a member to Parliament without the assistance of the Irish voters. The Irish party, he said, had taken an in- , dependent position in centres like Blackburn, where they had something like thirteen hundred Irish voters. The Liberals there had a majority of 142, but what would become of Mr. Briggs without the Irish vote. They "'were not going to consider Mr. Briggs at all in Blackburn. They considered him at the last general election when Lord Beaconsfield's manifesto was on the walls of the town. Mr. Briggs said he evould not vote for coercion, but that was a matter of small moment when he got into the House'of Commons. Mr. McMinnies who professed indeed in an indirect manner to be an Irishman or descended in- directly from Irish parents, or had some Irish blood mixed up somewhat in his anatomy, forgot all his pledges and went right up to the House of Commons and voted for coercion. It Was their duty to avenge this. They could avenge it by holding aloof and voting in the direction the Rich leaders told them. (Slight dissent.) He (Mr. Conway) thought he detected in the person who dissented a gentleman who when he applied for a certain hall in this town point blank refused him and said he could not let him have a Liberal ball for an Irish meeting. This was the character of the Liberalism they had up and down all England. But they were deter- mined to stamp this kind of Liberalism out of existence so far as Irishmen could do it, and so in Warrington, as in Blackburn, they were holding aloof from both parties, and would accept the advice their,leaders sent them, and though their policy be a zig-zag one—for the Tory here and for the Liberal there—it did not matter if they equalised parties. If they made the strength of the Conservatives and the strength of the Liberals so much they left the Irish members in pos- session of the situation and they could put time destinies of this great empire into the hands of which party they liked. They could say to each party that if they did not accept the conditions they imposed the other party should go into power. The Irish party should then have its programme extracted from the ministry of this country in all its ful- ness. Their duty was to give their members that power. Would they in Warrington be behind their brothers in this matter? He felt aesured they would not. Mr. Conway then referred to the previous Irish meeting in Warrington, when he said there was one gentleman of venerable appearance who met him in the most kindly spirit, and helped him as much as he poesibly could. It was with great grief and really sincere sorrow that he saw this gentleman had unfortunately committed the weHare of their couatrymen politically speak- ing, into the hands of the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) The Liberals, he said. had always looked upon the Irish as the tail end of their party; they had always looked upon the Irieh voter with a sort of despicable feeling. It Was the renegade and Total )—who was taken

I by the hand, but they were determined that until justice I was in the sscendant.they should sever their connection with the Liberal party. (Applause.) Mr. MANNion proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers. He had intended, he said, to have said a few words about the Liberal deputation that went to London and Liverpool, but as it was getting so late he would defer it until another time. Mr. STIRRUP seconded this proposal. In his opinion, he said, it would be folly on the part of the Irish party to send an Orangeman to Parliament. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) The vote of thanks being carr led, Mr. HUGHES, in responding, said it would be a deplorable thing if the Irishmen were to vote for an Orangeman, but in spite of his strong feeling against them if he thought he would forward the cause of Ireland by supporting an Orangeman he would sacrifice his own feeling and support him. The meeting then terminated, and a considerable number of those present gave in their names as members of the pro- posed branch of the Land League at Warrington.

, MARRIAGE or THE MlDGETS.—Francis Joseph Flynn and Millie Edwards, leette-r—known as the American Midgets, were married in Manchester on Wednesday. The bride- groom, who is in his twentieth year, weighs 9lb. and the bride, who is in her seventeenth year, weighs 21b. less. The civil contract was entered into before the Superintendent Registrar of the Chorlton Union, and aftereards the pair went through a religious ceremony, conducted by the Rev. J. Mackie, according to the forms of the Presbyterian Church, in the St. James's Hall. The latter was witnessed by a large number of spectators. EXECUTION am LINCOLN.—Mary Sefiley was banged at Lincola at nine o'clock On Monday morning, for the mords.r , of her husband .bv poison, 4. Wrangle, near Boston, on Feb- ruary 9th. Berry, of Bradford, was the executioner. Reporters were not admitted. Berry, it appears, carried out , all the arrangements in a satisfactory manner, giving the culprit a drop of nine feet. A Wesleyan minister attended her up to the time of the execution, when the chaplain of the prison continued the Ministrations to the end. Prisoner wrs in a very desponding condition. She screamed with terror while being pinioned, and her lamentations are de- scribed as having been heartrending. As she was being led to her deom she had to be assisted on to the scaffold, and en the white cap being placed over her face, and just as the bolt was withdrawn, she gave a long despairing cry. She aeserted her innocence to the Wesleyan minister,-shortly be- fore he left her, and to the last hoped a reprieve would be forthcoming. MR. WILLIAM CROSFIELD JP • • Ir. William Crosfield, of 16, Alexandra Drive, Liverpool, who has been selected as the Liberal can- didate for Warrington at the next election, is the eldest son of the late William Crosfield, Esq., T.P., who at the commencement of his business life resided in Warrington, assisting his eldest brother Joseph, who founded the Bank Quay Soap Works. He sub- sequently settled in 1827 in Livarpool, and became one of the partners in the well-known firm of Geo. Crosfield and Co., which continues its existence up to

the present time. The name of ‘,,‘ Crotheld " is "a house- hold word" in Liverpool, and by a double tradition has been made the synonym of all that is upright and thorough, just, and true. For until but the ether day (as it seeress to those who knew both) there were two William Crosfields—the father, who for more than half a century had actively supported with purse and influence every beneficient public movement, and the son, who from mannood had been following dili- gently the same honourable part. Among his fellow citizens the latter is even yet spoken of as William Orosfield, jun., by many whose memories are loth to part with the venerable and kindly senior of the well- known counting house in Temple Court. The first thing that occurs to the mind on mention of the name of Crosfield is a vision of sturdy and unflinching Nonconformity, for almost every scion of the family (wide though it be in its Liverpool ramifi- cations) remained faithful to the principles of Volun- taryism and Dissent, not a few having been the victims of the State Church bailiff in the times so vacantly flown—when furniture and sponns were periodically colleoted (at an expense of about 80 per (sent. super-added costs) from all who declined to bow the knee to the religious supremacy of a sect. Crosfield senior having suffered many thiegs at the hands of State Churchistn, it is not surprising that Crosfield junior should have his heart set upoa the attainment of complete religious equality. The vein of continuity is not always preserved thus intact. still less fr(quently have we found, as with this father and son, that the same ac- tivity in the same offices and agencies characterizes successive generations. And there is something surely of that quality we term " true Eng lish "—for want of a better phrase—in a man who follows his father mot otly in the headship of a commercial firm, the diaconate of a Congregational Church, the functions of the City Bench, and the honours of the Munici- pal Council, but follows with equal faithfulness in liberally subscribing in aid of all worthy objects. And yet Mr. William Crosfield who now presents himself to the electors of Warrington is not the mere echo of a departed father, for he has built up a dis- tinct reputation by dint of a certain sturdy grain of character that is all his own. Since Mr. Crosfield's retirement from business, he has added greatly to his public activities. Elected to the select vestry of the parish of Liverpool, he has obtained a valuable practical acquaintance with the working of the Poor Laws, which for good or evil so largely affect the mass of the labouring class and the payers of local taxation, while as chairman of the Industrial Schools Committee he is qualifying him- self to assist Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P., in future reforms for the benefit of the outcast children of our great cities. Nor will he be less useful in this par- ticular sphere by reason of his long and personal activity—a period of 30 years—as a teacher and pro- moter of Ragged Schools, and a member of the com- mittee of those training ships for boys, several of which vessels are moored in the Mersey. Selected by Her Matesta's Government to represent their interests in the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, Mr. Crosfield occupies a position of experi- ence which in the past has been a training sellout for a whole brigade of members cf Parliament, and retains in it ranks to-day the cream of the repre- sentation of Liverpool mercantile and shipping princes. The successful establishment of "Hospital Sandty" in Liverpool, with the great benefits accruing there- from to the mass of local hospitals and dispensaries, was largely, if not mainly, due to Mr. Crosfield, whose active and generous interest in the leading Liverpool charities pointed him out _as first treasurer of the movement. In the achievement ef Liverpool University College, with its ample and magnificent endowments, Mr. CrosSeld took a prominent part, contributing liter- ally to the general fund, besides providing (with his partners and Mr. A. H. Brown M.P.) the entire sum for the chair of history. In ;his yeoman service to the cause of education, Mr. Crosfield seems only to have been pursuing the natural inclination of his early life. Mr. Crosfield is, and has been all his life a Liberals advanced as to his views, sound as to its policy, and faithful in all respects to the leaders of the party. In the up-hill fight that for two generations the Liberals of Liverpool have had to sustain, a Crosfield has never been wanting to help with hand, and voice, and purse, the candidatures of its representatives, be it for parish vestrymen, town councillor, or members of Parliament. The Crosfield of whom we write is now the oldest member connected with the manage- ment of the Liberal Association of Liverpool, having been associated therewith for over 22 years. He has also held the post of treasurer to the Association, and has acted in that capacity at most of the Parliamen- tary contests for 12 years. As one of the ward chair- men of the " Teo," he preeided over those two suo- °armful elections of Mr. Smith in Castle-street ward, which lead to the selection of the latter as the Liberal Parliamentary candidate against M. A. B. Forwood. Until very recently, Mr. Crosfield was not put for- ward in public as a speaker for the party, and a natural shyness led him to dissuade others from pres- sing that particular form of party service upon him. But it has been noted with pleasure that during the last three years he has accepted opportunities of this nature, and his utterances have been characterized by much aptitude and an increasing ability. At a recent banquet at the Reform Club, when the Earls of Derby, Sefton, and Dalhousie were entertained, he was selected to propose the Itoast of the Rouse of Lords; and at the annual meeting of the National Liberal Federation, held in Liverpool, which was attended by the Right Hon. J. Chamberlain, M.P., he was requested to second a vote of confidence in the Government. Upon both occasions he displayed great tact and judgment in the treatment of his subject, and his speeches were warmly applauded. He was not less successful, we may add, on Wednesday ' night, in addressing the Liberal Council of War- rington, as will be seen from the full report which we give of it in another column.

MR. WILLIAM CROSFIRLD Of SUNDAY SCHOOL WORK. On Saturday afternoon last the foundation stone of a new Sunday school, in connection with the Skelmersdale Con- gregational Charcb, was laid by Mr. Wm. Crosfieici. The Rev. T. Willis (Manchester), in introducing Mr. Crosfield, said that gentleman came of a good stock, and was well known throughout Lancashire. He had recently, so he (Mr. Willis) was informed, become the Parliamentary can- didate for the borough of Warrington. (Applause, and Mr. Crosfield "No, no.") They trusted that 'when he canto to contest that borough his colours would be found flying triumphantly. (Loud applause.) They all knew that, if he became a member of Parliament, they would have in him a thoroughly good and Christian man and a Congregationalist, and ,a man ready for every good work. 1 (Applause.)—After the stone had been laid, Mr. Ccosflold remarked that Mr. Willis bad referred to the representa- tion of Warrington, and had said more about the matter than was strictly correct, and had also bestowed more honour upon him (Mr. Grosfield) than he deserved. ("No, no.") It was quite true that he had a number of friends in Warrington who were convinced that they could send him from Warrington to represent the electors of that borough in another place: but if they did not know it was well they should that anyone who appealed to an intelligent constitu- ency like Warrington, and was successful, would not be the wan selected by the few, but the man selected by the many (Hear. hear.) He had still to submit himself to the many, and until he did so he could not accept absolutely the honour Mr. Willis had given him. (Applause.) Referring to the work they were then engaged in Mr. Crosfield said at was a great work in which Sunday School teachers were engaged, and on their labours at present depended to a large extent the welfare of the Christian Church in the future. The Christian Church of the future would be very much as the children of to-day made it. They had the benefit of an admirable ,wsek-day education in the place, an education in whichCtirunian principles, though not Christian doctrines, wereinstilled. R beeline, therefore, the duty of the Christian Church and of Christian men and women to instil the doctrines of Christianity, so far as they could, into the hearts of the children. The work in which most of them were engaged was a dangerous one, and to them it was of vital importance that they should always be prepared for every contingency. The Sunday Schools th‘le would do a noble work, and he wished them every success (Appl —The proceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to 111 r. Crosfield.

SIR GILBERT GREENALL AND THE FISHiNG Al' THE WATERWORKS. am sure every working man in Warrington was pleased to hear from Sir Gilbert Greenall's speech. at a Twat meeting of working-men in the North-West Ward, that he has thought of again throwing open the fishing lathe reservoir at Walton to the public of Warrington and neigh- bourhood. Sir Gilbert is well known to be a generous thongh prudent and unostentatious benefactor to toe whole of this neighbourhood, and had half the money he has ex- pended for the good of Warrington been laid out in the same manner and trumpeted abroad as persistently and as loudly as much smaller benefits bestowed on the town by Liberals have been, there would be small chance of a Radical being returned to Parliament as member for the borough. Now there are a few Radicals in Warrington who call themselves working-men, and think themselves leaders of working-men, and who have occasionally led them into diffi- culties from which they themselves have managed to escape with more p[Ofit than some of the men whom they misled, as witness the recent struggle between the wiredrawers and their employers, to which, I think, may be added a previous strike. One of these men must be an extraordinary gram- marian, for he scarcely ever writes without finding fault with some one's grammar: so the present writer, whose educational advantages have been very few, does not expect , to escape his learned wrath Well, writing on the subject of fishing in the Walton reservoir, this person challenges ' the accuracy of Sir Gilbert's statement "that the fishing was stopped because the reservoir was completely fished out," and says "We all know very well that the reservoir is simply snewing ' with fish at the present moment." Working-men, beware of him! He is misleading you again. I happen to know that quite recently a Warrington man tried his hand at fishing in the reservoir in question, and after toiling all the day caught nothing. But, mark you, although he contradicts Sir Gilbert and says this reservoir is full of fish, and evidently thinks it wrong to prevent working-rcen from fishing therein, he does his best to pre- vent the possibility of that boon being given by maliciously holding over Sir Gilbert the threat of future proceedings in an election court for bribery should he allow the working- men of Warrington to fish in the reservoir, even though per- mission to do so is accompanied by regulations which would prove highly beneficial to that noble working-man's institu- tion—the Warrington Infirmary. Could political spite go further? Working-men of Warrington, will you be led by such men 7—Yours, dac., PAIR PLAY. Warrington, May 25th, 1834.

Sir,—The various letters which have from time to time appeared in your valuable paper have evidently struck home, and a little more information on the subject may not prove unacceptable to those interested. As an old fisherman, I have in former years occasionally bought a ticket from the Waterworks Company which enabled me to fish from any part of the lake side. In the year 1878, however, the Waterworks Company made over to Sir Gilbert the sole right of fishing in the reservoir, and immediately a now condition of things arose. The public were only allowed to fish from the road side—which forms a very small portion of the total circumference of the lake—an 4 which is, as we all know, the worst possible place to fish from. This arrange- ment alone completely put a stop to anything like a decent "catch." Before a man began to fish, he was required to enter his name in a book kept for the purpose at the keeper's house, and when he had finished to enter the number, description, and weight of the fish caught. It was in this way that Sir Gilbert became aware of the big catch of 460 fish in 16 days' fishing—which was by no means a remarka- ble feat, being less than 30 per day. But the curious fact is this—the fishing had become more and more restricted over since its present owner became possessor of it ; but the per- mission previously given to the public with such a "niggard hand" was entirely withdrawn soon after the election of 1880, because " the people of Warrington deserve no consideration at the bands of Sir Gilbert." This, and this alone, is the explanation of the case. Had the electors of our good old town been silly enough to have again returned the "odd, old fellow," as their member, they might still have enjoyed (?) their fishing in the reservoir under the restrictions already named. From 1878 to 1880 very few fish were taken out of the reservoir, and for three years past fishing has been altogether stopped. A short time ago many, if not all, of the pits on the neighbouring farms were netted, aud the fish so caught were turned into the reservoir. Fish are most prolific in the propagation of their species, so that Sir Gilbert's etaternent that he is waiting for the fish to increase acid multiply, before be can renew his permission, may be safely taken for what it is worth. It is mere nonsense, and can only deeds.° those who have no practical knowledge of the "gentle art." Sir Gilbert's angling days are over, the people will not be " gudgeoned" by tarn any longer, and if he is foolish enough to allow himself to go to the poll, be will receive such a " chousing " at the next election as will put the thrashing he got in 1830 completely into the shade.—Yours 4c., PISCATOIL

am pleased hi MO that tha way id which you he exposed the mean and shabby conduct of Sir Gilbert in reference to this matter has put him on his defence. I for , one refuse to accept Sir Gilbert's explanation of the matter, and have no hesitation in saving that It is an idle excuse. I fished at the Waterworks years before Sir Gilbert acquired the monopoly and am sure that all the other fishermen in the town will bear me out in saying that the great drawbar* to the place has always been that it has been overstocked with fish and is to-day. The fact of their being so many small fish is proof of this. Sir Gilbert's excuse why he would not allow people to fish was that it disturbed his game. I know several gentlemen in the town, who scarcely believing that Sir Gilbert would refuse them have written simply for tke purpose of knowing whether he would or not, and in each instance he flatly refused to allow them to fish. One of his own tenants told me that Sir Gil- bert had netted every pit and pond upon his own and his tenants' ground and turned the fish into the reservoir to prevent his tenants giving permission to fish and ao that his game would not be disturbed. Further than this, he informed me that Sir Gilbert has had the Waterworks netted several time and has sent the fish to his servants' table. I sum Sir Gilbert's explanation up as an evasion of the truth, and I flatly contradict him in his statement that the Water- works is short of fish. As an old fisherman, I perhaps know as much aboot fish and fishing as he does, and I state that 20 men fishing continually for a year with rod and line would not be able to take all the fish out of the reser- voir, and that at the end of that time the fah would b 3 in a better condition and the place plentifully stocked. Let Sir Gilbert stop h i is netting and try the experiment for 12 i months. I think t s a crying shame that one man should have it in hie power Is deprive the working-saen of War- rington of an enjoymrmt which properly belorm to them. What right has Sir Gilbert to the fishing? The Water- works were made for the inhabitants of Warringten. Does Sir Gilbert alone maintain the Waterworks Company I" It might be so judging from the way the Company treat the rest of their customers.—Your obedient servant, "IZAAK WALTN." THE VIC&

R V. THE SCHOOLMASTER OF STOCKTON HEATH. Sir,-1 have taken the trouble to inquire into this dispute. The facts are simply these :—Mr. Timson endeavoured to get up a free entertainment in connection with the Public Reading-room, and had engaged several friends to give mange on a certaia Saturday night. He mentioned it to the Vicar the night previous, expecting that he would be pleased with the news. However, the Vicar was not in a happy frame of mind and put his clerical heel upon it, Mr. Timson, naturally as everybody else would do after making all the arrary,ements, replied that "as schoolmaster he thought he could do what he liked in his own school," hilt when he saw the tantrum into which the Vicar worked himself he quickly withdrew the remark and apologised to him. The entertain- ment was not held, and Mr. Timson sent a written apology to the Vicar for his terrible misconduct. The mighty man of the parish would not relax, but instantly called a meet- ing of his managers, and on the following day he sat in solemn conclave over them, at which they dismissed Mr. Timson. After they had decided to do this they called Mr. Timson into the room and asked him what he had to say about it.

I believe these are the true facts of the case; and it ap- pears to me, as it must appear to every right-thinking per- son, that the vicar has exhibited .1 vicious and arbitrary spirit in the matter. The mission of a minister, I was taught at school to believe, was to spread peace and en- courage good will among his flock, but it is evident from the dissensions just now going on in different parts of the country that some of them have forgotten, if they ever knew, the simplest principles of religion. I observe that Mr. Robert Davies has taken up cudgels on the part of the par- son. I always thought that he, good man, would have been the last to have encouraged turmoil. I am, afraid now it is too late to bring about a reconciliation, but I think the parishioners should rightly understand a matter in which they are so deeply intrested. I quite agree with your sug- gestion that the parishioners ought to shaw their feeling in the matter by immediately calling for a School Board, and appointing Mr. TiCO5Ol2 as head master. I believe the meeting at which the managers decided to dismiss Mr. Timson NM held at Greenall's brewery, one of the managers of the school being a member of that firm; at all events it is certain that several meetings have been held there. It occurs to me that this is a strange place to transact church business in, but beer and the bible are all as one rani-a-days. I wonder whether Mr. Robert Davies' went to the meeting at the brewery, and whether the courage of the meeting to dismiss poor Mr. Timson was screwed up on "mild" or " bitter "—I should think the latter.—Yours I obediently, AN OUTSIDER.

TUB WARRINGTON MERSEY AMATEUR ROWING CLUB. —The headquarters are held at Mr. Capner's boating sta- tion, Wilderspool-road, where the committee meet every Monday evening at eight o'clock for the purpose of enrol- ling members. The subscriptions for rowing members is 10s. The club is now fairly under way, and has every prospect of a successful season. ALLEGED WILFUL MURDER.—About a fortnight ago, du- ring a quarrel, a man named Richard Saxon, who lived in Copestick-4treet, Ancoats, was struck upon the head by his son with a hammer. At the time flee wound was regarded as slight, but the injured man died on Tuesday morning last, the cause of death being, according to the medical evidence, pressure; on the brain and extrayasation of blood from external injury. A coroner's jury returned a ve:dict against the son (who is undergoing two months' imprison- ment for the assault) of wilful murder, upon which charge he will ultimately be tried.

CANON DODD AND THE STRETION SCHOOLMASTER. Since our last issue, we have received the following letter on this mater from Canon Dodd :—"Sir,—My attention has been drawn to a paragraph in your paper of the 24th inst headed 'Another Church and i3chool Dispute near Warrington.' May I request you to insert this letter in as prominent a position as you thought fit to assign to the paragraph, giving an unqualified denial to every statement contained in it, except one : • Within ' the last few weeks a letter determining his engagement has been sent to the schoolmaster.' That statement is correct. All the rest are false. There has been no dispute with any- body either about the church, or the schools, or the organ. There is no outbreak in the pari.li' or the least prospect of any. There are no managers • who corns as shadows and so depart.' No feeling of the parishioners has been re-resen- ted to me by anyone. You are kind enough to sayl have ! shown a conciliatory spirit. I hope I should always be ready to do this if occasion required. But I cannot accept the compliment, as I have not had the opportunity of show. log any spirit, conciliatory or otherwise. Lastly, the suc- cess or failure of Mr. Ellison as organist has nothing what- ever to do with his position as schoolmaster. The two offices are entirely distinct, and it is only within the last year or two they have been held by the same person. I have the authority of the schoolmaster to state that he has had nothing whatever to do with the paragraph in ques- tion, which indeed might prove of considerable injury to him, and that he is much annoyed at the statements con- tained in it, which are incorrect from beginning to end.—l am, yoars obediently, HENRY R. DODD." The Canon hae "gone oft" briskly, but some of his shots vire a little wide of the mark. Be begins by admitting that the statement in the paragraph in question upon which all the others in a was depend is not "false," whilst he con- chides by characterising the paragraph as incorrect from "beginning to and." In stating that representation of the feeling in his parish had been made to him, it was not meant that it had been made in the shape of a petition with more than five hundred names attached such as was pre- sented to his neighbour at Stockton Heath. But that re- presentttion in favour of the retention of Mr. Ellison has been made to him, though perhaps not formally in the name of the parishioners, we venture to re-affirm. Again, it was not stated that the two offices of schoolmaster and or- ganist had not been distinct. What was said was that the two offices are at present held by the same person. Nor was it suggested that the schoolmaster had anything to do with the information which reached us; we willingly corroborate the Canon's statement as to that. With regard to the man- agement of the school, if he means that up to last week there have been "no managers," he will perhaps tell us hew he has got the requisite signatures for securing the Go- vernment grant ? In suggesting that his managers came and went like shadows, we had an eye to the fact commen- ted on at the last vestry meeting that so far as the parishioners were concerned the managers were "an tinknown quantity." But all this is changed so we are informed. The reforming spirit which is abroad has visited Stretton, and, wonderful to say, since our last publication. Indeed, if we are not utterly misled, and the Canon will correct us if we are, there was a meeting no later than Thursday last, called by the Canon himself, at which amongst the select few present were Mr. Brockle- burst, Mr. Darbyshire, Mr. Whitley, and Churchwradens De Prez and Kerr. We are given to understand that the repre- sentatives of the parishioners, who know something of the feeling in the parish as to the notice of dismissal to the schoolmaster, were unanimous in desiring that he should be retained, and we are pleased to be able to add that an un- derstanding was come to that the objectionable notice should be withdrawn. Nay more, Mr. Ellison has to have a "lady help " in the school in addition to Mrs. Ellison. The "pet warden " seems to have been too much aghast at all this to be drawn even with the powerful eye-glass ; and so the thing was done. It forms a pretty postscript to the Canon's letter, and we must pay him the compliment of being conciliatory. We take no credit, of course, to our- selves, though it has happened that within a week of our calling attention to "the state of things "—we will not say " dispute "—the schoolmaster is reinstated, and a body of responsible managers is appointed. Truly, all is well that ends well. Let us hope that the good example will be con- tagious, and that the vicar of Stockton Heath will have the good sense to follow suit.

PENKETH. WritSLETAN SUNDAY SCHOOL SH6MONS, PSNIRTH,-011 Sunday, the anniversary sermons in connection with the above schools were preached, morning and evening, at the Wesleyan Chapel, Penketb, by the Rev. .1. A. Beet, of Wrexham (formerly of Warrington.) In the afternoon Mr. Beet delivered an address to the scholars, p.trents, and friends, which was listened to with pleasure. The sermons were highly commended, and the congregations were large. Suitable hymns were sung by the children, under the leadership of Mr. James Watson. Collections were made after each service, which reached the handsome sum of over £2l.

Dawns ov Ma. Witwat Jon.ll,7wlt is with regreE that we record the death of Mr. Jones, which took plaoe at his residence at renketh, where he had resided for the last 22 years, on Saturday morning. Mr. Jones, who was 84 years of age, had been confined to his house for over twelve months previous to his decease, which is attributed entirely to old age. His remains were interred in the Warrington Cemetery on Tuesday, the funeral arrangements being en- trusted to Messrs. Garnett and Sons. Mr. Jones was a na- tive of Shropshire, being born at Dawley Green in 1800. He comnlenced work in the collieries there at the early age of nine, but eventually apprenticed himself as a smith at the florseneys Ironworks, Salop. He first came to Warring- ton in 1822, and immediately found employment under the late Mr. William Wnitley, at the Bridge Foundry, Mersey- street, on the site of which Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Co.'s chemical works no stand. While with this firm Mr. Jones superintended the building of a number of boats for the Old Quay Canal Co., and also the building of "The War- rington,' the largest steamer which had been seen at War- rington at that time. The launching of this boat caused a great sensation in the town, considerable difficulty Ling experienced in getting her to leave the stays. Shortly after this, in 1840, Mr. Jones commenced business with Mr. John Rylands es partner, at the present works, Bewsey Mill Foundry, as boiler makers, it. Mr. Rylands withdrawing from the business in the course of a few years. Mr. Jones was the inventor at several improvements in boilers, en- gines, and soap makers' plant; the most important being thence of vertical tubes in horizontal steam boilers, which are now so general, the first boiler of this description being mode for Mr. Thomas Eskrigge, the Hope Mills, Dallarn- lane. The deceased gentleman was a Liberal in politics, and in that interest served as a Councillor for the North- West Ward from 1853 to 1858, when he retired In him the Wesleyane have lost an old friend, he having been identified with, that denomination ter over 60 years.

'ft[Err or TOOLS.—On Monday, at the Lymm Police Court, before Mr. T. P. Norris, David White, alias Archie Smith, and James Chantler, alias Weston, were charged with stealing a monkey-wrench, value 43 6d, and a screwdriver, value is 6d, the property of Thou3as Dalton, plumber, of Lymm.—lt appears that the prisoners, who are painters by trade, were passing through Lymm, and represented them. selves as "on the -oad " to the prosecutor, who supplied them with a dinner each. On leaving his house they had to pass through the shop, and in doing so stele the articles named.—Sergeant Harrington applied for a remand, in order that he might make inquiries, as he had reasonable sus- picions that one, if not both, of the men was " wanted " in various parts of the country for more or less serious offences. —They were remanded.—Yesterday morning the prisoners were again brought up before Mr. Ling, and were committed for trial at the next Quarter Sessions at Knutsford.

div.head: WILLOW BEETLE.
div.p: THE WILLOW BEETLE.

On Monday evening a meeting of gentlemen concerned in the willow growing industry in Lymm and the neigh- bourhood was h-ld at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, to receive reports on the attempts made to exterminate the willow beetle, and to consider the best method of getting rid of the pest, which has caused considerable damage to the crops. The chair was occupied by Mr. H. Cameron, and there were also present Meesrs. Wm. Blinstone, Joseph Marsh, Thos. Davis, George Leigh, J. Mort, Wibley, George Warbuton, and T. Hutchinsou.—Tbe Chairman said that since they met the last time observation had been taken as to how far the measures so far adopted to exterminate the willow beetle bad taken elect. He had not had much experience on the subject himself until he had ocuasion to plant three acres of willows the past winter, and be only found a few beetles here and there. His willows were a distance of about a mile and a half from the rest Of the plants, and how the beetles had got there he could not imagine. He was afraid they would spread over all the willows in the district. He went to Mr. Hutchinson's willows a few days ago to procure specimens to send to London, as an eminent naturalist in Manchester had asked him for some specimens of the beetle ea send to Miss Ormrod, also an eminent naturalist, who held the appointment of naturalist to the Royal Agricultural So- ciety. This gentleman had received a reply from Miss Ormrod to the effect that she was going from home, but in a few days she would write and give what information she coald for the use of the people of Lymm for getting rid of the pest, and he (the chairman) hoped that at their meeting some information would be forthcoming. Their businees that evening vess to receive the repeats of the several gentlemen I suffering from the beetle nuisance, and he hoped their re- ports would be encouraging so far as the destruction of the beetles were concerned, and that each gentleman had been doing his best in his own particular ground to destroy the pests.—Mr. Hutchinson said that since the previous meeting he had sent circulars Is the willow growers to stimulate them in destroying the pest; he thought that the circulars had had some effect. He found that there was not suffi- cient hands to be got in Lymm to undertake the work, so he had get labour from Warrington, and thought that they were now getting the mastery of the beetles. Where proper exertions had bees made they had had considerable success, and he was confident that lithe means recommended at the last meeting were continued day by day by each grower, the beetles would be soon nearly. if not quite, exterminated. What appeared to be the best method was shaking the beetles off the plants into the vessel containing the paraffin oil.—A discussion then took place as to the best method of applying the remedy, and Mr. Leigh said that instead of having men to go round each row of willows With the ves- sel of paraffin he mede a vessel similar to a dish cover, with a handle about three feet in length, so that it could be dragged along the ground in a straight line. This was , filled with paraffin, and as one man dragged it along the ground, another man followed blind and pressed the two rows together in such a Manner that t:e'!'y hung over the ves- sel. The beetles, being easily dislodged, dropped into the paraffin. He had tried allibore powder, but was not of much permanent benefit.—Mr. Hutchinson uri;ecd that all !t efforts must be made to destroy the beetles before 1,..1°Y d!3,- posited their progeny, and advocated stripping yonig lows of their leaves and thus taking the beetles away at the same time.—lt was then resolved, on the motion of Mr. Davies, seconded by Mr. Warburton, "That the secretary be instructed to write to those whom hi may conaidet to have been remiss as to attending to the extermination of the beetles on their respective holdings, and to urge upon them the importance of their strict and immediate attention to them with a view of their eitermination."—The meeting , concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

WE UNnentraten that owing to the increase in the num- ber of pupils, the governors of the Warrington Grammar School to enlarge the school. WE have received a copy of Dr. GornaWs annual report of the health and sanitary condition of the borough, but in the crowded state of our columns we are compelled to hold It over until our next issue. Sr. BAR as, Lovirae-Lawn.—lt is stated that the Rev, S. Allton, vicar of Coniston. Leeds, has been appointed by the patron, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar of St. Paul'e, to the incumbency of this new church. THE WARRIart IRO/WORKERS' Amateur Athletic Sports will take place to-day (Saturday) in a field adjoin- ing St. Jemes's Church. An excellent programme has been arranged, and it may be fairly expected that there will be many hotly contested events. The proceeds will he given in aid et the Infirmary. REDUCTI"ON OF WAGIIS ON Tan blow TRADIL--Th• wages of the men employed by the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company have been reduced 2i per cent., and the men, we understand, commenced work on that reduction on the 19th inst.. The reduction was the result of the award of Mr. Avery, of Birmingham, for the Arbitration Board of South Staffordshire some three or four weeks ago. The Warrington iron workers have for some time accepted the decisions of that Board, and in the present instance have followed their usual rule and been guided by it. There are about two thousand men employed at the works in question. SALVATION ARMY—At the afternoon meeting of the Salvation Army at Warrington on Sunday, it was announced that one of the members was about to take his farewell, prior to leaving for one of the Army's Training Mmes. The "captain "delivered an addreos, in the course of which she referred to the work carried on in the Homes, and to the alter lebours that followed it. The only difference, she said, between their "soldiers" and the soldiers of the Queen was that they (the Salvation Army) had got the great command- ing chief with them every day. She also announced that two of the members had, brought their infant child to the meeting to dedicate its life to the furtherance of the Army's objects. She prayed fervently that the child might be traiced up a true Christian and a faithful soldier. Daring the address she held the infant in her arms, and the 'pleura of the Army were held over it. COncauT AT BANE QtAT.—Another attractive concert was held at the Beak Quay Working Men's Mission School- room. on Saturday evening, when there was a moderate attendance. A programme, consisting principally of songs, was very well rendered, the various contributors being ac- corded well merited applause. A comic sketch, entitled "Ma', to be done," was productive of considerable merri- ment; and the comic songs given by Mr, Nash also caused mach fen and laughter. Mr. Cook was applauded for his song "Down in the deep," hat did not grant his audience a repetition. The ever popular song " khren en the Rhine " received full jnstice from Miss Booth, who was recalled. Miss Sykes made a good accompanist. The usual votes of thanks were given at the close. The following was the com- plete programme :—Pianoforte duet, Mimeo Sykes; song, " Out in etre streets," Miss Lockaley song, "The farmer's boy," Mr. Wm. Ford; song, "Sweet Ebren en the Rhine," Mies Booth (encore); song (comic), " ITp to Dick," Nash (encore) ; song, 'Pattering footsteps,"Mies J. monks pianoforte solo, Mies Lucy, Ashley;. song, "Only a sweet little letter," Miss Smith (Kidsgroye); song, "Down in the deep," Mr. Cook ; comic sketch, " What's to be done," Mr. Chrimes, Mr. Nash, bflr. Jones, and Mr. Baker ; pianoforte solo, Miss Sykes, sent.; song, " Strangers yet," MIS 9 Mills; song, "Show them how, to do it," Mr. Nash (encore); pianoforte duet, Misses Sykes, A CEL/7.0 DROWNED IS THE CANAL—On Tuesday Mr. Husbandedeputy coroner, held an. inquily at the Dog and Partridge Inn, Poulton, sear Warrington, into the circums- tances attending the death of a boy named Ben Jackson, six Years of age, the son of George Jackson, a glassblower, who. resides at Poulton. The deceased was found in the &mat near Wcolston on Saturday last. On the Friday previoea he left his home to plav with some other boys, and about five o'clock in the evening he was seen near the cinal by a woman named Mary Bibby, who lives in the neighbour- hood. He was then playing. As he did not return time at the time that he was expected information WAS given to the po:ice and a search was immediately instituted, with the result that his body was found in the canal by John Telt, a groom, of Poulton, who, with the assistance of P.C. Mae- (arises, got the body out of the water. It was at once re- moved to the hoe-se of the pirents of the deceassd.—The father of the deceased said that on Friday, the 23rd inst., he sate hi boy in front of the house, which was 140. yards dis- tant from the canal. He missed him at 5.30 Deceased had frequently wandered to Warringtcn, and inquiry was made at the police station. No information being obtained, however, a search was made through the night. The child's grandmother went next morning to a man named Toft, who lived near the caual,and got him to drag the water. The body was found about 10 o'clock in the morning.—The jury re- turned a verdict of "Accidental death."

FEENEY' AT THE PUBLIC HALL.— Last evening Mr. Patrick Feeney and his combination appeared befor a moder- ate audience at the Warrington Public Hall, and met with a flattering reception. The company appear again this (Saturday) evening, and in all probability there will be a crowded bones.

HOLY TRINITY SUNDAY Scnoms.—The anniversary in connection with Hoiy Trinity Schools were held on Sun- day last. At the morning service the sermon was preached! by the Rev. C. V. Merriman, M.A., Rector of St. Clement's, Salford. In the afternoon a scholars' service was neld, and the scholars were addressed by the the Vicar, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. Tha Rev. Canon Dodd, M.A., preached in the evening, There was a large congregation both morning and evening.

_ AN UNNasr CONSCIENCE—On Saturday last a respectable looking man, named John Roberts, was brought before Alderman Burgess, at the Warrington Police Court, on a charge of having stolen £8 and a lever watch.—lt was stated that Roberts bad come to the police office and confessed to , having stolen the watch and ZS from a patient in the Den- bigh Infirmary, whilst he was acting as attendant there. His reason for giving himself into the bands of the police was that he had never felt himself at ease since he commit- ted the theft —He was remanded till Monday, on which day he was brought before the Mayor and other magis- trates, who directed that he should be handed over to the Deabigh police. A WORTHLESS FELLOW.—At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, a charge was preferred against a man tamed Peter Ward, of Kinder's-yard, formerly a coachman, of leaving his family chargeable to the Warring- ton Union. He did not appear. The case was adjourned a month ago to give bim a chance to obtain work.--Mr. liar- bourne, relieving officer, now said that since the case was last before the magistrates he had visited the house of Ward several times, and found that there was no improvement in condition of the family. The house was filthy.—Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) said that from inquiries made he had reason to believe that the defendant had never tried to get work.—Sentence of one month's hard labour was passed.

TM! BIRTH AND DEATH RATH OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, May 24th, 1884. The mean temperature was 49 Fahrenheit, and therefore 2 degrees solder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 18 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 23rd met, and the minimum temperature 25 Fahrenheit on the 21st inst. The rainfall measured inches. The general direction of the wind was westerly. During the week, which was the 21st of the current year, 39 births and 8 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 93 per 1,000, against 159 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 207 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from measles, 1 from croup, 1 from old age, 2 from bronchitis, and 1 from heart disease. One case of smallpox was reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—Joww H. GORNALL, medical officer of health.

IMPUMINT ROBBRRY.—On Wednesday, at the Warrineton Borough Police Court, Thomas Oates and Margaret Flem- ing were charged before Alderman Chandley and Mr. John rairclough with stealing a shilling from the person of a woman named Hines, in Ituttermarketaitreet, on the previous evening,—The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that the prosecutor was the wife of Thomas Hines. The prissier Oates, VS years of age, was a native of Warrington and resided in Golden Grove-street. Fleming was a fustian cutter and had no permanent place of abode. On the pre- vious evening a man went to the house of the prosecutor for lodgings and handed Mrs. Hines a lion shilling with a hole in it. She went to buy some provisions at the shop of Mr Isaacs, who, however, refused to take the shilling in payment, advising her to get it changed at the post office or the bank. She then came out of the shop grumbling, and Oates, who was standing near at the time, said " Let me look at the shilling." She opened her hand and he snatched the shilling and handed it to the female prisoner' who ran swim—Prisoners, who pleaded not guilty and made a rambling and incoherent defence, were eacti aentenced to 14 days' hard labour. ALLSOBD PIO-KERPINS NOISANOI : CORPORATION PROSICUTION.—The Warrington Borough magistrates were engaged a considerable time on Monday morning in hearing Case in which James Caldwell, a baker, of Wakefield- street, was summoned for keeping pigs on premises near Enfield-street, that caused a nuisance injurious to health.— Mr. Whittle (deputy town clerk) prosecuted, and Mr. Jen- kins defended.—Mr. Whittle said that the pigs were not kept in near proximity to a dwelling-house, but were on a piece of waste land in close proximity to a large cutting shop, in which were employed between 70 and 80 persons. Over- looking the ground where the pigs were there were windows, and a medical gentlemen would tell them that the effluvia arising frona the place where the pigs were was of such a nature as to be injurious to health.—lnspector Norman said that on visiting the premises on the 18th inst. be found a quantity of manure and a number of pigs, the animals being in a deplorable state of filth. He considered them a serious nuisance.—Dr. Gornall, medical officer of health gave it as his opinion that the pigs wire a nuisance and in- jurious to the health of those working in the adjoining shop. Certainly not.—The' you come down upon the pigs and leave the noxious vaponre to take care of themselves F I come down upon an abominable nuisance.— Do you eat pork, doctor? Occasionally.—Would you eat any portion of these piee if they were killed? I do not think I need answer that question.—The Clerk : The pigs are not charged, it is the owners. (Laughter.)—For the de fence Mr. Jenkins caned one of the workpeople from the fustian cutting shop, who said that he had observed nothing in connection with the defend:oWe premises that could be construed into a nuisance.—Dr. Joseph was also called for the defence, and said that be saw the premises on &tardily last. He thought them very suitable premises on which to keep pigs. When he saw the pigs on Saturday he did not consider them a nuisance injurious to health.—Do you re- gard the way in which the pigetre is kept as suitable in all respects for the keeping of pigs F I do. I think it would be better if the premises were sevrered, but I do not think that a great objectioa in their present conditiose—The Mayor: Dr. Joseph says he only ears them on Saturday.— Mr. Jenkini pointed out that the information was only laid oaths 2ard inst.—Mr. Fairclough, one of the magistrateeon the Bench, said that at the request of t,..e defendant he had visited thy premises in question and did not observe any nuisance, but be thought it might be ran improvement if better drainage were provided—Mr. Weittle said that they did not ask that the defendant should give up keeping the pies, but only that no nuisance should be allowed to exist. —The B'encier adiourned the case for three weeks so that the defendant might make such improvements as would prevent the possibility of any nuisance occurring. ASSAULTS ON'THE POLICI4.—At the Warrington BoronTh Mice Court, on Monday, before the Mayor and other 'magistrates, a young man named Martin Griffith was lebarged with being drunk and disorderly in Wirovick-street, lon Saturday evening, and with assaulting P.C. Chantler at the same time and place.—The officer said that when in Winwick-street he saw the prisoner strike a young woman, and took him into custody. On the way to the police station the prisoner got hold of hie (the constable's) legs, threw him down, and got on to the top of him.—lnspector Stoinks corrouoratedeand said that he saw the prisoner throw Charmer. The prieoner was very violent.—The Bench sent prisoner to undergo two months' hard labour—At the sane court, Edward Griffin and Michael Callaghan, two youths, were charged' with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street, and Callaghan was also charged with assaulting P.C. Smith—P.C. Smith said that when he was apprehending Griffin Callaghan struck him first with his lit and then with a belt. Witness had to have the assist- ance of several constalfies, as there was a large and disor- derly crowd.—Mr. Hunt (chief constable) handed in a list of previous convictions against Callaghan.—Callagban : You can gife me seven days, if you like. (Laughter.)— The Mayor: You have already enjoyed a month; I am afrairrthat will not be sufficient. —Mr. Hunt: He has bad six months.—The Mayor (to Ca)laghan): You have the modesty to ask us to give you seven days, but we will be a little more generous with you, and, will give yoq two months, with hard labour. (Laughter.)—Griffin was fined 55 and costs, or seven days.—On Tuesday, Major Cart- wright and Councillor Monks had before them, at the Borough Court, three young women named Winifred Con- way, 27. Bank.street, Catherine O'Brien, Green's-court, and Eliza O'Brien, Greeth-court, who were charged with being drunk and disorderly the previous evening.—The O'Briens were also charged with assaulting the police.—P.C. Johnston stated that on Monday evening he saw prisoners Conway and Eliza O'Brien drank and fighting in Battersby-lane. He seised them to take them into cuseody, and Catherine O'Brien attempted to rescue her sister Eliza, striking and kicking him. Both the O'Briens assaulted him.—P.C. Whittingham deposed to going to the assistance a the last witness, and witnessing the emu:B.—Mr. Hunt said that the Bench had very seldom three such worthless characters of 'their sex to deal with as were the prisoners. Their conduct at the police station during the night iniel been most dis- ,gracefal. He then handed in a letter which had been 'received from the Station Hospital at the Barracks, reqaest- dog that some immediate steps should be taken to prevent • girls of the prisoners' character lounging ia the road at the back of the hospital and giving annoyance to the patients by the noise they made.—The Bench fined the prisoners 40s and costs each for being drunk and disorderly, and the O'Briens were committed to prison for three months with hard labour for the assault.--Al the same court, Frank Conway, brother of the girl Winifred Conway, was charged with being thank and disorderly in Bank-street, on Monday, with assaulting P.C. Bailey, and doing damage to his helmit to the amount of 7a 6d.—P.C. Bailey said that he was requested ca Montlay evening to go to the prisoner's house in Bank-street to prevent him beating his wife. When he got there the prisoner met him in the entry and struck him on the head with a chair, at the same time threatening to kill him. They afterwards had a severe struggle on the ground.--Mr. Runt: He has had six months for an mania —Major Cartwright (to prisoner): You don't feel sorry, I expect P—Prisoner : I do not see what is the use of being mrry.—He was fined 40s and costs or a month for the first offence, and was sentenced to three months hard labour' for Ike second.

Clough Mills, Oldham, containing 1,700 spindles, was totally destroyed by fire yesterday; damage £lO,OOO. Yesterday Australia made 269 in the second innings, and the Gentlemen of England had therefore 127 rune to get to win, of which they made 19 for one wicket, when stumps were drawn for the day. During the continued depression of trade other two ship- building yards on the Tees have been closed, and the num- ber of workmen at Mestirs. Raylton Dixon's yard ha been reduced from 2,500 to 200. At Halifax, yesterday, Charles Horst*ll Denham was committed for trial on charges of fraud and issuing false balance sheets whilst chairman and managing director of C. H. Denham and Co., Limited, stone merchants, Halifax. Tax AMERICAN MAILS.—The Postmaster General has ordered American mails for England and Scotland to be taken direct to Liverpool, instead of being landed at Queens- town. This arrangement has been rendered desirable owing to the great speed now attained by the mail steamers. AN EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE.—At Manchester yester- day, the Rev. Edward James Sylvester, Baptist minister, and Charles Calthorpe Milcheson, surgeon. were remanded en charges of conspiracy to defraud. Silvester has been giving health lectures in Manchester followed by consulta- tions in the Free Trade Hall, and it is alleged that the pri- soners treated persons for complaints that did not exist, charging high prices for simple medicines. Tax POSSESSION OF EXPLOSIVES.—At Bow-street, yester- day, Eugene Turnip, the Frenchman charged with unlawful possession of explosives, was again examined. On behalf of the defendant, it was urged he was under the impression that the Home Office had authorised him to bring explosives to England for use in certain experiments. Correspondence between the defendant and the Home Office having been read, the magistrate said it was necessary to show that ex- plosives and dangerous articles could not be imported with- out proper authority. The best way of making this known would be by inflicting a penalty, and be therefore fined defendant £5, and £5 costs.

div.head: EGYPTIAN EXPEDITION.
div.p: THE EGYPTIAN EXPEDITION.

_ The steam transport Dunluce left the royal arsenal, Woolwich, yesterday afternoon, with 1000 tons of war material, chiefly consisting of commissariat and miscella- neous stores, mountain guns, transport carts, dm, for Egypt. H. M. S. Wye arrived at Woolwich yesterday from Monte Video, and, after disembarking returned war stores, will proceed to Sheernes to be dry docked ; afterwards returning to Woolwich, where she will probably embark thirteea hun- dred tons war stores for Egypt. The authorities at Wool- wich are busily engaged despatshing stores to Sheerness for conveyance to Egypt by the store ship Humber.

TERRIFIC DYNAMITE EXPLOSIONS IN LONDON— GREAT DAMAGE—THREE MEN INJURED. At a quarter past nine o'clock last evening a terrific ex- plosion was heard in Whitehall, accompanied by clouds of dust and a tremendous noise as of falling masonry. The seat of the explosion was found to be in Scotland Yard where one of the buildings opposite the chief police offices was partly destroyed. The Rising Sun public-house oppo- site was greatly damaged and had all its windows smashed. Several cabs on the adjoining rank were blown over and several men injured. The police have formed a cordon to prevent access to the spot- The cause of the explosion is not yet known. The driver in charge of one of the vehicles and two or three other into were seriously injured, and were imme- diately conveyed to Charing Cross Hospital by the night watchmen of the Board of Trade offices adjacent. Two or three policemen and some firemen from the station in Scot- land Yard at once started removing the dibris, with the object of rescuing any persons that might be beneath, but no one was found. Almost immediately after the Scotland Yard explosion, another most violent one occurred in Pall Mall, near the Carlton Club. The whole of the club windows were , smashed, as were also those of other club buildings in the I neighbourhood, and at the seat of the explosion the pave- , ment was torn up for some distance. The streets in the neighbourhood are crowded with an immense concourse of people, and large bodies of police and many fire engines have arrived. As we telegraph a rumour is current that Victoria Station has been blown up. There is now no room for doubt that London has onc more been the scene of a deliberate and diabolical dynamite plot, exceeding in audacity, and it is feared so far as can at present be gleaned in the general alarm, in the damage to property and injury to human life and limb, anything that has yet been attempted by the desperadoes of the dyna- mite conspiracies. We have already stated the first intima- tion that anything sensational had occurred was conveyed by the report of a tremendous explosion, the seat of which was apparently in Whitehall. The streets in the neighbourhood of the Strand, and that Parliament-street and Trafalgar-square were at the time thronged with peOple a usual at this time of night. le the roadway were scores of vehicle, including I I a four-horse coach laden with pleasure seekers returning from the Oaks. The sound of the explosion was so palpable that it frightened the berses of cabs and carriages to such an extent that in some cases they bolted, thereby adding ! greatly to the alarm. Thousands of people were in an in- dant streaming towards Whitehall, where it was quickly discovered the explosion had actually taken place. Indeed, traces thereof were only too plainly visible In the shape of broken windows and clouds of blinding dust. The destruc- tive agent appeared to have been placed against or near a , building at the corner of Scotland Yard used by the Detec- tive Department, and this naturally bore the full brunt of the eljilosion. One corner of the building was completely wrecked. and a huge hole 25 feet high by go feet wide had been knocked into the wall, whilst such had been the tremendous force of the explosive agent that the massive Iron railings were wrenched bodily off the stone sockets and blown across the road to a distance of 85 feet, but there was not any very serious damage done, considering the quantity and quality of explosive evidently used.

St. Thomas's Church, Westfield-street, which was to have taken place last week, but had to be postponed in consequence of the sudden death of the wife of Bishole Hellmuth, late of Huron, Canada (acting on behalf of the Bishop of Liverpool), took place on Monday afternoon. In addition to Bishop lielimuth, the Rev. J. C. Plgot, vicar, and the Revs. T. S. Jagg and J. T. Canner, curates, were aloo present. In all 108 candidates were presented for confirma- tion, including 53 femalat and 30 males frees St. Thomas's. and 14 males and 14 females from St. PitulFCMisiOfl Church. After the hymn" Come gracious Spirit, heavenly Dove," the Vicar read the introductory portion, and he was followed by an address by the Bishop on the solemnity and importanae of confirmationt After the confirmation ceremony had been performed the hymn "Oh Jesus I have promised " was sung, and the Bisho,,gave another address. Ile ro' marked they had now been admitted by this solemn rite to all the privileges of the church. It was quite open for the* to come to.the Holy Communion and offer themselves to God with the earnestness and reality of which he had before spoken. He urged them to take heed and study the Bible earnestly and continuously, and not to forget to 'watch asd pray," His lordship then pronounced the benediction, sod the interesting service tame to a close. The candidates ad- journed to the school for tea, in order that they might all be present at an evening service, when the Rev. H. St Belton, of Ravenhead, addressed them further on the importance or the step they had each taken.
